questions.stem: A researcher studies protein digestion by measuring proteolytic activity across a range of pH values. One enzyme retains full activity at a pH of approximately 2.0. Which of the following enzymes is this most likely to be?

explanation.summary: Pepsin is the gastric protease that is activated by, and functions within, the acidic environment of the stomach.
explanation.whyCorrect: Pepsin is secreted as the zymogen pepsinogen and is activated by the acidic stomach environment, where it hydrolyzes peptide bonds with very broad specificity. Its activity at low pH is essential to begin digesting denatured dietary proteins.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Carboxypeptidase is a pancreatic enzyme secreted into the small intestine, where bicarbonate neutralizes the chyme; it does not function at pH 2.0.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Glutamate dehydrogenase is an intracellular nitrogen-handling enzyme of tissues such as liver and muscle, not an acid-active gastric protease.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Alanine transaminase acts within bodily tissues at near-neutral pH and does not operate in the acidic stomach.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Trypsin is a pancreatic protease that works in the small intestine after bicarbonate neutralizes the acidic chyme, not at pH 2.0.

questions.topicName: Amino Acid Metabolism I: Nitrogen Balance and Urea Cycle

questions.stem: During catabolism of an amino acid, the nitrogen is removed from the carbon skeleton and can be redirected into biosynthesis. Which of the following molecules can be synthesized using this liberated nitrogen?

explanation.summary: Nitrogen freed from amino acids is used to build nitrogen-containing biomolecules such as the purine and pyrimidine bases.
explanation.whyCorrect: One of the three defined fates of amino acid components is the biosynthesis of nitrogen-containing compounds, including nitrogenous bases for DNA and RNA. Adenine is a nitrogen-rich purine base whose synthesis requires nitrogen donors.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Alpha-ketoglutarate is the carbon skeleton left behind after nitrogen is removed from glutamate; the molecule itself contains no nitrogen.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Glucose can be made from the carbon skeleton of certain amino acids, but glucose contains no nitrogen and is not built from the liberated amino group.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Carbon dioxide arises from oxidative catabolism of the carbon backbone, not from the amino-group nitrogen.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Fumarate is a carbon-based TCA cycle intermediate that lacks nitrogen and does not incorporate the liberated amino group.

questions.topicName: Amino Acid Metabolism I: Nitrogen Balance and Urea Cycle

questions.stem: A 2-day-old male becomes progressively lethargic after feeding and begins to breathe rapidly. Within an hour he is nearly comatose, responding only to painful stimuli. Laboratory studies show marked hyperammonemia, and a urea cycle disorder is suspected. Which amino acid is most likely to be elevated in this patient before treatment?

explanation.summary: When ammonia is in excess, glutamine synthetase drives accumulation of glutamine, the osmotically active nitrogen carrier.
explanation.whyCorrect: Elevated ammonia stimulates glutamine synthetase, which consumes glutamate to package nitrogen into glutamine. Because glutamine is the predominant nitrogen transporter and accumulates when the liver cannot dispose of ammonia, it rises in hyperammonemic states.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Glutamate is typically depleted, not elevated, because it is rapidly consumed by glutamine synthetase as ammonia rises.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Glycine is not a primary participant in the ammonia-buffering shuttle and would not be expected to rise from hyperammonemia.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Histidine can be deaminated as a source of ammonia but is not the amino acid that accumulates in response to excess ammonia.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Asparagine can undergo deamination but does not accumulate as a nitrogen buffer during hyperammonemia.

questions.topicName: Amino Acid Metabolism I: Nitrogen Balance and Urea Cycle

questions.stem: A biochemist characterizes an enzyme that transfers the amino group of one amino acid onto an alpha-keto acid, effectively placing nitrogen on a new carbon skeleton without releasing free ammonia. This class of enzyme requires which of the following cofactors?

explanation.summary: Transaminases (aminotransferases) require pyridoxal phosphate, a vitamin B6 derivative, to swap amino and carbonyl groups.
explanation.whyCorrect: Nearly all aminotransferases use PLP, a vitamin B6 derivative, to move the amino group of an amino acid onto an alpha-keto acid. This allows nitrogen to flow safely between carbon carriers without being released as toxic ammonia.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Biotin is the cofactor for carboxylase reactions, not for amino-group transfer.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Thiamine pyrophosphate serves dehydrogenase and transketolase reactions, not transamination.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Cobalamin (B12) is used by methylmalonyl-CoA mutase and methionine synthase, not by transaminases.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Tetrahydrofolate carries one-carbon units and is not required for transamination.

questions.topicName: Amino Acid Metabolism I: Nitrogen Balance and Urea Cycle

questions.stem: In peripheral tissues, a carbon skeleton that has already accepted one nitrogen as glutamate accepts a second nitrogen in an ATP-dependent, irreversible reaction to form the nitrogen-rich blood carrier. Which enzyme catalyzes this step?

explanation.summary: Glutamine synthetase irreversibly adds a second ammonia onto glutamate, using ATP, to form glutamine.
explanation.whyCorrect: Glutamate can accept another nitrogen through the action of glutamine synthetase, producing the nitrogen-rich carrier glutamine. The reaction consumes ATP and is irreversible, so a separate enzyme is required to reverse it in the liver.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Glutaminase performs the opposite reaction, hydrolyzing glutamine back to glutamate and ammonia.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Glutamate dehydrogenase forms glutamate from alpha-ketoglutarate and ammonia; it does not make glutamine.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Aspartate transaminase swaps amino and keto groups between amino acids and does not incorporate free ammonia into glutamine.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I incorporates ammonia into carbamoyl phosphate for the urea cycle, not onto glutamate to form glutamine.

questions.topicName: Amino Acid Metabolism I: Nitrogen Balance and Urea Cycle

questions.stem: A patient develops metabolic acidosis, and the kidney responds by generating ammonia to buffer the urine. This process begins with an enzyme that hydrolyzes glutamine to glutamate while releasing an ammonium ion. Which enzyme catalyzes this reaction?

explanation.summary: Glutaminase uses water to cleave ammonia from glutamine, supplying ammonia the kidney uses to resolve acidosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Glutaminase hydrolyzes glutamine to glutamate and an ammonium ion. In the kidney it acts as an ammonia depot, using its ready supply of glutamine to liberate ammonia that buffers the urine and helps rapidly resolve metabolic acidosis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Glutamine synthetase makes glutamine by adding ammonia to glutamate, the reverse of what is needed here.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Glutamate dehydrogenase acts on glutamate (not glutamine) to release the second ammonia; the first ammonia comes from glutaminase.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Alanine transaminase swaps functional groups without releasing free ammonia from glutamine.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Pepsin is a gastric protease and has no role in renal ammonia generation.

questions.topicName: Amino Acid Metabolism I: Nitrogen Balance and Urea Cycle

questions.stem: A physiology lecture emphasizes how the body moves nitrogen safely between tissues to avoid releasing toxic ammonia. Which molecule serves as the predominant nitrogen transporter in the blood?

explanation.summary: Glutamine, which carries two nitrogens per molecule, is the predominant nitrogen transporter in the blood.
explanation.whyCorrect: Because glutamine holds two nitrogens per amino acid, it is nitrogen-rich and serves as the predominant ammonia transporter in the blood, shuttling nitrogen from peripheral tissues to the liver for urea production.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Alanine can carry nitrogen, but with only one amino group it is not the predominant blood carrier described here.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Glutamate is the substrate that is loaded and unloaded within cells rather than the main circulating nitrogen carrier.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Urea is the excretory waste form of nitrogen produced in the liver, not the amino acid transporter that delivers nitrogen to it.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Aspartate donates a nitrogen within the urea cycle but is not the predominant nitrogen carrier in the blood.

questions.topicName: Amino Acid Metabolism I: Nitrogen Balance and Urea Cycle

questions.stem: A 56-year-old man with a history of liver cirrhosis is brought to the emergency department by his daughter because he is confused and sleepy. He is disoriented to time, and when his wrists are extended his hands make a jerky, flapping movement. Which of the following laboratory tests will be most helpful in establishing the diagnosis?

explanation.summary: In suspected hepatic encephalopathy, a serum ammonia level confirms hyperammonemia from impaired hepatic urea production.
explanation.whyCorrect: The flapping tremor (asterixis), confusion, and lethargy in a cirrhotic patient point to hepatic encephalopathy. A greatly elevated serum ammonia reflects the failing liver's reduced ability to convert ammonia to urea and supports the diagnosis.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Serum glucose does not identify the ammonia-driven mechanism responsible for this presentation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Serum lipase is used to evaluate pancreatitis, not hepatic encephalopathy.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Serum creatinine assesses renal function and does not confirm hyperammonemic encephalopathy.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Serum albumin reflects hepatic synthetic capacity but does not directly demonstrate the elevated ammonia causing his symptoms.

questions.topicName: Amino Acid Metabolism I: Nitrogen Balance and Urea Cycle

questions.stem: A patient with severe hyperammonemia develops cerebral edema and rising intracranial pressure. Which of the following best explains the mechanism of the astrocyte swelling in this setting?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Accumulation of glutamine as an osmolyte draws water into astrocytes

choices.label: B
choices.text: Ammonia binds directly to neuronal membranes, rupturing them

choices.label: C
choices.text: Hyperglycemia increases plasma osmolarity and dehydrates neurons

choices.label: D
choices.text: Iron deposition within astrocytes triggers oxidative lysis

choices.label: E
choices.text: Lactate crossing the blood-brain barrier directly lyses astrocytes

explanation.summary: Excess ammonia drives glutamine synthesis, and glutamine acts as an osmolyte that pulls water into astrocytes.
explanation.whyCorrect: As ammonia rises, glutamine synthetase produces ever-increasing amounts of glutamine. Glutamine is an active osmolyte, so its accumulation promotes water influx and osmotic swelling of astrocytes, leading to cerebral edema and increased intracranial pressure.

whyWrongByChoice.B: The injury results from osmotic swelling, not from ammonia directly rupturing neuronal membranes.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hyperglycemia is not the described mechanism and would tend to draw water out of cells, not cause swelling.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Iron deposition is not part of the ammonia neurotoxicity mechanism taught here.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Although hyperammonemia can be associated with lactic acidosis, lactate is not the cause of the astrocyte osmotic swelling.

questions.topicName: Amino Acid Metabolism I: Nitrogen Balance and Urea Cycle

questions.stem: In peripheral tissues, free ammonia is captured by adding it to a TCA cycle intermediate to form glutamate, and the same enzyme reverses the reaction in the liver to liberate ammonia for urea synthesis. Which enzyme catalyzes this reversible reaction?

explanation.summary: Glutamate dehydrogenase reversibly incorporates ammonia into alpha-ketoglutarate to form glutamate, using NAD(P).
explanation.whyCorrect: Glutamate dehydrogenase reversibly joins free ammonia to the TCA intermediate alpha-ketoglutarate to make glutamate, using NAD(P)+/NAD(P)H. It loads nitrogen in peripheral tissues and runs in reverse in the liver to release ammonia for urea production.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Glutamine synthetase adds ammonia onto glutamate to form glutamine using ATP; it does not act on alpha-ketoglutarate.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Glutaminase removes ammonia from glutamine, not from alpha-ketoglutarate.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Pepsin is a gastric protease with no role in ammonia incorporation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Carboxypeptidase is a pancreatic protease and does not handle nitrogen incorporation.

questions.topicName: Amino Acid Metabolism I: Nitrogen Balance and Urea Cycle

questions.stem: A digestive enzyme is secreted in an inactive form and only functions after bicarbonate neutralizes the acidic chyme entering the small intestine. Which of the following enzymes best fits this description?

explanation.summary: Trypsin is a pancreatic protease secreted into the small intestine, where bicarbonate neutralizes the acidic chyme.
explanation.whyCorrect: Trypsin, along with chymotrypsin and carboxypeptidase, is a pancreatic enzyme secreted into the small intestine together with bicarbonate that neutralizes the acidic chyme. These enzymes collectively cleave peptides from a variety of proteins.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Pepsin works in the acidic stomach and does not depend on bicarbonate neutralization.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Glutaminase is an intracellular nitrogen-handling enzyme, not a secreted digestive protease.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Glutamate dehydrogenase is an intracellular enzyme of nitrogen metabolism, not a luminal digestive enzyme.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Aminopeptidases are produced by brush border cells rather than secreted by the pancreas with bicarbonate.

questions.topicName: Amino Acid Metabolism I: Nitrogen Balance and Urea Cycle

questions.stem: A patient with hyperammonemia is hyperventilating despite normal oxygenation and no metabolic acidosis. An arterial blood gas shows a low pCO2 and an elevated pH. Which of the following best explains this acid-base disturbance?

explanation.summary: Ammonia compromises the brainstem respiratory centers, driving hyperventilation that produces respiratory alkalosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Ammonia toxicity compromises the brainstem respiratory centers and causes hyperventilation in the absence of hypoxia or metabolic acidosis. Excessive exhalation of CO2 lowers arterial pCO2, raising blood pH and producing respiratory alkalosis.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Metabolic acidosis would lower the pH, whereas this patient has an elevated pH.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Respiratory acidosis is caused by hypoventilation with a high pCO2, the opposite of the low pCO2 seen here.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Metabolic alkalosis from vomiting is not the ammonia-driven respiratory mechanism described, and the low pCO2 reflects a respiratory process.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The abnormal low pCO2 and elevated pH indicate a true acid-base disturbance, not a normal state.

questions.topicName: Amino Acid Metabolism I: Nitrogen Balance and Urea Cycle

questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman takes a high-dose proton pump inhibitor that sharply reduces gastric acid secretion. Her physician explains that acid in the stomach performs a specific structural task on dietary protein before any protease can act. Which of the following is that task?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Denaturing the 3-D structure so peptide bonds are accessible

choices.label: C
choices.text: Hydrolyzing terminal residues into single amino acids

choices.label: D
choices.text: Neutralizing chyme so pancreatic enzymes can function

choices.label: E
choices.text: Transporting amino acids across the intestinal epithelium

explanation.summary: Gastric acid denatures dietary protein so that its peptide bonds become accessible to digestive proteases.
explanation.whyCorrect: For amino acids to be extracted from dietary proteins, the 3-D structure must first be denatured and then the peptide bonds hydrolyzed. Denaturation occurs within the acidic environment of the stomach, which ensures that the peptide bonds are exposed to the proteases that follow.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Gastric acid activates pepsinogen to pepsin in the stomach; trypsin is a pancreatic enzyme that acts in the small intestine after bicarbonate neutralization.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hydrolysis into single amino acids is completed by brush border aminopeptidases in the small intestine, not by stomach acid.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Neutralization of acidic chyme is performed by pancreatic bicarbonate in the small intestine, the opposite of what gastric acid does.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Amino acid absorption occurs through active transport in the intestinal epithelium and is unrelated to gastric acid.

questions.topicName: Amino Acid Metabolism I: Nitrogen Balance and Urea Cycle

questions.stem: A researcher isolates a protease from the luminal surface of intestinal epithelial cells rather than from pancreatic secretions. The enzyme trims small peptides down to single amino acids or very short peptides just before absorption. Which of the following enzymes has been isolated?

explanation.summary: Aminopeptidases are produced by brush border cells and complete protein digestion into single amino acids or small peptides.
explanation.whyCorrect: The third area of protein digestion is the brush border of the intestinal epithelium. Aminopeptidases are produced by brush border cells to complete digestion into single amino acids or small peptides, which are then absorbed via active transport.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Pepsin is a gastric protease produced from pepsinogen in the stomach, not a brush border enzyme.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Chymotrypsin is a pancreatic enzyme secreted into the small intestine with bicarbonate, not produced by epithelial cells.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Carboxypeptidase is one of the three pancreatic proteases secreted into the intestinal lumen, not a brush border product.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Trypsin is a pancreatic enzyme that cleaves peptides in the intestinal lumen rather than an epithelial brush border enzyme.

questions.topicName: Amino Acid Metabolism I: Nitrogen Balance and Urea Cycle

questions.stem: After a protein-rich meal, single amino acids are absorbed across the intestinal epithelium. Which of the following best describes the route these amino acids take immediately after absorption and the primary tissue that first receives them?

explanation.summary: Absorbed amino acids enter the portal circulation and travel to the liver, which allocates them to protein synthesis, energy production, or other biomolecules.
explanation.whyCorrect: Liberated amino acids are absorbed through the intestinal epithelium via active transport mechanisms. They then enter the portal circulation and are transported to the liver, where they are used for protein synthesis, energy production, or conversion to other biomolecules depending on bodily demand.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Amino acids do not enter lymphatic vessels for delivery to muscle; they enter the portal blood destined for the liver.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The kidney expresses amino acid transporters for reabsorption, but it is not the first tissue to receive newly absorbed dietary amino acids.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The pulmonary circulation is not the route by which absorbed amino acids are first distributed.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The pancreatic duct carries secretions into the intestine; it does not carry absorbed nutrients to the pancreas.

questions.topicName: Amino Acid Metabolism I: Nitrogen Balance and Urea Cycle

questions.stem: A pharmacology student notes that the same family of amino acid transporters expressed in the intestinal epithelium is also expressed in another organ, where it serves a distinct physiologic purpose. Which of the following correctly pairs that second organ with its transporter function?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Liver; secretion of amino acids into bile

choices.label: B
choices.text: Skeletal muscle; excretion of amino acids into sweat

choices.label: C
choices.text: Kidney; reabsorption of amino acids from filtrate

choices.label: D
choices.text: Pancreas; release of amino acids into the duct

choices.label: E
choices.text: Brain; export of amino acids into the blood

explanation.summary: Amino acid transporters in the intestine promote absorption, while the same transporters in the kidney promote reabsorption.
explanation.whyCorrect: Similar to carbohydrates, amino acid transporters are expressed within the intestinal epithelium and the kidney to promote absorption or reabsorption, respectively. Deficiencies of these transporters are clinically relevant inborn errors of amino acid metabolism.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The liver receives amino acids from the portal circulation for synthesis and energy use; biliary secretion is not the transporter role described.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Skeletal muscle is not identified as a site of amino acid transporter-mediated excretion.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The pancreas secretes proteases and bicarbonate into the duct, not amino acids via transporters.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The brain is not the paired organ described; the transporters of interest promote intestinal absorption and renal reabsorption.

questions.topicName: Amino Acid Metabolism I: Nitrogen Balance and Urea Cycle

questions.stem: A bodybuilder consumes far more dietary protein than his physiologic needs, expecting to build up a large internal reserve of amino acids. Which of the following best describes what happens to the excess amino acids?

choices.label: A
choices.text: They are stored in adipose tissue as an amino acid reserve

choices.label: B
choices.text: They expand the free amino acid pool to several kilograms

choices.label: C
choices.text: They are polymerized into a storage protein analogous to glycogen

choices.label: D
choices.text: They are retained unchanged in the portal circulation

choices.label: E
choices.text: They are catabolized because the free pool cannot expand

explanation.summary: Unlike fats and carbohydrates, excess amino acids cannot be stored; the free pool cannot expand, so surplus is catabolized.
explanation.whyCorrect: Excess amino acids cannot be stored in the body. An average healthy adult contains about 100 grams of free amino acids, and this pool cannot really expand like fat or glycogen stores. When dietary intake exceeds physiological needs, amino acids are catabolized instead.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Adipose tissue stores fat, not amino acids; amino acids have no dedicated storage depot.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The free amino acid pool is only about 100 grams and cannot expand to a great extent.
whyWrongByChoice.C: There is no storage polymer for amino acids equivalent to glycogen; tissue proteins serve only as emergency reserves.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Amino acids do not accumulate unchanged in the portal blood; they are delivered to the liver and used or catabolized.

questions.topicName: Amino Acid Metabolism I: Nitrogen Balance and Urea Cycle

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man has been fasting for 3 days as part of a religious observance. His body has begun breaking down tissue proteins. Which of the following best explains why amino acid catabolism increases under this condition?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Dietary intake of amino acids has exceeded physiologic needs

choices.label: B
choices.text: Carbohydrates are restricted, so carbon backbones are needed for ATP

choices.label: C
choices.text: The free amino acid pool has expanded beyond its capacity

choices.label: D
choices.text: Tissue proteins are being renewed at their normal turnover rate

choices.label: E
choices.text: Portal ammonia from gut bacteria has saturated the liver

explanation.summary: When carbohydrates are restricted, as in prolonged fasting, tissue proteins serve as emergency reserves whose carbon backbones fuel oxidative catabolism.
explanation.whyCorrect: Amino acids are catabolized when carbohydrates are restricted in the diet, typically during an overnight fast progressing into a prolonged starvation state. Proteins in tissues serve as emergency reserves and are catabolized largely to obtain their carbon backbones, which serve as substrates for oxidative catabolism to support ATP production.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Dietary excess is a separate trigger for amino acid catabolism; a fasting patient has no dietary intake at all.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The free amino acid pool cannot expand; fasting depletes rather than overfills it.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Normal synthesis and turnover of proteins occurs continuously and does not explain the increased catabolism of a prolonged fast.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Gut ammonia handling by the liver is not the reason tissue proteins are broken down during starvation.

questions.topicName: Amino Acid Metabolism I: Nitrogen Balance and Urea Cycle

questions.stem: A researcher measures the capacity of various tissues to convert ammonia into urea. Which of the following tissues is the only one that performs this process to an appreciable extent?

explanation.summary: The liver is the only tissue that performs the urea cycle to an appreciable extent, producing urea as a major excretory form of nitrogen.
explanation.whyCorrect: The goal of the nitrogen-handling enzymes is to deliver nitrogen to the liver, which produces urea, a major excretory form of nitrogen. The liver is the only tissue that performs the urea cycle to an appreciable extent, which is why liver dysfunction leads to hyperammonemia.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Skeletal muscle loads nitrogen onto carbon skeletons to form glutamine for transport but does not run the urea cycle.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The kidney uses glutaminase and GDH to generate ammonia for urine pH balance; it does not produce urea to an appreciable extent.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The brain cannot use the urea cycle to detoxify ammonia, which is why excess ammonia saturates its glutamate and glutamine system.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The intestine uses glutaminase to make glutamate for fuel, not to synthesize urea.

questions.topicName: Amino Acid Metabolism I: Nitrogen Balance and Urea Cycle

questions.stem: In a transaminase reaction, the amino group of alanine is transferred onto alpha-ketoglutarate, generating glutamate. Which of the following alpha-keto acids is produced from alanine in this reaction?

explanation.summary: Alanine and pyruvate are a transaminase amino acid/keto acid pair; losing its amino group converts alanine into pyruvate.
explanation.whyCorrect: Transaminases swap the amino group of an amino acid for the carbonyl of an alpha-keto acid. The paired amino acid/keto acid partners are glutamate/alpha-ketoglutarate, alanine/pyruvate, and aspartate/oxaloacetate, so when alanine donates its nitrogen it becomes pyruvate.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Oxaloacetate is the keto acid partner of aspartate, not alanine.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Succinyl-CoA is the TCA entry product of methylmalonyl-CoA mutase, not a transamination product of alanine.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Fumarate is released from the urea cycle and is not the keto acid formed from alanine.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Carbamoyl phosphate is the urea cycle entry compound and is not generated by transamination.

questions.topicName: Amino Acid Metabolism I: Nitrogen Balance and Urea Cycle

questions.stem: When glutamate dehydrogenase runs in the liver, it liberates ammonia for urea production and regenerates alpha-ketoglutarate. Which of the following best describes the additional metabolic value of the alpha-ketoglutarate formed in this reaction?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It serves as the direct nitrogen donor to carbamoyl phosphate

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is exported to muscle as the primary blood nitrogen carrier

choices.label: C
choices.text: It replenishes TCA cycle intermediates in an anaplerotic reaction

choices.label: D
choices.text: It provides the cofactor required by aminotransferases

choices.label: E
choices.text: It is converted to lactate to correct hepatic acidosis

explanation.summary: The alpha-ketoglutarate reformed by hepatic GDH can feed anaplerotic reactions that refill the TCA cycle.
explanation.whyCorrect: In the liver, GDH liberates nitrogen from glutamate, reforming alpha-ketoglutarate. The nitrogen is used in urea production and the alpha-ketoglutarate can be used in anaplerotic reactions of the TCA cycle. Anaplerotic is a term derived from Greek meaning to fill, and many reactions in amino acid metabolism are anaplerotic in nature.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Alpha-ketoglutarate contains no nitrogen and therefore cannot donate nitrogen to carbamoyl phosphate.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Glutamine, not alpha-ketoglutarate, is the predominant nitrogen carrier in the blood.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Aminotransferases require PLP, a vitamin B6 derivative; alpha-ketoglutarate is a substrate, not a cofactor.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Alpha-ketoglutarate is not converted to lactate; lactate production in liver failure is a consequence of hepatic dysfunction, not a corrective pathway.

questions.topicName: Amino Acid Metabolism I: Nitrogen Balance and Urea Cycle

questions.stem: A 62-year-old woman with pernicious anemia has a cofactor deficiency that impairs a mutase enzyme. Metabolites derived from odd-chain fatty acids, leucine, and cholesterol can no longer be connected to the TCA cycle. Which of the following products is this mutase unable to form?

explanation.summary: Vitamin B12-dependent methylmalonyl-CoA mutase is an anaplerotic enzyme that forms succinyl-CoA to feed the TCA cycle.
explanation.whyCorrect: A prime example of anaplerosis is the function of vitamin B12 in methylmalonyl-CoA mutase, which connects various molecules such as cholesterol, leucine, and odd-chain fatty acids to the TCA cycle by forming succinyl-CoA. Without B12, this anaplerotic entry point is lost.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Alpha-ketoglutarate is the anaplerotic product of glutamate dehydrogenase, not of the B12-dependent mutase.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Oxaloacetate is the keto acid partner of aspartate in transamination and is not the product of methylmalonyl-CoA mutase.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Pyruvate is the keto acid partner of alanine and is not formed by the mutase reaction.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Fumarate is released from the urea cycle; it is not the product of methylmalonyl-CoA mutase.

questions.topicName: Amino Acid Metabolism I: Nitrogen Balance and Urea Cycle

questions.stem: A biochemist compares the cofactor requirements of the four main enzymes of nitrogen handling. One enzyme reversibly interconverts glutamate and alpha-ketoglutarate while releasing or consuming free ammonium. Which of the following cofactors does this enzyme use?

explanation.summary: Glutamate dehydrogenase uses NAD(P)+/NAD(P)H as it reversibly converts glutamate to alpha-ketoglutarate plus ammonium.
explanation.whyCorrect: The reversible GDH reaction is written as glutamate + NAD(P)+ + H2O going to alpha-ketoglutarate + NAD(P)H + NH4+. In peripheral tissue, GDH consumes NADPH to load nitrogen onto alpha-ketoglutarate; in liver the reverse reaction liberates ammonia for urea production.

whyWrongByChoice.A: ATP is consumed by glutamine synthetase to add ammonia onto glutamate, not by glutamate dehydrogenase.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Pyridoxal phosphate is the vitamin B6 derivative required by transaminases, not by GDH.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Biotin is not a cofactor for any of the four nitrogen-handling enzymes described.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Cobalamin is the cofactor of methylmalonyl-CoA mutase, an anaplerotic enzyme, not of glutamate dehydrogenase.

questions.topicName: Amino Acid Metabolism I: Nitrogen Balance and Urea Cycle

questions.stem: Immunohistochemistry of a healthy liver shows that glutamine synthetase, although present in nearly all tissues, is especially enriched in hepatocytes around the hepatic portal vein. Which of the following best explains this distribution?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Portal blood carries the highest concentration of bile acids

choices.label: B
choices.text: Portal blood delivers pancreatic proteases that need inactivation

choices.label: C
choices.text: Portal blood contains the urea that must be recycled

choices.label: D
choices.text: Portal blood carries free ammonia from gut bacteria and diet

choices.label: E
choices.text: Portal blood has the lowest oxygen tension in the liver

explanation.summary: Glutamine synthetase is enriched around the hepatic portal vein to capture the free ammonia arriving from the gut.
explanation.whyCorrect: Glutamine synthetase is expressed in nearly all tissues to ensure proper nitrogen handling and prevent ammonia toxicity. It is enriched around the hepatic portal vein because that blood comes from the GI tract and commonly has increased levels of free ammonia from bacterial metabolism and dietary intake.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Bile acid content is not the reason for glutamine synthetase enrichment; the enzyme handles ammonia, not bile acids.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Pancreatic proteases act in the intestinal lumen and are not the trigger for glutamine synthetase localization.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Urea is the end product exported for excretion; portal ammonia, not urea, is what glutamine synthetase captures.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Oxygen tension is not the described basis for the enzyme's enrichment near the portal vein.

questions.topicName: Amino Acid Metabolism I: Nitrogen Balance and Urea Cycle

questions.stem: A cell biologist fractionates hepatocytes and assays each compartment for enzymes of nitrogen metabolism. Which of the following correctly pairs each enzyme with the compartment in which it is found?

explanation.summary: Glutamine synthetase is a cytoplasmic enzyme, whereas glutaminase is a mitochondrial enzyme.
explanation.whyCorrect: Glutamine synthetase is described as a fairly ubiquitous cytoplasmic enzyme, located in the liver around the portal vein. Glutaminase is a mitochondrial enzyme responsible for urea production in the liver, ammonia generation for acid-base balance in the kidney, and glutamate production for fuel in the intestine.

whyWrongByChoice.B: This reverses the compartments; glutaminase is mitochondrial and glutamine synthetase is cytoplasmic.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Neither enzyme is lysosomal, and glutaminase is mitochondrial rather than cytoplasmic.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Glutamine synthetase is cytoplasmic, not nuclear, although glutaminase is correctly mitochondrial.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Glutamine synthetase is cytoplasmic, not mitochondrial, and glutaminase is mitochondrial, not peroxisomal.

questions.topicName: Amino Acid Metabolism I: Nitrogen Balance and Urea Cycle

questions.stem: Glutaminase is expressed in three organs, and in each it serves a different physiologic purpose. In the intestine, which of the following is the primary purpose of glutaminase activity?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Generating ammonia to buffer luminal pH

choices.label: C
choices.text: Making glutamate for use as fuel

choices.label: D
choices.text: Forming glutamine for export to the blood

explanation.summary: In the intestine, glutaminase cleaves glutamine to make glutamate that the tissue uses as fuel.
explanation.whyCorrect: Glutaminase is a mitochondrial enzyme with organ-specific roles: urea production in the liver, ammonia generation for acid-base balance in the kidney, and making glutamate for fuel in the intestine. The intestine therefore uses glutamine as an energy substrate rather than for nitrogen disposal.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Producing ammonia for urea synthesis is the role of glutaminase in the liver, the only tissue that performs the urea cycle appreciably.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Generating ammonia for pH balance is the role of glutaminase in the kidney, where it buffers the urine during metabolic acidosis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Glutamine formation is performed by glutamine synthetase, which runs the opposite reaction from glutaminase.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Nucleotide nitrogen donation is a biosynthetic fate of nitrogen, not the organ-specific purpose of intestinal glutaminase.

questions.topicName: Amino Acid Metabolism I: Nitrogen Balance and Urea Cycle

questions.stem: During metabolic acidosis, renal tubular cells take up glutamine and fully process it to alpha-ketoglutarate. How many ammonia molecules are liberated per glutamine, and which enzyme releases the final one?

explanation.summary: Complete renal processing of glutamine liberates two ammonia molecules: the first by glutaminase and the second by glutamate dehydrogenase.
explanation.whyCorrect: The kidney has a ready supply of glutamine and converts it into glutamate via glutaminase and subsequently to alpha-ketoglutarate via GDH. This process liberates two ammonia molecules, preventing the urine from becoming too acidic. Glutaminase removes the first ammonia and glutamate dehydrogenase liberates the second.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Glutaminase releases the first ammonia, but the process continues through GDH to release a second, so only one is incorrect.
whyWrongByChoice.B: GDH does release the final ammonia, but two molecules, not one, are liberated from each glutamine.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Glutamine synthetase adds ammonia to glutamate rather than releasing it, so it cannot be the final ammonia-releasing enzyme.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Alanine transaminase swaps functional groups without releasing free ammonia; it is not part of the renal glutamine pathway.

questions.topicName: Amino Acid Metabolism I: Nitrogen Balance and Urea Cycle

questions.stem: In skeletal muscle, a nitrogen-free carbon skeleton undergoes back-to-back nitrogen additions to become glutamine, which travels to the liver where back-to-back reactions strip both nitrogens off for urea production. Which of the following is the carbon skeleton that is regenerated in the liver at the end of this shuttle?

explanation.summary: The glutamine nitrogen shuttle begins and ends with alpha-ketoglutarate, which is reformed in the liver after both nitrogens are stripped.
explanation.whyCorrect: A single carbon skeleton of alpha-ketoglutarate that contains no nitrogen undergoes back-to-back nitrogen additions in tissues (GDH then glutamine synthetase) to become glutamine. In the liver, glutaminase then GDH strip the nitrogen back off for urea production, reforming the original carbon skeleton of alpha-ketoglutarate.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Pyruvate is the keto acid partner of alanine in transamination, not the skeleton of the glutamine shuttle.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Oxaloacetate is the keto acid partner of aspartate; it is not regenerated by the glutamine shuttle.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Succinyl-CoA is the product of methylmalonyl-CoA mutase and is not part of the glutamine shuttle.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Citrulline is a urea cycle intermediate, not the nitrogen-free carbon skeleton of glutamine.

questions.topicName: Amino Acid Metabolism I: Nitrogen Balance and Urea Cycle

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man with cirrhosis has recurrent hepatic encephalopathy. His physician explains that a large share of the ammonia reaching his portal blood is generated in the intestinal lumen by bacteria acting on a nitrogenous compound. Which of the following reactions best describes this bacterial source of ammonia?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Glutamate + NAD(P)+ + H2O to alpha-ketoglutarate + NH4+

choices.label: E
choices.text: Glutamate + ATP + NH4+ to glutamine + ADP + Pi

explanation.summary: Gut bacterial urease hydrolyzes urea into two ammonia molecules and carbon dioxide, a major intestinal source of ammonia.
explanation.whyCorrect: Gut metabolism is one of the four predominant sources of ammonia, arising from amino acid degradation and bacterial urease activity. The urease reaction converts urea plus water into 2 NH3 plus CO2, and this ammonia enters the portal circulation, where glutamine synthetase around the portal vein normally captures it.

whyWrongByChoice.A: This is the glutamate dehydrogenase reaction, an intracellular ammonia source in host tissue, not a bacterial reaction in the gut lumen.
whyWrongByChoice.C: This is the glutaminase reaction, which occurs in liver, kidney, and intestinal cells rather than in luminal bacteria acting on urea.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Adenosine deaminase activity is a purine metabolism source of ammonia, not the bacterial urea-derived source.
whyWrongByChoice.E: This is the glutamine synthetase reaction, which consumes ammonia rather than generating it.

questions.topicName: Amino Acid Metabolism I: Nitrogen Balance and Urea Cycle

questions.stem: A 7-year-old boy with a lymphoproliferative disorder receives chemotherapy that causes massive breakdown of tumor cell DNA and RNA. His ammonia level rises. Which of the following categories of ammonia source is most directly responsible for this rise?

choices.label: C
choices.text: Bacterial urease activity in the colon

explanation.summary: Purine and pyrimidine metabolism, including adenosine deaminase activity, is one of the four predominant sources of ammonia in the body.
explanation.whyCorrect: The four predominant sources of ammonia are purine and pyrimidine metabolism (e.g., ADA activity), gut metabolism, glutamate dehydrogenase, and deamination of select amino acids. Breakdown of nucleic acids from lysed cells drives nucleotide catabolism, releasing ammonia via purine and pyrimidine metabolism.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Deamination of histidine, threonine, glutamine, and asparagine is a separate amino acid source and does not arise from nucleic acid breakdown.
whyWrongByChoice.B: GDH liberates ammonia from glutamate; it is not the pathway by which DNA and RNA degradation releases nitrogen.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Bacterial urease produces ammonia in the gut from urea and is unrelated to tumor cell nucleic acid breakdown.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Renal glutaminase generates ammonia for urine pH balance, not from nucleotide catabolism.

questions.topicName: Amino Acid Metabolism I: Nitrogen Balance and Urea Cycle

questions.stem: Beyond glutamate dehydrogenase, certain amino acids can be directly deaminated to release free ammonia. Which of the following amino acids is a source of ammonia through direct deamination?

explanation.summary: Histidine, threonine, glutamine, and asparagine are the select amino acids whose deamination is a predominant source of ammonia.
explanation.whyCorrect: One of the four predominant sources of ammonia is deamination of select amino acids, specifically histidine, threonine, glutamine, and asparagine. Threonine therefore contributes free ammonia directly rather than passing its nitrogen through a transaminase.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Alanine handles its nitrogen by transamination with pyruvate as its keto acid partner, not by direct deamination.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Aspartate transfers nitrogen by transamination with oxaloacetate and is not listed among the directly deaminated amino acids.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Glycine is not among the select amino acids identified as deaminated ammonia sources.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Leucine is connected to the TCA via methylmalonyl-CoA mutase and succinyl-CoA; it is not a listed deamination source of ammonia.

questions.topicName: Amino Acid Metabolism I: Nitrogen Balance and Urea Cycle

questions.stem: A neurologist explains why hyperammonemia produces brain-centered symptoms even though the underlying problem is in the liver. Which of the following best explains why the brain is uniquely vulnerable to circulating ammonia?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The brain lacks glutamate dehydrogenase and cannot capture ammonia at all

choices.label: B
choices.text: The blood-brain barrier actively pumps ammonia into astrocytes

choices.label: C
choices.text: The brain lacks glutamine synthetase and cannot form glutamine

choices.label: D
choices.text: Ammonia is converted to urea in the brain, which is osmotically active

choices.label: E
choices.text: Ammonia crosses the blood-brain barrier and the brain has no urea cycle

explanation.summary: Ammonia freely traverses the blood-brain barrier and lipid bilayers, and the brain cannot use the urea cycle to detoxify it.
explanation.whyCorrect: Ammonia readily transverses the blood-brain barrier and lipid bilayers to access intracellular niches. At normal levels the brain incorporates ammonia into alpha-ketoglutarate via GDH and then into glutamine via glutamine synthetase, but the brain cannot manage ammonia like the liver and cannot use the urea cycle, so excess ammonia saturates this system.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The brain does have glutamate dehydrogenase and uses it to incorporate ammonia into alpha-ketoglutarate at normal levels.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Ammonia crosses passively through lipid bilayers; there is no active pump driving it into astrocytes.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The brain expresses glutamine synthetase, and its overactivity is precisely what depletes glutamate and ATP during hyperammonemia.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The brain cannot perform the urea cycle; glutamine, not urea, is the osmolyte that accumulates.

questions.topicName: Amino Acid Metabolism I: Nitrogen Balance and Urea Cycle

questions.stem: A 49-year-old woman with acute liver failure and marked hyperammonemia develops a generalized seizure. Her physician attributes the seizure partly to loss of a specific inhibitory neurotransmitter. Which of the following best explains the mechanism of that loss?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Glutamate, the precursor of GABA, is siphoned into glutamine

choices.label: B
choices.text: Ammonia directly hydrolyzes GABA at the synapse

choices.label: C
choices.text: Glutamine synthetase converts GABA into glutamate

explanation.summary: Excess ammonia drives glutamine synthetase to consume glutamate, which is both a neurotransmitter and the precursor of GABA.
explanation.whyCorrect: Ammonia increases glutamine synthetase activity, consuming glutamate and ATP while producing ever-increasing amounts of glutamine. Rapid depletion of glutamate within the CNS adversely impacts neurotransmission because glutamate is itself a neurotransmitter and also the precursor of gamma-aminobutyrate (GABA), the primary inhibitory neurotransmitter. Seizure is one of the listed manifestations of hepatic encephalopathy.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Ammonia does not hydrolyze GABA; the deficit arises upstream from depletion of the glutamate precursor.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Glutamine synthetase acts on glutamate to form glutamine; it does not act on GABA.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Alpha-ketoglutarate depletion slows the TCA and ATP production; it is not described as blocking GABA reuptake.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Aminopeptidases are brush border digestive enzymes and play no role in CNS GABA metabolism.

questions.topicName: Amino Acid Metabolism I: Nitrogen Balance and Urea Cycle

questions.stem: In an astrocyte exposed to high ammonia, glutamate dehydrogenase is driven toward glutamate formation to replace glutamate consumed by glutamine synthetase. Which of the following is the most direct consequence of this shift for cellular energy metabolism?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Alpha-ketoglutarate depletion lowers oxaloacetate and slows the TCA

choices.label: C
choices.text: Glutamine accumulation directly uncouples the electron transport chain

choices.label: D
choices.text: Pyruvate is diverted to alanine, starving glycolysis

choices.label: E
choices.text: Succinyl-CoA accumulates and inhibits citrate synthase

explanation.summary: Ammonia-driven GDH activity consumes alpha-ketoglutarate, causing a fall in oxaloacetate that slows the TCA cycle and OXPHOS.
explanation.whyCorrect: High ammonia and depletion of glutamate stimulate glutamate dehydrogenase, which consumes alpha-ketoglutarate in an effort to reduce ammonia and restore glutamate. Because alpha-ketoglutarate is a key TCA intermediate, its rapid depletion causes a fall in oxaloacetate, slowing the TCA and OXPHOS. This ineffective TCA exacerbates the ATP depletion already caused by heightened glutamine synthetase activity.

whyWrongByChoice.A: GDH running toward glutamate consumes rather than produces NAD(P)H, and NADPH excess is not the described mechanism.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Glutamine acts as an osmolyte causing astrocyte swelling; it is not described as uncoupling the electron transport chain.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Pyruvate diversion to alanine is not the energy consequence described; the problem lies in TCA intermediate depletion.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Succinyl-CoA accumulation is not part of the ammonia toxicity mechanism; the deficit is in alpha-ketoglutarate and oxaloacetate.

questions.topicName: Amino Acid Metabolism I: Nitrogen Balance and Urea Cycle

questions.stem: A 60-year-old man with cirrhosis has recovered from an episode of hepatic encephalopathy. To reduce the risk of recurrence, his physician makes a dietary recommendation grounded in the principle that excess protein is not stored and will yield nitrogen. Which of the following is the most appropriate recommendation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: High-protein diet to rebuild hepatic reserves

choices.label: B
choices.text: Carbohydrate-free diet to promote amino acid oxidation

choices.label: C
choices.text: High-fat diet to spare tissue protein

choices.label: D
choices.text: Protein-restricted diet to limit ammonia production

explanation.summary: Patients at risk of hyperammonemia are placed on a protein-restricted diet because excess protein cannot be stored and yields nitrogen.
explanation.whyCorrect: Patients at risk of hyperammonemia are usually placed on a protein-restricted diet to prevent ammonia production. Because excess proteins are not stored and will yield nitrogen, limiting protein intake limits the ammonia load the failing liver must handle. Protein-restricted diets and lactulose mitigate the risk associated with hepatic encephalopathy.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A high-protein diet would increase nitrogen and ammonia production, worsening the risk of encephalopathy.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Carbohydrate restriction drives catabolism of tissue proteins for carbon backbones, which would liberate more nitrogen, not less.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A high-fat diet is not the described intervention; the goal is to reduce the nitrogen load from dietary protein.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Glutamine is the osmolyte that accumulates and swells astrocytes in hyperammonemia; supplementing it is not the recommended strategy.

questions.topicName: Amino Acid Metabolism I: Nitrogen Balance and Urea Cycle

questions.stem: A 52-year-old man with acute liver failure has a serum ammonia level three times the upper limit of normal. Blood gas analysis unexpectedly reveals an elevated lactate with a low pH. A student is puzzled, noting that ammonia is a base. Which of the following best explains the finding?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Ammonia is directly converted to lactate in astrocytes

choices.label: B
choices.text: Respiratory alkalosis from ammonia triggers compensatory lactate release

choices.label: C
choices.text: The failing liver itself causes lactate production

choices.label: D
choices.text: Renal glutaminase overactivity acidifies the blood

choices.label: E
choices.text: Bacterial urease in the gut generates lactic acid

explanation.summary: Hyperammonemia is often accompanied by lactic acidosis because both result from hepatic dysfunction, and liver failure causes lactate production.
explanation.whyCorrect: Hyperammonemia can be associated with lactic acidosis. This may be counterintuitive because ammonia is basic, but hyperammonemia is often caused by hepatic dysfunction, and liver failure causes lactate production. The acidosis therefore reflects the underlying liver failure rather than the ammonia itself.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Ammonia is not converted to lactate; in astrocytes it is incorporated into glutamate and glutamine.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Ammonia-mediated hyperventilation produces respiratory alkalosis, but that is not described as causing lactate release; the lactate comes from liver failure.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Renal glutaminase generates ammonia to buffer urine and combat acidosis; it does not acidify the blood.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Bacterial urease converts urea into ammonia and carbon dioxide; it does not produce lactic acid.

questions.topicName: Amino Acid Metabolism I: Nitrogen Balance and Urea Cycle

questions.stem: A full-term male newborn is well until 24 hours of life, when he becomes irritable and feeds poorly, then develops lethargy, vomiting, and tachypnea. Arterial blood gas shows a respiratory alkalosis. Serum ammonia is 2,800 micromol/L and serum glutamine is elevated. Urinalysis shows orotic aciduria, and a complete blood count is normal. Which of the following enzyme deficiencies is the most likely cause?

explanation.summary: OTC deficiency is the most common urea cycle defect and uniquely produces orotic aciduria with hyperammonemia but no anemia.
explanation.whyCorrect: Ornithine transcarbamylase deficiency is the most common urea cycle disorder. Without OTC, carbamoyl phosphate accumulates, leaks into the cytosol, and is diverted into the pyrimidine synthesis pathway to form orotic acid. This yields the combination of hyperammonemia, elevated glutamine, low/absent citrulline, and orotic aciduria with a normal CBC.

whyWrongByChoice.A: CPS-I deficiency causes low citrulline and hyperammonemia but produces normal or low orotic acid, because carbamoyl phosphate is not made.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Argininosuccinate synthetase deficiency (citrullinemia) causes elevated, not low, citrulline and does not cause orotic aciduria.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Arginase deficiency presents later with spasticity and markedly elevated arginine, not neonatal orotic aciduria.
whyWrongByChoice.E: UMP synthase deficiency (hereditary orotic aciduria) causes orotic aciduria with megaloblastic anemia and NO hyperammonemia.

questions.topicName: Amino Acid Metabolism I: Nitrogen Balance and Urea Cycle

questions.stem: A 3-day-old infant with lethargy and vomiting is found to have marked hyperammonemia and orotic aciduria. Genetic and metabolic workup is pending. Which additional finding would best distinguish ornithine transcarbamylase deficiency from hereditary orotic aciduria (UMP synthase deficiency)?

explanation.summary: OTC deficiency causes hyperammonemia without anemia, whereas hereditary orotic aciduria causes anemia without hyperammonemia.
explanation.whyCorrect: Both disorders present with high orotic acid, so they must be differentiated. UMP synthase deficiency causes classic orotic aciduria with megaloblastic anemia but does NOT cause hyperammonemia. In contrast, OTC deficiency does present with hyperammonemia but does not cause megaloblastic anemia.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Megaloblastic anemia points toward hereditary orotic aciduria, not OTC deficiency, so it would not identify OTC.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Both conditions share elevated orotic acid, so this cannot distinguish them.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Low BUN reflects impaired urea synthesis but is not specific and would not separate these two possibilities cleanly.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Elevated glutamine accompanies hyperammonemia of urea cycle defects but is not the defining discriminator between these two.

questions.topicName: Amino Acid Metabolism I: Nitrogen Balance and Urea Cycle

questions.stem: A neonate presents with hyperammonemia and elevated serum glutamine. Plasma amino acid analysis reveals markedly elevated citrulline with low argininosuccinic acid. Which enzyme is most likely deficient?

explanation.summary: Argininosuccinate synthetase deficiency (citrullinemia) causes citrulline buildup with low argininosuccinic acid.
explanation.whyCorrect: Argininosuccinate synthetase converts citrulline into argininosuccinate. When it is deficient, its substrate citrulline accumulates while its product argininosuccinic acid (ASA) remains low. This pattern of high citrulline with low ASA defines citrullinemia and distinguishes it from lyase deficiency.

whyWrongByChoice.A: OTC deficiency causes low or absent citrulline, not elevated citrulline.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Argininosuccinate lyase deficiency elevates BOTH citrulline and argininosuccinic acid, not low ASA.
whyWrongByChoice.D: CPS-I deficiency causes low citrulline because upstream carbamoyl phosphate is not produced.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Arginase deficiency elevates arginine and presents with spasticity, not a citrulline/ASA imbalance.

questions.topicName: Amino Acid Metabolism I: Nitrogen Balance and Urea Cycle

questions.stem: A hyperammonemic infant has plasma studies showing elevated citrulline and elevated argininosuccinic acid. Which enzyme deficiency best explains these findings?

explanation.summary: Argininosuccinate lyase deficiency (argininosuccinic aciduria) elevates both citrulline and argininosuccinic acid.
explanation.whyCorrect: Argininosuccinate lyase cleaves argininosuccinate into arginine and fumarate. When it is deficient, argininosuccinic acid accumulates, and citrulline upstream also rises. The presence of high ASA together with high citrulline defines argininosuccinic aciduria and separates it from citrullinemia, where ASA is low.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Synthetase deficiency (citrullinemia) elevates citrulline but keeps argininosuccinic acid LOW.
whyWrongByChoice.C: OTC deficiency causes low citrulline and high orotic acid, not elevated ASA.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Arginase deficiency elevates arginine, not citrulline and ASA.
whyWrongByChoice.E: NAGS deficiency causes low urea cycle intermediates from impaired CPS-I activation, not ASA accumulation.

questions.topicName: Amino Acid Metabolism I: Nitrogen Balance and Urea Cycle

questions.stem: A 2-year-old child has progressive spasticity and stiff, scissoring gait present since infancy, and was initially thought to have cerebral palsy. Serum ammonia is only mildly elevated, but plasma arginine is nearly four-fold above the upper reference limit. Which enzyme is most likely deficient?

explanation.summary: Arginase deficiency uniquely presents with progressive spasticity mimicking cerebral palsy and markedly elevated arginine with only mild hyperammonemia.
explanation.whyCorrect: Arginase cleaves arginine into ornithine and urea. Its deficiency causes arginine to rise three- to four-fold above normal, and the elevated arginine and arginine-derived compounds drive the neurological picture. Symptoms progress from birth with mean onset around 2 years and are often mistaken for cerebral palsy, while ammonia is only mildly high.

whyWrongByChoice.B: OTC deficiency typically presents in the neonatal period with severe hyperammonemia and orotic aciduria, not late spasticity.
whyWrongByChoice.C: CPS-I deficiency causes severe neonatal hyperammonemia with low intermediates, not elevated arginine.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Synthetase deficiency causes citrullinemia with high citrulline, not high arginine.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Lyase deficiency elevates citrulline and argininosuccinic acid, not isolated arginine with spasticity.

questions.topicName: Amino Acid Metabolism I: Nitrogen Balance and Urea Cycle

questions.stem: An infant with recurrent hyperammonemia has a complete but poorly stimulated urea cycle. Enzymatic studies show that carbamoyl phosphate synthetase-I fails to be activated normally. Administration of carbamylglutamate corrects the hyperammonemia. Which of the following best explains why this therapy works in this patient?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It supplies the missing carbamoyl phosphate directly

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is a synthetic N-acetylglutamate analog

choices.label: C
choices.text: It inhibits pyrimidine synthesis to lower orotic acid

choices.label: D
choices.text: It scavenges glutamine for urinary excretion

explanation.summary: In NAGS deficiency, carbamylglutamate is a synthetic NAG analog that directly activates CPS-I, bypassing the need for endogenous NAG.
explanation.whyCorrect: CPS-I is allosterically activated by N-acetylglutamate (NAG), which is made by NAG synthetase (NAGS). In NAGS deficiency the urea cycle enzymes are intact but cannot be stimulated. Carbamylglutamate is a synthetic analog of NAG that activates CPS-I directly, restoring flux; this is well tolerated and often eliminates the need for protein restriction. CPS-I deficiency itself, by contrast, is non-responsive to carbamylglutamate.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Carbamylglutamate is an activator of CPS-I, not a source of carbamoyl phosphate.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Its benefit is activation of the urea cycle, not inhibition of pyrimidine synthesis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Glutamine scavenging is the action of phenylbutyrate, not carbamylglutamate.
whyWrongByChoice.E: It does not substitute for arginase; it acts at the CPS-I regulatory step.

questions.topicName: Amino Acid Metabolism I: Nitrogen Balance and Urea Cycle

questions.stem: A researcher studies the first committed step of the urea cycle in isolated hepatocyte mitochondria. Which of the following molecules is the physiologic allosteric activator required for carbamoyl phosphate synthetase-I activity?

explanation.summary: CPS-I is allosterically activated by N-acetylglutamate (NAG).
explanation.whyCorrect: Carbamoyl phosphate synthetase-I converts ammonia and CO2 into carbamoyl phosphate and requires allosteric activation by N-acetylglutamate. Arginine, a urea cycle intermediate, further stimulates NAG synthase to increase NAG when nitrogen-rich intermediates accumulate, ensuring augmented nitrogen disposal.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Aspartate is a substrate that donates the second nitrogen at the argininosuccinate synthetase step, not a CPS-I activator.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Ornithine combines with carbamoyl phosphate at the OTC step; it does not allosterically activate CPS-I.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Fumarate is a product of the lyase step that links to the TCA cycle, not a regulator of CPS-I.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Argininosuccinate is a downstream intermediate, not the CPS-I activator.

questions.topicName: Amino Acid Metabolism I: Nitrogen Balance and Urea Cycle

questions.stem: In the urea cycle, one nitrogen of urea is derived from free ammonia, and the second nitrogen is supplied by another amino acid. This second nitrogen donor is regenerated from fumarate by way of malate and oxaloacetate. Which molecule provides this second nitrogen atom to the urea cycle?

explanation.summary: Aspartate supplies the second nitrogen of urea and is regenerated from fumarate via malate, oxaloacetate, and AST.
explanation.whyCorrect: Argininosuccinate synthetase uses aspartate to add the second nitrogen atom. The fumarate released by argininosuccinate lyase is converted to malate and then oxaloacetate, which is transaminated by aspartate aminotransferase (AST) using glutamate as the nitrogen donor to regenerate aspartate, sustaining nitrogen flow into urea.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Glutamine is a major nitrogen transporter to the liver but is not the direct second-nitrogen donor within the cycle.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Ornithine is the carrier that accepts carbamoyl phosphate and is regenerated by arginase; it does not donate the second nitrogen.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Alanine transports nitrogen to the liver in the Cahill cycle but does not directly provide the second urea nitrogen.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Citrulline is an intermediate that accepts aspartate; it is not itself the second nitrogen donor.

questions.topicName: Amino Acid Metabolism I: Nitrogen Balance and Urea Cycle

questions.stem: A child with a urea cycle defect and chronic hyperammonemia is treated with sodium phenylbutyrate. Which of the following best describes why removing this drug's target molecule helps control the patient's ammonia levels?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It binds glutamine for urinary excretion

choices.label: B
choices.text: It binds urea directly to accelerate its transport to the kidney

choices.label: C
choices.text: It inhibits arginase to prevent ammonia release

choices.label: D
choices.text: It neutralizes ammonia by acidifying the blood

choices.label: E
choices.text: It replaces the deficient urea cycle enzyme

explanation.summary: Phenylbutyrate (via phenylacetate) conjugates glutamine, the predominant nitrogen transporter, providing a urea-independent route to excrete nitrogen.
explanation.whyCorrect: Phenylbutyrate is oxidized to phenylacetate, which covalently binds glutamine to form a derivative excreted in the urine. Because glutamine is the predominant nitrogen transporter in the body, its removal provides an alternative path for nitrogen disposal that bypasses the compromised urea cycle, keeping ammonia within a safer range.

whyWrongByChoice.B: It does not bind urea; it conjugates glutamine, and the whole point is to bypass urea production.
whyWrongByChoice.C: It works by scavenging glutamine, not by inhibiting arginase.
whyWrongByChoice.D: It does not lower ammonia through blood acidification; it removes nitrogen as a glutamine conjugate.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Nitrogen scavengers do not replace the deficient enzyme; they provide an alternate excretion route.

questions.topicName: Amino Acid Metabolism I: Nitrogen Balance and Urea Cycle

questions.stem: During prolonged vigorous exercise, skeletal muscle transfers amino acid nitrogen to a carrier that travels to the liver, where it is converted to pyruvate for gluconeogenesis and its nitrogen enters the urea cycle. Which molecule serves as this nitrogen carrier?

explanation.summary: In the glucose-alanine (Cahill) cycle, alanine carries nitrogen from muscle to the liver and its carbon skeleton becomes pyruvate for gluconeogenesis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Alanine is a key nitrogen transporter, especially during prolonged intense exercise. Via ALT, muscle nitrogen is loaded onto pyruvate to form alanine, which travels to the liver; there ALT converts alanine back to pyruvate for gluconeogenesis, and the released nitrogen feeds urea synthesis. This process is known as the Cahill cycle.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Lactate carries carbon in the Cori cycle but does not transport nitrogen, and no transaminase is involved.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Creatinine is a waste product of creatine metabolism, not a gluconeogenic nitrogen shuttle.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Urea is the excreted nitrogen end product, not the muscle-to-liver carrier.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Oxaloacetate is an intermediate that regenerates aspartate; it is not the muscle nitrogen carrier.

questions.topicName: Amino Acid Metabolism I: Nitrogen Balance and Urea Cycle

questions.stem: A physiologist compares two interorgan shuttles. In one, muscle and erythrocytes send a three-carbon molecule to the liver to be remade into glucose without any amino acid metabolism. Which statement best characterizes this Cori cycle relative to the glucose-alanine cycle?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It transports lactate and requires no transaminase enzymes

choices.label: B
choices.text: It transports alanine and requires ALT

choices.label: C
choices.text: It generates urea directly in skeletal muscle

choices.label: D
choices.text: It occurs only in the presence of insulin

choices.label: E
choices.text: It converts ammonia to glutamine in erythrocytes

explanation.summary: The Cori cycle recycles lactate from muscle and erythrocytes back to glucose in the liver and, unlike the Cahill cycle, needs no transaminases.
explanation.whyCorrect: The Cori cycle allows lactate produced by anaerobic glycolysis in muscle or by erythrocytes to be returned to the liver and remade into glucose. Because it does not involve amino acid metabolism, no amino transaminases are required, in contrast to the glucose-alanine cycle which relies on ALT.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Transporting alanine and requiring ALT describes the glucose-alanine (Cahill) cycle, not the Cori cycle.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Skeletal muscle does not run the urea cycle; urea is made in the liver.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The lactate-recycling Cori cycle is not defined by insulin presence; the glucose-alanine cycle notably does not occur when insulin is present.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Erythrocytes releasing lactate is central to the Cori cycle; it does not convert ammonia to glutamine here.

questions.topicName: Amino Acid Metabolism I: Nitrogen Balance and Urea Cycle

questions.stem: A previously healthy adult undergoes a prolonged fast during which glucagon promotes breakdown of body protein for energy. Compared with a fed state, which of the following best describes this person's nitrogen balance and its cause?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Negative nitrogen balance because protein catabolism causes nitrogen loss

choices.label: B
choices.text: Positive nitrogen balance because tissue is being actively built

choices.label: C
choices.text: Nitrogen equilibrium because intake equals loss

choices.label: D
choices.text: Positive nitrogen balance because the urea cycle is downregulated

choices.label: E
choices.text: Negative nitrogen balance because urea synthesis is suppressed by glucagon

explanation.summary: Fasting drives a catabolic, negative nitrogen balance because nitrogen loss exceeds intake as body protein is broken down.
explanation.whyCorrect: Negative nitrogen balance occurs when nitrogen loss exceeds intake, indicating a catabolic state in which the body breaks down its own proteins. During fasting, glucagon promotes protein catabolism for energy from the amino acid carbon skeletons; this generates ammonia that is converted to urea and upregulates the urea cycle, pushing the individual toward negative nitrogen balance.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Positive nitrogen balance is an anabolic state seen in growth, pregnancy, and recovery, not fasting.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Equilibrium is typical of healthy adults on a balanced diet, not during a prolonged fast.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Starvation actually upregulates the urea cycle to increase urea excretion, and the balance is negative, not positive.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Glucagon during fasting increases, not suppresses, urea synthesis; the balance is negative because of increased catabolism.

questions.topicName: Amino Acid Metabolism I: Nitrogen Balance and Urea Cycle

questions.stem: A 27-year-old woman at 24 weeks' gestation undergoes a nutritional assessment. Over a 24-hour period, her dietary nitrogen intake substantially exceeds her urine urea nitrogen and other nitrogen losses. Which of the following best characterizes her nitrogen balance and the metabolic state it indicates?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Positive nitrogen balance reflecting an anabolic state

choices.label: B
choices.text: Negative nitrogen balance reflecting a catabolic state

choices.label: C
choices.text: Nitrogen equilibrium reflecting stable protein turnover

choices.label: D
choices.text: Positive nitrogen balance reflecting a catabolic state

choices.label: E
choices.text: Negative nitrogen balance reflecting an anabolic state

explanation.summary: Positive nitrogen balance (intake exceeds loss) indicates an anabolic state and is seen in pregnancy, childhood growth, and convalescence.
explanation.whyCorrect: Nitrogen balance compares nitrogen consumed with nitrogen depleted from the amino acid pool into waste such as urine urea nitrogen. When intake exceeds loss the balance is positive, indicating the body is building more tissue than it breaks down. Pregnancy, rapid growth in children, and recovery from severe illness are the classic settings.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Negative balance means loss exceeds intake, the opposite of this patient's measurements, and signals catabolism as in starvation or chronic illness.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Equilibrium requires intake to equal loss, which is typical of a healthy non-pregnant adult on a balanced diet, not a pregnant woman retaining nitrogen.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Positive balance is by definition anabolic; a catabolic state produces negative, not positive, balance.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Negative balance is never anabolic; it reflects the body breaking down its own protein.

questions.topicName: Amino Acid Metabolism I: Nitrogen Balance and Urea Cycle

questions.stem: A biochemist maps the fates of the free amino acid pool. In addition to tissue protein synthesis and catabolism to urea or carbon skeletons, the pool supplies nitrogen for a class of nonprotein nitrogen compounds. Which of the following belongs to that class?

explanation.summary: Heme/porphyrins, purines, pyrimidines, and nitric oxide are the nonprotein nitrogen compounds built from the amino acid pool.
explanation.whyCorrect: The amino acid pool is dynamic but stable. Besides tissue protein, it is drawn on to make nonprotein nitrogen compounds, which include heme and porphyrins, purines and pyrimidines, and nitric oxide. Heme synthesis is a major nitrogen sink; a single porphyrin ring requires eight glycines.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Lactate is a nitrogen-free product of anaerobic glycolysis recycled in the Cori cycle.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Acetoacetate is a ketone body formed from carbon skeletons after nitrogen has been removed.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Oxaloacetate is a citric acid cycle intermediate and gluconeogenic precursor; it carries no nitrogen.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Palmitate is a fatty acid made from acetyl-CoA carbon; it contains no nitrogen.

questions.topicName: Amino Acid Metabolism I: Nitrogen Balance and Urea Cycle

questions.stem: A researcher studies isolated hepatocyte mitochondria and confirms that only the first two reactions of the urea cycle occur inside them. Which of the following urea cycle intermediates must be carried across the mitochondrial membrane by transporters so that the remaining three reactions can proceed in the cytoplasm?

explanation.summary: Citrulline is the product of the two mitochondrial reactions and is transported into the cytoplasm for the rest of the urea cycle.
explanation.whyCorrect: The urea cycle begins in the mitochondria, where CPS-I forms carbamoyl phosphate and OTC combines it with ornithine to make citrulline. Mitochondrial membrane transporters move citrulline into the cytoplasm, where argininosuccinate synthetase, argininosuccinate lyase, and arginase complete the cycle.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Carbamoyl phosphate is consumed by OTC inside the mitochondria; it only leaks into the cytosol pathologically in OTC deficiency.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Argininosuccinate is formed and cleaved in the cytoplasm, so it never needs to cross the mitochondrial membrane.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Arginine is generated by the cytoplasmic lyase step and cleaved by cytoplasmic arginase.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Fumarate is released in the cytoplasm by argininosuccinate lyase; it is not the intermediate exported from the mitochondria.

questions.topicName: Amino Acid Metabolism I: Nitrogen Balance and Urea Cycle

questions.stem: In the cytoplasm of a hepatocyte, citrulline is converted to argininosuccinate. Which of the following pairs of substances is required for this reaction?

explanation.summary: Argininosuccinate synthetase joins citrulline with aspartate at the expense of ATP.
explanation.whyCorrect: Argininosuccinate synthetase is the first cytoplasmic enzyme of the urea cycle. It condenses citrulline with aspartate, which donates the second urea nitrogen, and the reaction requires ATP.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Ornithine is the substrate of the mitochondrial OTC step, not the synthetase step, and NAD+ is used at the malate-to-oxaloacetate step.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Glutamate donates nitrogen to oxaloacetate through AST to regenerate aspartate; it is not a direct synthetase substrate.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Carbamoyl phosphate and NAG belong to the mitochondrial CPS-I and OTC steps.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Fumarate is a product of the following lyase reaction, and water is consumed by arginase.

questions.topicName: Amino Acid Metabolism I: Nitrogen Balance and Urea Cycle

questions.stem: Argininosuccinate lyase releases fumarate during the urea cycle. Most of this fumarate is recycled to regenerate aspartate, but a smaller fraction is diverted to another use. Which of the following is that alternative fate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Direct conjugation with glycine for urinary excretion

choices.label: B
choices.text: Conversion to orotic acid in pyrimidine synthesis

choices.label: D
choices.text: Transport to skeletal muscle as a nitrogen carrier

choices.label: E
choices.text: Entry into gluconeogenesis by way of oxaloacetate

explanation.summary: Fumarate from the lyase step can feed the TCA cycle or, via oxaloacetate, gluconeogenesis to a much smaller extent.
explanation.whyCorrect: Fumarate produced by argininosuccinate lyase is primarily converted through malate to oxaloacetate and transaminated back to aspartate, sustaining nitrogen flow into urea. Because fumarate is also a TCA cycle metabolite, a small portion can instead be used in the TCA cycle or in gluconeogenesis via oxaloacetate.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Glycine conjugation is the action of sodium benzoate on glycine, not a fate of fumarate.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Orotic acid arises from carbamoyl phosphate spilling into pyrimidine synthesis; fumarate is not a pyrimidine precursor.
whyWrongByChoice.C: NAG synthase is stimulated by arginine, not by fumarate.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Fumarate carries no nitrogen; alanine and glutamine are the interorgan nitrogen carriers.

questions.topicName: Amino Acid Metabolism I: Nitrogen Balance and Urea Cycle

questions.stem: After a large protein meal, nitrogen-rich intermediates accumulate in hepatocytes. One of these urea cycle intermediates stimulates N-acetylglutamate synthase, raising NAG levels and thereby augmenting nitrogen disposal. Which intermediate provides this signal?

explanation.summary: Arginine stimulates NAG synthase (NAGS), increasing NAG and hence CPS-I activation when nitrogen-rich intermediates build up.
explanation.whyCorrect: CPS-I requires allosteric activation by N-acetylglutamate. Arginine, a urea cycle intermediate, stimulates the activity of NAG synthase, ensuring that when nitrogen-rich intermediates accumulate, NAG rises and the cycle is driven harder to dispose of excess nitrogen. This is why NAGS deficiency is described as ineffective CPS-I activation when arginine levels increase.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Citrulline is the mitochondrial product exported to the cytoplasm; it does not regulate NAGS.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Ornithine accepts carbamoyl phosphate at the OTC step and has no described role in stimulating NAGS.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Argininosuccinate is the substrate of the lyase and is not the NAGS signal.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Carbamoyl phosphate is the product of CPS-I, downstream of NAG regulation, not the stimulator of NAGS.

questions.topicName: Amino Acid Metabolism I: Nitrogen Balance and Urea Cycle

questions.stem: A 6-year-old boy with acute lymphoblastic leukemia is enrolled in a trial of recombinant arginase. Although arginine is a nonessential amino acid, the therapy is expected to starve the leukemic cells while sparing normal cells. Which of the following best explains this selectivity?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Leukemic cells overexpress ornithine transcarbamylase and deplete their own ornithine

choices.label: B
choices.text: Leukemic cells lack key enzymes of arginine synthesis and depend on external arginine

choices.label: C
