A mutation in which of the following genes is most likely?

explanation.summary: Hartnup disease is a defect of the SLC6A19 neutral amino acid transporter causing neutral hyperaminoaciduria.
explanation.whyCorrect: Hartnup disease results in a defective neutral amino acid transporter (Phe, Ile, Leu, Thr, Trp, Val, Ser, Ala, Tyr) encoded by the SLC6A19 gene, causing neutral hyperaminoaciduria. The normal basic amino acids (lysine, arginine, ornithine) exclude cystinuria. Hartnup disease is largely asymptomatic until stressors such as dietary changes or increased sun exposure provoke pellagra-like symptoms.

whyWrongByChoice.A: SLC3A1 encodes a subunit of the basic amino acid transporter defective in cystinuria, which causes basic hyperaminoaciduria with elevated lysine, arginine, ornithine, and cystine.
whyWrongByChoice.C: SLC7A9 is the other gene encoding the cystinuria transporter complex, again affecting basic amino acids rather than neutral ones.
whyWrongByChoice.D: PAH mutations cause PKU with elevated plasma phenylalanine, not a generalized neutral aminoaciduria.
whyWrongByChoice.E: CBS mutations cause homocystinuria with elevated homocysteine, not urinary loss of neutral amino acids.

questions.topicName: Inborn Errors of Amino Acid Metabolism

questions.stem: A 19-year-old woman presents with radiating flank pain and hematuria. Urine microscopy shows hexagonal crystals, and the nurse notes that the urine has a rotten egg odor. The odor is most directly attributable to which of the following?

explanation.summary: The rotten egg odor of cystinuria comes from sulfur in the excreted cystine.
explanation.whyCorrect: Cystinuria is caused by defects in the SLC3A1 or SLC7A9 genes, which encode subunits of the basic amino acid transporter that also carries the disulfide-linked cysteine dimer, cystine. Excreted cystine gives the urine a rotten egg smell due to its sulfur content, and precipitates into hexagonal kidney stones that can cause flank pain, infection, and blood in the urine.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Phenylacetate produces the musty, mousey odor of PKU.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Isovaleric acid produces the sweaty feet odor of isovaleric acidemia.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Accumulated alpha-keto acids of the BCAAs produce the maple syrup or burnt sugar odor of MSUD.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Homogentisic acid causes dark urine in alkaptonuria rather than a rotten egg odor.

questions.topicName: Inborn Errors of Amino Acid Metabolism

questions.stem: A 5-day-old boy with newly diagnosed maple syrup urine disease is comatose despite aggressive fluid and electrolyte therapy and intravenous glucose. Plasma leucine remains markedly elevated. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

choices.label: E
choices.text: Alkalinizing agents to raise urine pH

explanation.summary: When toxic intermediates accumulate to the point of coma in an acute inborn error, hemodialysis may be needed.
explanation.whyCorrect: Acute newborn presentations of inborn errors of amino acid metabolism are managed with a multifaceted approach: aggressive fluid and electrolyte therapy, caloric supplementation with glucose to promote insulin-driven anabolism and prevent protein and fatty acid breakdown, and antibiotics when warranted because metabolically compromised children are prone to infections. Hemodialysis may be needed if toxic intermediates have accumulated to the point of inducing a coma, as in this infant.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Thiamine can partially rescue select MSUD variants over time, but it alone will not clear toxic alpha-keto acids from a comatose infant.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A high-protein formula would supply more BCAAs; MSUD treatment requires protein restriction with a formula lacking BCAAs.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Carnitine supplementation is part of the strategy for propionic acidemia, conjugating excess propionic acid, not for MSUD coma.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Urine alkalinization prevents cystine stone formation in cystinuria and does not address accumulated BCAA alpha-keto acids.

questions.topicName: Inborn Errors of Amino Acid Metabolism

questions.stem: A healthy full-term newborn develops yellowing of the skin and sclerae on the third day of life. He is feeding well and is otherwise vigorous. Total bilirubin is elevated with a predominantly unconjugated (indirect) fraction, and the jaundice resolves by two weeks of age. Which of the following mechanisms best explains the elevated bilirubin?

choices.label: C
choices.text: Extrahepatic obstruction of the common bile duct

choices.label: E
choices.text: Mutation in the ABCC2 (MRP2) canalicular transporter

explanation.summary: Physiologic neonatal jaundice reflects immature hepatic conjugation combined with high red-cell turnover.
explanation.whyCorrect: In newborns the liver is still maturing, so UDP-glucuronosyltransferase (UDPGT) activity is transiently reduced. Combined with increased breakdown of a large, short-lived neonatal red-cell mass, this produces a benign unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia that resolves as the liver matures over 1-2 weeks.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Autoimmune hepatocyte destruction is not the cause of routine physiologic neonatal jaundice, which is developmental and self-limited.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Bile duct obstruction would raise the conjugated (direct) fraction and cause pale stools and dark urine, not a self-resolving indirect hyperbilirubinemia.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Absent ferrochelatase impairs heme synthesis and does not describe the mechanism of physiologic neonatal jaundice.
whyWrongByChoice.E: An ABCC2/MRP2 mutation (Dubin-Johnson) causes a conjugated hyperbilirubinemia, not the transient unconjugated jaundice of the newborn.

questions.topicName: Porphyrins and Iron Homeostasis (1 of 2)

questions.stem: A 3-year-old who lives in a home built in the 1940s presents with irritability, abdominal pain, and loss of previously acquired developmental milestones. A complete blood count shows a microcytic anemia, and delta-aminolevulinic acid (ALA) is elevated. Which pair of enzymes is most directly inhibited by the responsible toxin?

choices.label: D
choices.text: Porphobilinogen deaminase and uroporphyrinogen III synthase

explanation.summary: Lead poisoning blocks ALA dehydratase and ferrochelatase, causing ALA buildup and reduced heme.
explanation.whyCorrect: Lead inhibits ALA dehydratase (causing accumulation of neurotoxic ALA) and ferrochelatase (preventing insertion of iron into protoporphyrin IX). The result is decreased heme production with microcytic anemia plus the neurologic findings of ALA accumulation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: ALA synthase is the rate-limiting enzyme but is not the target of lead, and biliverdin reductase acts in heme degradation, not synthesis.
whyWrongByChoice.B: UDP-glucuronosyltransferase and heme oxygenase participate in bilirubin metabolism, not the steps blocked by lead.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Porphobilinogen deaminase and uroporphyrinogen III synthase are not the enzymes classically inhibited by lead.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The coproporphyrinogen and protoporphyrinogen oxidases are not the primary lead-sensitive steps described in the pathway.

questions.topicName: Porphyrins and Iron Homeostasis (1 of 2)

questions.stem: A 2-month-old boy is brought in for failure to thrive that began shortly after birth. Laboratory studies confirm a microcytic anemia, and a Prussian blue stain of the bone marrow shows ringed sideroblasts (iron-laden mitochondria encircling the nucleus of erythroid precursors). Which of the following is the most likely cause of his condition?

explanation.summary: X-linked sideroblastic anemia results from deficient ALAS2, the erythroid-specific isoform.
explanation.whyCorrect: ALAS2 is the erythroid isoform that drives heme synthesis for hemoglobin. Its deficiency impairs heme production, so iron accumulates in the mitochondria of erythroid precursors, forming ringed sideroblasts and causing an X-linked microcytic anemia.

whyWrongByChoice.A: ALAS1 predominates in the liver and non-erythroid tissues, not the erythroid precursors affected in ringed sideroblastic anemia.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Folate deficiency causes a macrocytic (megaloblastic) anemia, whereas impaired heme synthesis produces microcytosis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Increased ferrochelatase activity would enhance iron incorporation into heme, the opposite of the defect seen here.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Excess heme oxygenase accelerates heme degradation and does not explain ringed sideroblasts or microcytic anemia.

questions.topicName: Porphyrins and Iron Homeostasis (1 of 2)

questions.stem: The committed, rate-limiting step of heme synthesis condenses glycine and succinyl-CoA to form delta-aminolevulinic acid. Which of the following cofactors is required for this reaction, such that its deficiency can produce a microcytic (sideroblastic) anemia?

explanation.summary: ALA synthase is a PLP (vitamin B6)-dependent enzyme catalyzing the first step of heme synthesis.
explanation.whyCorrect: The first step of heme synthesis, catalyzed by ALA synthase, requires pyridoxal phosphate (the active form of vitamin B6). Because this step is essential for heme production, B6/PLP deficiency impairs heme synthesis and can cause a microcytic, sideroblastic anemia.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Vitamin B12 deficiency causes a macrocytic megaloblastic anemia and is not the cofactor for ALA synthase.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Folate is required for one-carbon transfer and DNA synthesis, not for the ALA synthase reaction.
whyWrongByChoice.D: NADPH is used by biliverdin reductase in heme degradation, not for the condensation of glycine and succinyl-CoA.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Biotin is a cofactor for carboxylase reactions and is not involved in the first step of heme synthesis.

questions.topicName: Porphyrins and Iron Homeostasis (1 of 2)

questions.stem: Before bilirubin can be excreted into bile, it must be conjugated with glucuronic acid to become water-soluble. In which of the following cells does this conjugation reaction occur?

explanation.summary: Bilirubin is conjugated with glucuronic acid by UDP-glucuronosyltransferase inside hepatocytes.
explanation.whyCorrect: Unconjugated bilirubin is taken up by hepatocytes, where UDP-glucuronosyltransferase (UDPGT) covalently links it to glucuronic acid. This produces water-soluble conjugated bilirubin that can then be excreted into bile.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Macrophages break down red cells and generate unconjugated bilirubin, but they do not conjugate it.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Renal tubular cells excrete water-soluble conjugated bilirubin but do not perform the conjugation reaction.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Gut bacteria convert conjugated bilirubin to urobilinogen; they do not conjugate bilirubin.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Erythroid precursors synthesize hemoglobin and are not sites of bilirubin conjugation.

questions.topicName: Porphyrins and Iron Homeostasis (1 of 2)

questions.stem: During degradation of heme within splenic macrophages, the porphyrin ring is cleaved to form biliverdin. Which of the following byproducts are released in this heme oxygenase-catalyzed reaction?

explanation.summary: Heme oxygenase cleaves heme to biliverdin, releasing carbon monoxide and Fe2+.
explanation.whyCorrect: Heme oxygenase opens the porphyrin ring of heme, producing biliverdin while liberating carbon monoxide and ferrous iron (Fe2+). The iron is recycled, and this reaction is the source of endogenous CO.

whyWrongByChoice.A: NADPH is a reactant for the next step (biliverdin reductase), and glucuronic acid is added later in the liver; neither is released by heme oxygenase.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Ammonia and succinyl-CoA are not products of heme cleavage; succinyl-CoA is a substrate of heme synthesis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Urobilinogen and stercobilin are downstream gut bacterial products of conjugated bilirubin, not products of heme oxygenase.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Glycine and CO2 relate to the synthetic (ALA synthase) side of heme metabolism, not to heme degradation.

questions.topicName: Porphyrins and Iron Homeostasis (1 of 2)

questions.stem: A newborn with a markedly elevated unconjugated bilirubin that is not promptly treated becomes lethargic and later develops cerebral palsy and hearing loss. Which property of unconjugated bilirubin best accounts for this neurologic injury?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It is water-soluble and freely filtered by the kidney

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is lipid-soluble and can cross the blood-brain barrier

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is covalently bound to glucuronic acid

choices.label: D
choices.text: It is efficiently excreted into bile

choices.label: E
choices.text: It accumulates as ringed sideroblasts in the brain

explanation.summary: Lipid-soluble unconjugated bilirubin crosses the blood-brain barrier, causing kernicterus.
explanation.whyCorrect: Unconjugated bilirubin is hydrophobic and lipid-soluble. When it accumulates because conjugation cannot keep pace, it crosses the blood-brain barrier and deposits in the brain, producing the irreversible neurologic damage of kernicterus (cerebral palsy, hearing/vision problems).

whyWrongByChoice.A: Unconjugated bilirubin is water-insoluble and is not filtered by the kidney; only the conjugated form is renally excreted.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Conjugation with glucuronic acid defines conjugated bilirubin, which does not cross the blood-brain barrier.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Only conjugated bilirubin is efficiently excreted into bile; the unconjugated form is the neurotoxic species.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Ringed sideroblasts are marrow erythroid precursors in sideroblastic anemia and have nothing to do with kernicterus.

questions.topicName: Porphyrins and Iron Homeostasis (1 of 2)

questions.stem: A jaundiced neonate is placed under blue-green phototherapy lamps, and the serum bilirubin falls even though hepatic conjugation is unchanged. Which of the following best explains how phototherapy lowers the bilirubin level?

choices.label: B
choices.text: It photo-isomerizes bilirubin into a water-soluble form

choices.label: C
choices.text: It degrades bilirubin into carbon monoxide and iron

choices.label: D
choices.text: It increases albumin binding of bilirubin in the blood

choices.label: E
choices.text: It stimulates ferrochelatase to consume bilirubin

explanation.summary: Phototherapy isomerizes unconjugated bilirubin in the skin into a water-soluble form for excretion.
explanation.whyCorrect: The conjugated ring system of bilirubin absorbs blue-green light (most effective around 460-490 nm). This energy isomerizes unconjugated bilirubin in the skin capillaries into a more water-soluble isomer that can be excreted in bile and urine without requiring hepatic conjugation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Phototherapy works independently of hepatic conjugation; the stem specifies conjugation is unchanged.
whyWrongByChoice.C: CO and iron are released by heme oxygenase acting on heme, not by light acting on bilirubin.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Increasing albumin binding would keep bilirubin in the blood rather than promote its excretion.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Ferrochelatase inserts iron into protoporphyrin during heme synthesis and does not consume bilirubin.

questions.topicName: Porphyrins and Iron Homeostasis (1 of 2)

questions.stem: A young adult with a history of mild, intermittent jaundice undergoes laparoscopy for an unrelated reason, and the surgeon notes a strikingly glossy black liver. Laboratory studies show a predominantly conjugated (direct) hyperbilirubinemia. Which of the following defects is most likely responsible?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Defective canalicular MRP2 transporter due to an ABCC2 mutation

choices.label: C
choices.text: A slight reduction in UDP-glucuronosyltransferase activity

choices.label: E
choices.text: Excessive hemolysis of red blood cells

explanation.summary: Dubin-Johnson syndrome is a conjugated hyperbilirubinemia from a defective MRP2 (ABCC2) transporter, marked by a black liver.
explanation.whyCorrect: Dubin-Johnson syndrome is an autosomal recessive defect of the ABCC2 gene encoding MRP2, which normally exports conjugated bilirubin from hepatocytes into bile. Impaired excretion raises conjugated bilirubin and produces the characteristic glossy black liver.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Complete absence of UDPGT is Crigler-Najjar type 1, which causes severe unconjugated (not conjugated) hyperbilirubinemia.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A slight decrease in UDPGT describes Gilbert syndrome, an unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia without a black liver.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Lead inhibition of ferrochelatase impairs heme synthesis and causes anemia, not a conjugated hyperbilirubinemia with a black liver.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Hemolysis produces an unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia because it overwhelms conjugation, not a conjugated one.

questions.topicName: Porphyrins and Iron Homeostasis (1 of 2)

questions.stem: A 19-year-old man notices mild scleral icterus during a febrile illness and again after fasting for a religious observance; each episode resolves on its own. Labs show a mildly elevated, predominantly unconjugated bilirubin with normal liver enzymes and no evidence of hemolysis. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanation.summary: Gilbert syndrome causes mild, stress- or fasting-provoked unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia and is benign.
explanation.whyCorrect: Gilbert syndrome is a common (3-7%), benign disorder with a slight decrease in UDPGT. Conjugation still occurs, but stressors such as infection or fasting let heme breakdown outpace conjugation, producing a transient, self-limited unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia that needs no treatment.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Crigler-Najjar type 1 has complete absence of UDPGT and presents in infancy with severe jaundice and kernicterus, not mild episodic icterus in a young adult.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Dubin-Johnson causes a conjugated hyperbilirubinemia with a black liver, not an unconjugated one triggered by fasting.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Rotor syndrome causes a conjugated hyperbilirubinemia from impaired hepatic excretion, unlike this unconjugated pattern.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Biliary obstruction produces a conjugated hyperbilirubinemia with pale stools and dark urine, not a benign unconjugated pattern.

questions.topicName: Porphyrins and Iron Homeostasis (1 of 2)

questions.stem: A 55-year-old woman with a gallstone lodged in her common bile duct develops jaundice, pale clay-colored stools, and dark urine. Which of the following laboratory findings best fits her condition?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Elevated unconjugated bilirubin with absent bilirubin in the urine

choices.label: B
choices.text: Elevated conjugated bilirubin that spills over into the urine

choices.label: C
choices.text: Increased stercobilin production in the gut

choices.label: D
choices.text: Ringed sideroblasts in the bone marrow

explanation.summary: Post-hepatic obstruction backs up conjugated bilirubin into blood and urine, causing pale stools and dark urine.
explanation.whyCorrect: With a bile duct obstruction the liver still conjugates bilirubin, but the water-soluble conjugated form cannot reach the gut and backs up into the blood (post-hepatic jaundice). It is then abnormally excreted in urine (dark urine), while reduced bilirubin delivery to the gut produces pale stools.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The obstruction raises the conjugated fraction, and because conjugated bilirubin is water-soluble it does appear in the urine.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Obstruction reduces conjugated bilirubin reaching the gut, so stercobilin falls and stools become pale, not increased.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Ringed sideroblasts reflect a heme synthesis defect in the marrow, unrelated to biliary obstruction.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Serum conjugated bilirubin rises, not falls, when it cannot be routed out through the obstructed bile duct.

questions.topicName: Porphyrins and Iron Homeostasis (1 of 2)

questions.stem: A patient with acute intermittent porphyria has an attack after starting a barbiturate and drinking alcohol, both of which induce hepatic ALAS1. The clinical team wants to reduce ALAS1-driven flux through the pathway. Which of the following most directly opposes ALAS1 induction and is used to dampen such attacks?

explanation.summary: Glucose (and heme/hemin) suppresses ALAS1, so glucose loading helps dampen porphyria attacks.
explanation.whyCorrect: Low glucose indirectly stimulates ALAS1 expression, so maintaining or raising blood glucose suppresses ALAS1 and reduces flux through the heme pathway. This is why glucose loading (and hemin, which acts like heme's feedback signal) is used to blunt acute porphyria attacks.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Hypoxia is a stimulator of ALAS activity, which would worsen rather than dampen an attack.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Erythropoietin induces the erythroid isoform ALAS2, not the hepatic ALAS1 relevant to this scenario.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Lead inhibits downstream enzymes (ALA dehydratase, ferrochelatase) but does not suppress ALAS1 expression.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Iron chelation does not suppress ALAS1; if anything, intracellular iron regulates the erythroid isoform ALAS2.

questions.topicName: Porphyrins and Iron Homeostasis (1 of 2)

questions.stem: Heme is produced in several tissues, but the bulk of the body's heme synthesis takes place in one location. Which of the following tissues accounts for roughly 80% of total heme synthesis?

explanation.summary: About 80% of heme is made in the bone marrow for hemoglobin, 15% in the liver, and 5% elsewhere.
explanation.whyCorrect: Heme synthesis is distributed roughly 80% bone marrow (heme for hemoglobin), 15% liver (heme for cytochrome P450 used in phase I detoxification), and 5% other tissues. The erythroid demand for hemoglobin makes the marrow the dominant site.

whyWrongByChoice.B: The liver contributes about 15%, mainly to supply heme for cytochrome P450 enzymes, not the majority.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The kidney falls within the roughly 5% of synthesis attributed to all other tissues combined.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The spleen is a site of red cell breakdown and heme degradation, not the major site of heme synthesis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Skeletal muscle uses heme in myoglobin but is part of the small remainder of synthesis, not the major site.

questions.topicName: Porphyrins and Iron Homeostasis (1 of 2)

questions.stem: A biochemistry student is asked to write the overall stoichiometry for building one porphyrin ring from its two carbon sources. Which of the following correctly states the number of precursor molecules consumed?

explanation.summary: All porphyrin ring carbons come from glycine and succinyl-CoA; 8 of each are needed per ring.
explanation.whyCorrect: Every carbon in the porphyrin ring is derived from glycine and succinyl-CoA. The overall reaction consumes 8 glycines plus 8 succinyl-CoA molecules to produce one porphyrin ring, since each ALA molecule is built from one glycine and one succinyl-CoA and eight ALA units are assembled into the ring.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Four of each would supply only half the carbons required for the four-pyrrole ring.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Two of each would form only two ALA molecules, far short of the eight needed.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Glycine and succinyl-CoA are consumed in equal numbers because each ALA is made from one of each.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The precursors are used in a 1:1 ratio, so unequal numbers of glycine and succinyl-CoA are incorrect.

questions.topicName: Porphyrins and Iron Homeostasis (1 of 2)

questions.stem: In the last step of heme synthesis, ferrochelatase inserts ferrous iron into a fully formed ring system. Which of the following is the direct substrate for this iron insertion?

explanation.summary: Ferrochelatase adds iron to protoporphyrin IX to form heme.
explanation.whyCorrect: Heme is a porphyrin with a bound iron. Before iron is added, the ring system is called protoporphyrin IX; ferrochelatase, located in the mitochondria, inserts Fe2+ into protoporphyrin IX to produce heme.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Coproporphyrinogen III is a cytosolic intermediate that must still be converted by coproporphyrinogen oxidase and protoporphyrinogen oxidase.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Uroporphyrinogen III is an early cytosolic intermediate acted on by uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase, several steps before iron insertion.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Hydroxymethylbilane is the linear product of porphobilinogen deaminase and is not the substrate of ferrochelatase.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Protoporphyrinogen IX must first be oxidized by protoporphyrinogen oxidase to protoporphyrin IX before iron can be inserted.

questions.topicName: Porphyrins and Iron Homeostasis (1 of 2)

questions.stem: A researcher separates erythroid precursor cells into cytosolic and mitochondrial fractions and assays each for enzymes of heme synthesis. Which of the following enzymes would be recovered in the cytosolic fraction?

explanation.summary: The middle steps of heme synthesis (ALA dehydratase through uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase) occur in the cytosol; the first and last steps are mitochondrial.
explanation.whyCorrect: Heme synthesis begins in the mitochondria (ALA synthase), moves to the cytosol for ALA dehydratase, porphobilinogen deaminase, uroporphyrinogen III synthase, and uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase, then returns to the mitochondria for the final oxidase steps and ferrochelatase. Uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase, which converts uroporphyrinogen III to coproporphyrinogen III, is therefore cytosolic.

whyWrongByChoice.A: ALA synthase catalyzes the first step inside the mitochondria, condensing glycine and succinyl-CoA.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Ferrochelatase is mitochondrial, inserting Fe2+ into protoporphyrin IX in the final step.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Protoporphyrinogen oxidase acts in the mitochondria to form protoporphyrin IX.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Coproporphyrinogen oxidase is a mitochondrial enzyme that converts coproporphyrinogen III to protoporphyrinogen IX as the pathway re-enters the mitochondria.

questions.topicName: Porphyrins and Iron Homeostasis (1 of 2)

questions.stem: In the cytosol, individual porphobilinogen molecules are joined into a linear tetrapyrrole before the ring is closed. Which of the following is the direct product of the porphobilinogen deaminase reaction?

explanation.summary: Porphobilinogen deaminase converts porphobilinogen into the linear intermediate hydroxymethylbilane.
explanation.whyCorrect: After ALA dehydratase forms porphobilinogen, porphobilinogen deaminase links porphobilinogen units into hydroxymethylbilane (uroporphyrinogen I precursor). Uroporphyrinogen III synthase then closes and rearranges this into uroporphyrinogen III.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Porphobilinogen is the substrate of the deaminase, not its product; it is made from ALA by ALA dehydratase.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Uroporphyrinogen III is formed one step later by uroporphyrinogen III synthase acting on hydroxymethylbilane.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Coproporphyrinogen III is produced further downstream by uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Delta-aminolevulinic acid is the product of ALA synthase, upstream of porphobilinogen.

questions.topicName: Porphyrins and Iron Homeostasis (1 of 2)

questions.stem: Two patients each have an inherited enzyme defect in the porphyrin synthetic pathway. One has an acute porphyria with intermittent attacks and a normal hemoglobin; the other has an erythropoietic porphyria with severe anemia. Which of the following best explains why porphyrin synthesis defects differ in their effect on red cell production?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Tissue-specific enzyme isoforms let some defects spare erythroid heme production

choices.label: B
choices.text: Compensatory up-regulation of ALAS2 fully offsets the enzyme defect in acute porphyria

choices.label: C
choices.text: Erythropoietic porphyrias primarily disrupt globin chain rather than heme production

choices.label: D
choices.text: Acute and cutaneous porphyrias affect heme degradation rather than heme synthesis

choices.label: E
choices.text: The liver rather than the bone marrow supplies most of the heme used for hemoglobin

explanation.summary: Because heme-synthetic enzymes have tissue-specific isoforms, some porphyrias do not cause anemia while the erythropoietic porphyrias do.
explanation.whyCorrect: There are multiple tissue-specific isoforms of the enzymes used to synthesize porphyrin. Even though porphyrin is required for hemoglobin production, defects such as the acute and cutaneous porphyrias do not cause anemia, whereas the erythropoietic porphyrias cause severe anemia because the affected enzyme activity is critical in erythroid cells.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Acute porphyrias spare red cell production because of isoform specificity, not because ALAS2 compensates for a downstream block.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Erythropoietic porphyrias are defects of porphyrin (heme) synthesis, not of globin synthesis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Acute and cutaneous porphyrias are defects in the heme synthetic pathway, not in degradation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: About 80% of heme synthesis occurs in the bone marrow, which is where hemoglobin heme is made.

questions.topicName: Porphyrins and Iron Homeostasis (1 of 2)

questions.stem: Heme controls its own production through several mechanisms directed at ALA synthase. Besides repressing transcription of the ALAS gene and allosterically inhibiting existing enzyme, heme limits which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Release of ALA from the mitochondrion into the cytosol

choices.label: B
choices.text: Movement of ALA synthase into the mitochondrial matrix

choices.label: C
choices.text: Uptake of glycine across the mitochondrial membrane

choices.label: D
choices.text: Oxidation of protoporphyrinogen IX to protoporphyrin IX

choices.label: E
choices.text: Binding of pyridoxal phosphate to ALA dehydratase

explanation.summary: Heme reduces the transport of ALA synthase into the mitochondrial matrix as one of its self-regulatory mechanisms.
explanation.whyCorrect: Heme regulates its own synthesis by repressing production of ALA synthase from the ALAS gene, allosterically inhibiting existing ALA synthase, reducing the movement of ALA synthase enzymes into the mitochondrial matrix, and inducing heme oxygenase when in excess. Since ALA synthase must act inside the mitochondrion, limiting its import throttles the rate-limiting step.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Heme's regulatory actions target the ALA synthase enzyme itself, not the export of its product ALA.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Glycine uptake is not a described site of heme feedback regulation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Protoporphyrinogen oxidase is a late step and is not the target of heme's feedback control.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Pyridoxal phosphate is the cofactor of ALA synthase, not ALA dehydratase, and heme does not act by blocking cofactor binding.

questions.topicName: Porphyrins and Iron Homeostasis (1 of 2)

questions.stem: In erythroid precursors, heme production is coordinated with production of its protein partner so that hemoglobin is assembled in balanced amounts. Heme promotes globin synthesis by regulating which of the following steps?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Transcriptional activation of the globin gene promoter

choices.label: B
choices.text: Splicing of the globin precursor mRNA in the nucleus

choices.label: C
choices.text: Formation of the ribosomal initiation complex for translation

choices.label: D
choices.text: Export of mature globin mRNA through the nuclear pore

choices.label: E
choices.text: Chaperone-assisted folding of the finished globin chain

explanation.summary: Heme regulates globin synthesis in erythroid tissue by controlling formation of the ribosomal initiation complex.
explanation.whyCorrect: In addition to its inhibitory roles on its own synthesis, heme regulates synthesis of globin protein in erythroid tissues by regulating the formation of the ribosomal initiation complex for protein synthesis. This couples globin translation to heme availability so hemoglobin production stays balanced.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Heme's described action on globin is at the level of translation initiation, not gene transcription.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Splicing of globin mRNA is not the step regulated by heme.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Nuclear export of globin mRNA is not the described point of heme control.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Heme acts before the globin chain is made, at ribosomal initiation, not at folding of the finished protein.

questions.topicName: Porphyrins and Iron Homeostasis (1 of 2)

questions.stem: A 60-year-old man with chronic lung disease and long-standing hypoxemia has a markedly elevated serum erythropoietin. Which of the following effects on heme synthesis in his bone marrow erythroid progenitors is expected?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Decreased ALAS1 expression in erythroid progenitors

choices.label: C
choices.text: Increased sensitivity of ALAS2 to allosteric inhibition by heme

explanation.summary: Erythropoietin triggers expression of the erythroid isoform ALAS2, boosting heme production for hemoglobin.
explanation.whyCorrect: Because erythrocyte demand is high in the bone marrow, the ALAS2 isoform is expressed in erythroid progenitor cells. The hormone EPO triggers expression of ALAS2, and ALAS2 is less sensitive to heme allosteric inhibition than ALAS1, allowing high heme output for hemoglobin synthesis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: EPO induces rather than represses ALAS2, since more heme is needed for new red cells.
whyWrongByChoice.B: ALAS1 is the non-erythroid (hepatocyte) isoform; the erythroid response to EPO involves ALAS2.
whyWrongByChoice.C: ALAS2 is inherently less sensitive to heme allosteric inhibition than ALAS1; EPO does not increase its sensitivity.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Ferrochelatase is inhibited by lead, not by erythropoietin; EPO promotes, not blocks, heme formation.

questions.topicName: Porphyrins and Iron Homeostasis (1 of 2)

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man is started on a chronic medication that is cleared by hepatic cytochrome P450 enzymes. Over the following weeks, hepatic ALAS1 expression rises. Which of the following best explains this induction?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The drug chelates ferrous iron and prevents heme formation

choices.label: B
choices.text: The drug inhibits heme oxygenase and raises hepatic heme

choices.label: C
choices.text: The drug blocks ALA dehydratase, causing ALA to accumulate

choices.label: D
choices.text: The drug stimulates erythropoietin release from the kidney

choices.label: E
choices.text: Increased P450 synthesis demands more heme as a prosthetic group

explanation.summary: Drugs detoxified by phase I cytochrome P450 induce hepatic ALAS1 to supply heme prosthetic groups for the new enzymes.
explanation.whyCorrect: Drugs and chemicals that require detoxification through the phase I cytochrome P450 enzymes induce ALAS1 expression in the liver to provide sufficient prosthetic groups (heme) to support enzymatic function. Cytochrome P450 enzymes are heme proteins, so ramping up their synthesis creates demand for more hepatic heme.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Iron chelation is not the mechanism; the induction reflects increased demand for heme, not a block in its synthesis.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Raising hepatic heme would suppress ALAS1 through feedback inhibition, the opposite of what is observed.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Blocking ALA dehydratase is the action of lead, and it would not explain a rise in ALAS1 expression.
whyWrongByChoice.D: EPO acts on the erythroid isoform ALAS2 in bone marrow, not on hepatic ALAS1.

questions.topicName: Porphyrins and Iron Homeostasis (1 of 2)

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman with a known porphyria has attacks that recur with her menstrual cycle, when heme synthesis is stimulated. During an attack she is treated with intravenous hemin, a compound isolated from human blood. Which of the following best describes how hemin relieves her symptoms?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Mimics heme's feedback inhibition of ALA synthase, reducing pathway flux

choices.label: B
choices.text: Binds and inactivates the accumulated ALA in the circulation

choices.label: C
choices.text: Supplies the ferrous iron required by ferrochelatase

choices.label: D
choices.text: Induces hepatic UDP-glucuronosyltransferase to clear intermediates

choices.label: E
choices.text: Directly inhibits ALA dehydratase to halt porphobilinogen formation

explanation.summary: Hemin dampens heme synthesis by the same feedback mechanism heme uses naturally, controlling attacks triggered by increased heme production.
explanation.whyCorrect: Hemin is made naturally from the breakdown of RBCs and can be isolated from human blood as a therapeutic. Because it is very similar to heme itself, administering it dampens heme synthesis by the same mechanism heme does naturally (feedback on ALA synthase). It is used for occasional porphyria attacks, such as those stimulated by the menstrual cycle, when heme synthesis is turned on.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Hemin does not neutralize ALA directly; it reduces the upstream production of intermediates.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hemin is not given as an iron source; ferrochelatase supply of iron is not the problem in a porphyria attack.
whyWrongByChoice.D: UDP-glucuronosyltransferase conjugates bilirubin during heme degradation and is unrelated to controlling heme synthesis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Inhibiting ALA dehydratase is the action of lead and would worsen ALA accumulation and neurotoxicity.

questions.topicName: Porphyrins and Iron Homeostasis (1 of 2)

questions.stem: A 32-year-old woman presents with abdominal pain, tachycardia, hypertension, anxiety, and burning pain with numbness in her hands and feet. She has an inherited defect in an early enzyme of heme synthesis. Blood lead level is normal. Accumulation of which of the following intermediates best accounts for her neurologic and autonomic findings?

explanation.summary: ALA accumulation, irrespective of its cause, is neurotoxic and produces peripheral neuropathy, CNS symptoms, and autonomic dysfunction.
explanation.whyCorrect: ALA accumulation is neurotoxic regardless of the reason it builds up. It is most often associated with peripheral neuropathy (numbness, tingling, burning pain, motor weakness), CNS symptoms (anxiety, confusion, psychosis, seizures), and autonomic dysfunction (tachycardia, hypertension, GI dysmotility), matching this patient's presentation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Protoporphyrin IX is the late ring intermediate that receives iron; it is not the neurotoxic species described.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Unconjugated bilirubin is a heme degradation product that causes kernicterus in neonates, not this adult autonomic and neuropathic picture.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Biliverdin is the green degradation product of heme oxygenase and is not implicated in neurotoxicity.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Coproporphyrinogen III is a mid-pathway intermediate; the neurotoxic intermediate is ALA.

questions.topicName: Porphyrins and Iron Homeostasis (1 of 2)

questions.stem: A 12-year-old boy with X-linked sideroblastic anemia due to an ALAS2 variant has a microcytic anemia with ringed sideroblasts on marrow examination. Supplementation with which of the following may increase his hemoglobin concentration and hematocrit?

explanation.summary: Select ALAS2 variants respond to pyridoxine supplementation with increased hemoglobin and hematocrit.
explanation.whyCorrect: ALAS2 requires pyridoxal phosphate, the active form of vitamin B6. Select ALAS2 variants in X-linked sideroblastic anemia demonstrate increased Hb concentration and HCT upon pyridoxine supplementation, because higher cofactor availability supports residual enzyme activity.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Folate deficiency causes macrocytic anemia; it is not the cofactor for ALAS2 and does not correct this microcytic defect.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Vitamin B12 deficiency produces macrocytic anemia and is unrelated to the ALAS2 reaction.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Iron is already accumulating in the mitochondria of these erythroid precursors (ringed sideroblasts); the defect is failed incorporation, not iron lack.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Vitamin C is not the cofactor required by ALA synthase.

questions.topicName: Porphyrins and Iron Homeostasis (1 of 2)

questions.stem: A patient with hyperbilirubinemia develops yellow discoloration of the skin and sclerae. Which of the following properties of bilirubin accounts for this visible color change?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Its tight binding to serum albumin

choices.label: C
choices.text: The iron atom retained in its structure

choices.label: D
choices.text: Its conjugated ring system absorbs light

choices.label: E
choices.text: Its oxidation to urobilin within the skin

explanation.summary: Bilirubin, like heme, has a conjugated ring system whose double bonds absorb light, producing yellow skin and sclerae when it accumulates.
explanation.whyCorrect: Both heme and bilirubin possess a conjugated ring system. Bilirubin absorbs light because of these conjugated double bonds, which accounts for the yellowing of skin tones and the sclera of the eye when it abnormally accumulates in the body.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Albumin binding allows transport of unconjugated bilirubin but does not itself produce color.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Water solubility determines how bilirubin is excreted, not why it appears yellow.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Iron is released as Fe2+ when heme oxygenase opens the ring; bilirubin contains no iron.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Urobilin forms from urobilinogen after gut bacterial metabolism and gives urine its tint; it is not formed in the skin.

questions.topicName: Porphyrins and Iron Homeostasis (1 of 2)

questions.stem: A 3-week-old infant has severe unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia and early signs of kernicterus. Enzyme studies show complete absence of UDP-glucuronosyltransferase. Phototherapy and plasmapheresis are started to lower the bilirubin. Which of the following interventions offers the potential for a lasting correction of the underlying defect?

explanation.summary: In Crigler-Najjar type 1, liver transplantation is potentially lifesaving because the transplanted liver can conjugate bilirubin.
explanation.whyCorrect: Crigler-Najjar type 1 results from complete absence of UDPGT, presents in infancy with jaundice, kernicterus, and high unconjugated bilirubin, and leads to death within a few years. Plasmapheresis and phototherapy help lower bilirubin, but liver transplantation is potentially lifesaving because the transplanted liver can conjugate bilirubin properly.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Phenobarbital increases liver enzyme synthesis and works in type 2, where UDPGT is present but reduced; with no enzyme at all there is nothing to induce.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Sunlight or phototherapy only solubilizes existing unconjugated bilirubin; it does not correct the absent conjugation enzyme.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Iron is not the problem in a bilirubin conjugation defect.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Hemin dampens heme synthesis in porphyria attacks and does not restore bilirubin conjugation.

questions.topicName: Porphyrins and Iron Homeostasis (1 of 2)

questions.stem: After macrophages convert heme into water-insoluble unconjugated bilirubin, the bilirubin must travel through the bloodstream to the liver. Which of the following carries unconjugated bilirubin in the plasma?

explanation.summary: Unconjugated bilirubin is bound to serum albumin for transport in blood to the liver.
explanation.whyCorrect: Unconjugated bilirubin is hydrophobic and water-insoluble. To allow transport in the blood to the liver, it is bound to serum albumin and circulates as a bilirubin-albumin complex until it is taken up by hepatocytes for conjugation.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Transferrin is an iron-transport protein and does not carry bilirubin.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hemoglobin is the source of heme that is degraded to bilirubin; it does not transport bilirubin.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Glucuronic acid is covalently attached to bilirubin inside hepatocytes during conjugation, not a plasma carrier.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Biliverdin is the intermediate reduced to bilirubin by biliverdin reductase, not a transport molecule.

questions.topicName: Porphyrins and Iron Homeostasis (1 of 2)

questions.stem: A pharmacology student notes that the hepatic enzyme that attaches glucuronic acid to bilirubin also acts on certain drugs. This enzyme, UDP-glucuronosyltransferase, is best classified as part of which detoxification system?

explanation.summary: UDPGT is a phase II detoxification enzyme that conjugates bilirubin (and drugs) with glucuronic acid.
explanation.whyCorrect: In hepatocytes, unconjugated bilirubin is conjugated (covalently linked) with glucuronic acid by UDP-glucuronosyltransferase. This liver enzyme is part of the phase II enzyme system involved in detoxification, producing water-soluble conjugates that can be excreted.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Phase I cytochrome P450 enzymes carry out oxidation reactions and require heme; they do not perform glucuronidation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Heme oxygenase cleaves heme to biliverdin and is a degradation enzyme, not a conjugation enzyme.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Gut bacteria act on conjugated bilirubin to form urobilinogen; they do not glucuronidate.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Esterase hydrolysis is not the reaction catalyzed by UDPGT.

questions.topicName: Porphyrins and Iron Homeostasis (1 of 2)

questions.stem: A medical student asks why normal urine is yellow while normal stool is brown. Which of the following compounds is responsible for the typical yellowish tint of urine?

explanation.summary: Reabsorbed urobilinogen is converted to urobilin and secreted in urine, giving it its yellow color.
explanation.whyCorrect: Once bile containing conjugated bilirubin enters the gut, bacterial metabolism generates urobilinogen. Some urobilinogen is reabsorbed, converted to urobilin, and secreted in the urine, where it contributes the typical yellowish tint. The remainder is oxidized in the gut to stercobilin, which colors the stool brown.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Stercobilin is formed by intestinal bacteria from urobilinogen and gives stool its brown color.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Conjugated bilirubin appears in urine only abnormally, as in bile duct obstruction, where it darkens the urine.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Unconjugated bilirubin is albumin-bound and water-insoluble, so it is not excreted by the kidneys.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Biliverdin is the green intermediate formed by heme oxygenase in macrophages, not a urinary pigment.

questions.topicName: Porphyrins and Iron Homeostasis (1 of 2)

questions.stem: A clinical laboratory measures bilirubin by splitting a serum sample into two aliquots. The assay reagents are applied directly to the first aliquot, while a protein denaturant is added to the second before the reagents. Which of the following is the purpose of the denaturant?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Convert conjugated bilirubin back to the unconjugated form

choices.label: B
choices.text: Precipitate the conjugated fraction so only unconjugated is measured

choices.label: C
choices.text: Hydrolyze glucuronic acid from conjugated bilirubin

choices.label: D
choices.text: Free albumin-bound unconjugated bilirubin so the reagents can reach it

choices.label: E
choices.text: Isomerize the bilirubin into a more water-soluble configuration

explanation.summary: A denaturant removes albumin so the assay can detect unconjugated bilirubin, yielding the total; the first aliquot gives the direct (conjugated) value.
explanation.whyCorrect: The assay directly detects conjugated bilirubin because it is water-soluble and accessible to the reagents. Unconjugated bilirubin is bound by albumin, which prevents detection, so a protein denaturant is added to a second aliquot to remove the albumin and let the reagents reach the unconjugated bilirubin. Because the conjugated fraction is still detected too, this aliquot gives total bilirubin.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The denaturant does not change conjugation status; it removes the albumin barrier to detection.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The conjugated fraction remains present and detected in the denatured aliquot, which is why it yields the total rather than unconjugated alone.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Removing glucuronic acid is not the purpose; conjugated bilirubin is already detectable.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Isomerization to a water-soluble form is what phototherapy does in the skin, not what the laboratory denaturant does.

questions.topicName: Porphyrins and Iron Homeostasis (1 of 2)

questions.stem: A 22-year-old man with a hemolytic anemia has the following laboratory results: total bilirubin (TBIL) 4.2 mg/dL and direct bilirubin 0.4 mg/dL. Which of the following is his indirect bilirubin?

explanation.summary: Indirect bilirubin is derived mathematically: total bilirubin minus direct bilirubin.
explanation.whyCorrect: Two separate values are measured: direct (conjugated) bilirubin and total bilirubin (conjugated plus unconjugated). Indirect bilirubin is obtained indirectly by calculation: total bilirubin minus direct bilirubin equals indirect bilirubin, so 4.2 minus 0.4 equals 3.8 mg/dL. This elevated unconjugated fraction fits excessive RBC breakdown.

whyWrongByChoice.A: 0.4 mg/dL is the direct (conjugated) value, not the indirect fraction.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Adding the two values is incorrect; the total already includes the direct fraction.
whyWrongByChoice.C: 4.2 mg/dL is the total bilirubin, which includes both fractions.
whyWrongByChoice.D: 0.2 mg/dL is the upper reference limit for direct bilirubin, not the calculated indirect value.

questions.topicName: Porphyrins and Iron Homeostasis (1 of 2)

questions.stem: A 25-year-old woman with an autoimmune hemolytic anemia develops scleral icterus. Her stools are normally brown and her urine is its usual color. Which of the following laboratory patterns is most consistent with her jaundice?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Elevated indirect bilirubin with direct bilirubin below 0.2 mg/dL

choices.label: B
choices.text: Elevated direct bilirubin with reduced stercobilin in stool

choices.label: C
choices.text: Elevated direct bilirubin with bilirubin present in urine

choices.label: D
choices.text: Elevated indirect bilirubin with bilirubin present in urine

choices.label: E
choices.text: Normal total bilirubin with elevated urobilinogen only

explanation.summary: Hemolysis produces an unconjugated (indirect) hyperbilirubinemia; the conjugated fraction stays normal and no bilirubin reaches the urine.
explanation.whyCorrect: Unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia occurs through two mechanisms: excessive RBC breakdown (hemolysis) overwhelming conjugation, or reduced UDPGT activity. In hemolysis the liver still conjugates and excretes normally, so direct bilirubin stays within its reference range (below 0.2 mg/dL), stool remains brown, and the water-insoluble indirect bilirubin is not excreted by the kidneys.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Reduced stercobilin with a direct hyperbilirubinemia describes biliary obstruction, where stools become pale.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Direct hyperbilirubinemia with bilirubinuria is the post-hepatic pattern of obstruction, not hemolysis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Indirect bilirubin is albumin-bound and water-insoluble, so it is not excreted in the urine.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Hemolysis raises total bilirubin; a normal total would not produce visible jaundice.

questions.topicName: Porphyrins and Iron Homeostasis (1 of 2)

questions.stem: The parents of a child recently diagnosed with a hereditary hyperbilirubinemia ask about the chance that future children will be affected. Gilbert, Crigler-Najjar, Dubin-Johnson, and Rotor syndromes all share which of the following inheritance patterns?

explanation.summary: All of the hereditary hyperbilirubinemias are autosomal recessive; only Gilbert syndrome is common.
explanation.whyCorrect: The genetic disorders of bilirubin conjugation (Gilbert and Crigler-Najjar, with decreased or absent UDPGT) and excretion (Dubin-Johnson and Rotor, with limited excretion of conjugated bilirubin) are all autosomal recessive. Of these, only Gilbert syndrome is common.

whyWrongByChoice.A: X-linked recessive inheritance describes sideroblastic anemia from ALAS2 mutations, not the hyperbilirubinemias.
whyWrongByChoice.C: These disorders are recessive, requiring two defective alleles, not dominant.
whyWrongByChoice.D: None of the hereditary hyperbilirubinemias are mitochondrially inherited.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The hyperbilirubinemias are autosomal, not X-linked.

questions.topicName: Porphyrins and Iron Homeostasis (1 of 2)

questions.stem: A 16-year-old boy has had persistent mild jaundice since childhood with a predominantly unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia. Testing shows UDP-glucuronosyltransferase is present but markedly reduced; he has never had kernicterus. He is started on phenobarbital. Which of the following best explains how this drug lowers his bilirubin?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It isomerizes unconjugated bilirubin in skin capillaries

choices.label: B
choices.text: It inhibits heme oxygenase in splenic macrophages

choices.label: C
choices.text: It increases hepatic synthesis of the conjugating enzyme

choices.label: D
choices.text: It displaces bilirubin from albumin for renal excretion

choices.label: E
choices.text: It enhances MRP2-mediated export into bile

explanation.summary: Crigler-Najjar type 2 has reduced but present UDPGT and is treated with phenobarbital to increase liver enzyme synthesis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Crigler-Najjar type 2 is less serious than type 1, is sometimes diagnosed later in life, and has UDPGT that is present but reduced; kernicterus is rare. It is treated with phenobarbital to increase liver enzyme synthesis, boosting the residual conjugating capacity.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Isomerization of bilirubin in the skin is the mechanism of phototherapy, not of phenobarbital.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Blocking heme oxygenase is not how phenobarbital acts; the treatment aims to increase conjugation, not reduce bilirubin formation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Displacing bilirubin from albumin would free lipid-soluble unconjugated bilirubin, which is not renally excreted and could reach the brain.
whyWrongByChoice.E: MRP2 export is defective in Dubin-Johnson syndrome; it is not the target of phenobarbital in a conjugation defect.

questions.topicName: Porphyrins and Iron Homeostasis (1 of 2)

questions.stem: A 20-year-old man has mild, intermittent jaundice with a predominantly conjugated hyperbilirubinemia and normal liver enzymes. Ultrasound shows a normal-sized gallbladder, and a liver biopsy obtained for another reason shows normally colored tissue without pigment deposition. Which of the following is the most likely genetic basis of his condition?

explanation.summary: Rotor syndrome is a benign conjugated hyperbilirubinemia from SLCO1B1/SLCO1B3 mutations, without the black liver or small gallbladder of Dubin-Johnson.
explanation.whyCorrect: Rotor syndrome resembles Dubin-Johnson in that bilirubin is conjugated but cannot be correctly trafficked, giving a fairly benign conjugated hyperbilirubinemia. It presents without a black liver and with a normal gallbladder because the impact on excretion is indirect. It results from mutations in the SLCO1B1 and SLCO1B3 genes required for uptake or reuptake of bilirubin from the bile.

whyWrongByChoice.A: An ABCC2 (MRP2) mutation causes Dubin-Johnson syndrome, which features a glossy black liver and a markedly small gallbladder, both absent here.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Complete absence of UDPGT (Crigler-Najjar type 1) causes severe unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia in infancy, not a mild conjugated pattern.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A slight decrease in UDPGT (Gilbert syndrome) produces an unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia, not a conjugated one.
whyWrongByChoice.E: ALAS2 deficiency causes X-linked sideroblastic anemia and does not produce conjugated hyperbilirubinemia.

questions.topicName: Porphyrins and Iron Homeostasis (1 of 2)

questions.stem: A 24-year-old woman presents with recurrent attacks of severe, diffuse abdominal pain lasting several days, accompanied by nausea, tingling in her arms, and anxiety. The attacks tend to coincide with her menstrual cycle and a recent low-calorie diet. Her abdomen is soft with no peritoneal signs, and a urine sample left at the bedside darkens to a port-wine color on standing. Which of the following enzyme deficiencies is most likely responsible?

explanation.summary: Acute intermittent porphyria is caused by porphobilinogen deaminase deficiency and presents with neurovisceral attacks.
explanation.whyCorrect: Acute intermittent porphyria (AIP) results from deficiency of porphobilinogen deaminase (PBGD), causing accumulation of the neurotoxic intermediates ALA and PBG. This produces episodic severe abdominal pain, peripheral neuropathy, and neuropsychiatric symptoms, often triggered by fasting and hormonal changes, and the urine turns port-wine colored on standing or light exposure.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Ferrochelatase deficiency causes erythropoietic protoporphyria, which presents with painful cutaneous photosensitivity, not neurovisceral abdominal attacks.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase deficiency causes porphyria cutanea tarda, a cutaneous porphyria with blistering photosensitivity rather than acute abdominal pain.
whyWrongByChoice.D: ALA synthase is the rate-limiting enzyme that is upregulated in attacks; its deficiency does not cause AIP and would reduce, not increase, ALA and PBG.
whyWrongByChoice.E: ALA dehydrase deficiency is a different, far rarer porphyria and is not the classic cause of the described AIP presentation.

questions.topicName: Porphyrins and Iron Homeostasis (2 of 2)

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman is admitted with an acute attack of acute intermittent porphyria marked by severe abdominal pain and confusion. Which of the following is the most appropriate intervention to abort the attack, and what is its mechanism?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Oral iron supplementation, which restores heme synthesis

choices.label: B
choices.text: A barbiturate sedative, which calms neurovisceral symptoms

choices.label: C
choices.text: Intravenous glucose and hemin, which downregulate ALA synthase

choices.label: E
choices.text: High-dose vitamin C, which enhances porphyrin excretion

explanation.summary: Acute porphyria attacks are treated by suppressing ALA synthase with glucose or hemin.
explanation.whyCorrect: Acute attacks are managed with glucose or hemin infusions, which downregulate ALA synthase (ALAS1). This reduces production of the upstream neurotoxic intermediates ALA and PBG that drive the neurovisceral symptoms. Givosiran, an siRNA against the ALAS1 transcript, works by the same principle of lowering ALA synthase activity.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Iron is a substrate for the final ferrochelatase step but does not treat AIP; the defect is upstream at PBGD, and giving iron would not lower ALA and PBG.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Barbiturates induce cytochrome P450 enzymes and increase heme demand, which is a classic trigger that worsens AIP attacks.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Phlebotomy is a treatment for iron-overload states such as PCT or hemochromatosis, not for aborting an acute AIP attack.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Vitamin C aids dietary iron reduction and absorption but has no role in downregulating ALA synthase or aborting acute porphyria attacks.

questions.topicName: Porphyrins and Iron Homeostasis (2 of 2)

questions.stem: A 49-year-old man is referred to dermatology for painful, blistering lesions on the dorsum of both hands that appeared after a beach vacation, though he never developed a frank sunburn. Exam shows 1-2 cm blisters, some ruptured, with fragile skin over the hands and forearms. He drinks alcohol regularly, and labs reveal elevated liver enzymes. Which enzyme deficiency best explains his condition?

explanation.summary: Porphyria cutanea tarda is due to reduced uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase activity and causes delayed blistering photosensitivity.
explanation.whyCorrect: Porphyria cutanea tarda (PCT), the most common porphyria, results from deficiency or inhibition of uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase (UROD). Uroporphyrinogen III accumulates and is oxidized to photosensitive uroporphyrin, which deposits in skin and causes delayed blistering and skin fragility on sun-exposed areas. Alcohol use, iron overload, and hepatitis are well-known triggers, consistent with his elevated liver enzymes.

whyWrongByChoice.A: PBGD deficiency causes acute intermittent porphyria with neurovisceral attacks, not delayed cutaneous blistering.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Ferrochelatase deficiency causes erythropoietic protoporphyria, which produces painful burning photosensitivity that usually lacks blistering and presents in childhood.
whyWrongByChoice.C: ALA synthase is the rate-limiting regulatory enzyme; PCT is notably not exacerbated by upregulation of this pathway.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Uroporphyrinogen III synthase acts one step earlier and is not the enzyme implicated in PCT.

questions.topicName: Porphyrins and Iron Homeostasis (2 of 2)

questions.stem: A 6-year-old boy develops intense burning, itching, and swelling of the skin within minutes of sun exposure, but rarely forms blisters. Over years, the backs of his hands have developed a waxy, pebbled thickening. Laboratory testing shows elevated protoporphyrin in red blood cells and dark-colored stool. Which enzyme is partially deficient?

explanation.summary: Erythropoietic protoporphyria results from partial ferrochelatase deficiency, causing painful photosensitivity with elevated RBC protoporphyrin.
explanation.whyCorrect: Erythropoietic protoporphyria (EPP) is caused by partial deficiency of ferrochelatase, the enzyme that inserts iron into protoporphyrin IX to form heme. Excess protoporphyrin accumulates in red blood cells, skin, and liver, generating reactive oxygen species on light exposure that cause painful, non-blistering photosensitivity beginning in childhood. Because protoporphyrin is water-insoluble, it is excreted in stool, giving it a dark color, and diagnosis relies on elevated RBC protoporphyrin.

whyWrongByChoice.B: UROD deficiency causes PCT, which produces frank blistering and skin fragility rather than the burning, non-blistering pain of EPP.
whyWrongByChoice.C: PBGD deficiency causes acute intermittent porphyria with neurovisceral attacks, not childhood cutaneous photosensitivity.
whyWrongByChoice.D: ALA dehydrase deficiency is an early cytosolic-step defect and would not cause protoporphyrin to accumulate in red cells.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Coproporphyrinogen oxidase acts earlier in the pathway and does not produce the isolated protoporphyrin accumulation seen in EPP.

questions.topicName: Porphyrins and Iron Homeostasis (2 of 2)

questions.stem: A researcher studies how dietary non-heme iron crosses the apical membrane of duodenal enterocytes. Non-heme iron in food is largely ferric (Fe3+) and cannot be taken up in that form. Which of the following correctly pairs the step with the protein responsible?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Fe3+ is oxidized to Fe2+ by hephaestin, then enters via ferroportin-1

choices.label: B
choices.text: Fe3+ binds transferrin at the lumen and enters via the transferrin receptor

choices.label: C
choices.text: Fe3+ enters directly via ferroportin-1 without a change in oxidation state

choices.label: D
choices.text: Fe3+ is stored as ferritin at the apical surface before absorption

choices.label: E
choices.text: Fe3+ is reduced to Fe2+ by duodenal cytochrome B, then enters via DMT-1

explanation.summary: Dietary Fe3+ is reduced to Fe2+ by duodenal cytochrome B and imported by DMT-1.
explanation.whyCorrect: Only ferrous iron (Fe2+) can be absorbed. Non-heme dietary Fe3+ is reduced to Fe2+ by the vitamin C-dependent duodenal cytochrome B on the apical surface, and this ferrous iron is then transported into the enterocyte by the divalent metal transporter-1 (DMT-1).

whyWrongByChoice.A: Hephaestin oxidizes Fe2+ to Fe3+ on the basal side after export; it does not act at apical uptake, and ferroportin exports rather than imports iron.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Transferrin transports iron in the blood as Fe3+; it is not the mechanism for luminal uptake across the apical enterocyte membrane.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Ferroportin-1 exports iron from the basolateral membrane into portal blood, not import at the apical surface, and iron must first be reduced.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Ferritin is an intracellular storage protein, not an apical uptake mechanism for luminal iron.

questions.topicName: Porphyrins and Iron Homeostasis (2 of 2)

questions.stem: A 9-month-old infant has microcytic anemia unresponsive to oral iron. Genetic testing reveals a mutation in SLC11A2, the gene encoding DMT-1. Which of the following best explains the anemia in this patient?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Iron is trapped in endosomal vesicles and cannot be released

choices.label: B
choices.text: Hepcidin is overexpressed, degrading all ferroportin

choices.label: C
choices.text: Transferrin cannot be synthesized by the liver

choices.label: D
choices.text: Ferrochelatase cannot insert iron into protoporphyrin IX

choices.label: E
choices.text: Excess iron is deposited as hemosiderin in macrophages

explanation.summary: A DMT-1 (SLC11A2) mutation traps iron intracellularly, causing functional iron deficiency and microcytic anemia.
explanation.whyCorrect: DMT-1 normally moves ferrous iron into cells and out of endosomes. When SLC11A2 is mutated, iron becomes trapped in endosomal vesicles and cannot be released to bind transferrin or be used in biosynthetic reactions. The resulting reduction in heme and globin synthesis produces a microcytic anemia.

whyWrongByChoice.B: The defect is in the iron transporter DMT-1, not in hepcidin; hepcidin overexpression is not the mechanism described in this inherited mutation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Transferrin is synthesized normally by the liver; the problem is that iron cannot reach transferrin because it is trapped in vesicles.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Ferrochelatase deficiency causes EPP, a porphyria, not a microcytic anemia from an SLC11A2 mutation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Hemosiderin deposition reflects iron overload, the opposite of the functional iron deficiency caused by DMT-1 loss.

questions.topicName: Porphyrins and Iron Homeostasis (2 of 2)

questions.stem: After ferroportin exports iron across the basolateral membrane of an enterocyte, the iron must be loaded onto plasma transferrin for transport. Because transferrin binds only ferric iron, which protein performs the required conversion?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Duodenal cytochrome B, a vitamin C-dependent reductase

explanation.summary: Hephaestin, a copper-dependent ferroxidase, oxidizes exported Fe2+ to Fe3+ so it can bind transferrin.
explanation.whyCorrect: Ferroportin exports iron in the ferrous (Fe2+) state, but transferrin transports only ferric (Fe3+) iron. Hephaestin is a copper-dependent ferroxidase that oxidizes the exported Fe2+ to Fe3+, enabling it to bind plasma transferrin for transport.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Duodenal cytochrome B reduces Fe3+ to Fe2+ at the apical surface for uptake; it performs the opposite reaction from what is needed here.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hepcidin regulates iron export by degrading ferroportin; it does not change the oxidation state of iron.
whyWrongByChoice.D: DMT-1 transports ferrous iron across membranes but has no ferroxidase activity to load transferrin.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Ferritin stores iron intracellularly and does not oxidize iron for transferrin loading.

questions.topicName: Porphyrins and Iron Homeostasis (2 of 2)

questions.stem: A hematology team reviews cases of hereditary hemochromatosis to identify the common consequence of an HFE gene mutation. Which of the following best describes the downstream effect of HFE dysfunction that produces iron overload?

explanation.summary: HFE mutations lower hepcidin activity, prolonging ferroportin function and driving iron overload.
explanation.whyCorrect: In hereditary hemochromatosis, an HFE mutation renders hepatocytes unable to produce adequately functioning hepcidin. Because hepcidin normally degrades ferroportin, reduced hepcidin allows ferroportin to remain active, prolonging iron export and increasing dietary iron absorption and release from macrophages. Homozygotes can absorb two to four times more iron than normal.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Increased hepcidin would degrade ferroportin and cause iron deficiency, the opposite of hemochromatosis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Iron overload lowers TIBC because most transferrin is already saturated with iron, so TIBC does not increase.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Serum iron is elevated in iron overload, not decreased.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Iron absorption is increased in hemochromatosis, not decreased, because ferroportin export is prolonged.

questions.topicName: Porphyrins and Iron Homeostasis (2 of 2)

questions.stem: A 47-year-old man reports fatigue, joint pain in his hands, and progressively bronzed skin. He was recently diagnosed with diabetes mellitus, and exam reveals hepatomegaly. Iron studies show markedly elevated ferritin and transferrin saturation. Which of the following best accounts for the combination of skin pigmentation and diabetes seen in this patient?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Uroporphyrin deposition generating reactive oxygen species in the skin

choices.label: B
choices.text: Accumulation of ALA and PBG damaging peripheral nerves

choices.label: C
choices.text: Iron overload causing hyperpigmentation and suppressed insulin release

choices.label: D
choices.text: Protoporphyrin accumulation in red blood cells and bile

choices.label: E
choices.text: Hepcidin excess trapping iron within macrophages

explanation.summary: Hemochromatosis causes 'bronze diabetes' from iron-driven hyperpigmentation plus pancreatic and hepatic dysfunction.
explanation.whyCorrect: Excess iron accumulates in and damages the liver, heart, skin, and pancreas. In the skin it drives hyperpigmentation (increased melanocyte-stimulating hormone effect plus hemosiderin deposition), the liver develops cirrhosis leading to insulin resistance, and the pancreas shows decreased insulin production. The combined effect is the classic 'bronze diabetes' of hemochromatosis, supported here by high ferritin and transferrin saturation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Uroporphyrin-mediated skin damage occurs in porphyria cutanea tarda, which does not cause diabetes or the elevated iron studies described.
whyWrongByChoice.B: ALA and PBG neurotoxicity causes the acute neurovisceral attacks of AIP, not bronze skin with diabetes.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Protoporphyrin accumulation characterizes EPP, which produces photosensitivity and gallstones, not diabetes and hyperpigmentation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Hepcidin excess causes iron sequestration and anemia of chronic disease, the opposite of the iron-overload picture here.

questions.topicName: Porphyrins and Iron Homeostasis (2 of 2)

questions.stem: A 60-year-old postmenopausal woman is found to have previously undiagnosed hereditary hemochromatosis. Compared with an unaffected person, which of the following patterns of iron studies would you most expect?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Serum iron increased, serum ferritin decreased, TIBC increased, transferrin saturation decreased

choices.label: B
choices.text: Serum iron decreased, serum ferritin increased, TIBC increased, transferrin saturation increased

choices.label: C
choices.text: Serum iron decreased, serum ferritin decreased, TIBC increased, transferrin saturation decreased

choices.label: D
choices.text: Serum iron increased, serum ferritin increased, TIBC decreased, transferrin saturation increased

choices.label: E
choices.text: Serum iron increased, serum ferritin increased, TIBC increased, transferrin saturation decreased

explanation.summary: Iron overload raises serum iron, ferritin, and transferrin saturation while lowering TIBC.
explanation.whyCorrect: In iron overload, excess circulating iron raises serum iron, and excess tissue stores spill ferritin into the serum. The abundance of iron saturates transferrin, raising transferrin saturation, while the amount of available unbound transferrin (TIBC) falls. Thus serum iron up, ferritin up, TIBC down, and transferrin saturation up.

whyWrongByChoice.A: This mixes overload and deficiency findings; ferritin and transferrin saturation should be increased, and TIBC decreased, in overload.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Decreased serum iron and increased TIBC are features of iron deficiency, not overload.
whyWrongByChoice.C: This is the classic iron-deficiency pattern, the opposite of hemochromatosis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: TIBC decreases and transferrin saturation increases in overload; both directions here are wrong.

questions.topicName: Porphyrins and Iron Homeostasis (2 of 2)

questions.stem: A 55-year-old woman with long-standing rheumatoid arthritis has a normocytic anemia. Labs show low serum iron, low TIBC, and an elevated serum ferritin. Which of the following best explains this pattern?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Chronic blood loss depleting total body iron stores

choices.label: B
choices.text: IL-6-driven inflammation raises hepcidin, reducing iron absorption

choices.label: C
choices.text: An HFE mutation lowering hepcidin activity

choices.label: D
choices.text: Deficiency of duodenal cytochrome B impairing dietary iron reduction

explanation.summary: Anemia of chronic disease reflects IL-6-induced hepcidin sequestering iron, giving low serum iron but high ferritin.
explanation.whyCorrect: Inflammation, classically via the IL-6 cytokine, induces hepcidin. Elevated hepcidin degrades ferroportin, reducing iron absorption in the gut and iron release from macrophage stores. This protective sequestration lowers circulating serum iron and TIBC while ferritin (reflecting retained tissue stores) is normal or elevated, producing anemia of chronic disease.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Chronic blood loss causes true iron deficiency with low ferritin and high TIBC, not the high ferritin and low TIBC seen here.
whyWrongByChoice.C: An HFE mutation lowers hepcidin and causes iron overload, which would raise serum iron and transferrin saturation, not lower serum iron.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Duodenal cytochrome B deficiency would impair absorption but does not explain the elevated ferritin of an inflammatory state.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Ferrochelatase deficiency causes erythropoietic protoporphyria, a photosensitivity disorder, not this inflammatory iron-sequestration pattern.

questions.topicName: Porphyrins and Iron Homeostasis (2 of 2)

questions.stem: A cell biologist examines how iron levels control ferritin production. Ferritin mRNA contains an iron response element (IRE) in its 5' untranslated region, which can be bound by iron regulatory protein (IRP). In a state of low intracellular iron, what happens to ferritin synthesis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: IRP dissociates from the IRE, increasing ferritin synthesis

choices.label: B
choices.text: IRP binds the IRE and stabilizes the mRNA, increasing ferritin synthesis

choices.label: C
choices.text: Ferritin is degraded into hemosiderin within lysosomes

choices.label: D
choices.text: Hepcidin binds the IRE and enhances ferritin translation

choices.label: E
choices.text: IRP binds the IRE and blocks translation, decreasing ferritin synthesis

explanation.summary: In low iron, IRP binds the 5' IRE of ferritin mRNA and blocks its translation.
explanation.whyCorrect: IRP binds IRE-containing transcripts when intracellular iron is low. For ferritin mRNA, the IRE sits in the 5' untranslated region, so IRP binding physically blocks translation, decreasing ferritin synthesis. This is appropriate because a cell that is iron-poor should not waste resources building an iron storage protein.

whyWrongByChoice.A: IRP dissociates from the IRE when iron is high, not low; it is bound in the low-iron state.
whyWrongByChoice.B: IRP binding stabilizes mRNA for the transferrin receptor (3' IRE), but for ferritin (5' IRE) it blocks translation rather than stabilizing it.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hemosiderin forms from denatured ferritin in iron excess, which is unrelated to the low-iron translational control described.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Hepcidin is a hormone that regulates ferroportin; it does not bind iron response elements or control ferritin translation.

questions.topicName: Porphyrins and Iron Homeostasis (2 of 2)

questions.stem: A 26-year-old woman presents with 3 days of severe, diffuse abdominal pain, vomiting, and new anxiety. Her abdomen is soft, and imaging is unremarkable. She has had similar episodes in the past that were never explained. Acute intermittent porphyria is suspected. Which of the following laboratory findings alone is sufficient to establish this diagnosis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Elevated protoporphyrin in red blood cells

explanation.summary: The diagnosis of AIP may be established solely with elevated urinary porphobilinogen.
explanation.whyCorrect: Without functional porphobilinogen deaminase, porphobilinogen (PBG) accumulates and is excreted in the urine. Because this intermediate is specific to the block in AIP, the diagnosis may be established solely with elevated urinary PBG; measuring elevated urinary ALA and PBG is key to the workup of a suspected acute neurovisceral attack.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Elevated red blood cell protoporphyrin confirms erythropoietic protoporphyria, a cutaneous porphyria, not AIP.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Elevated urinary uroporphyrin (with heptacarboxylporphyrin) is the diagnostic confirmation for porphyria cutanea tarda, not AIP.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Serum ferritin reflects tissue iron stores and rises in iron overload; it says nothing about heme intermediates in AIP.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Protoporphyrin is water-insoluble and is excreted in stool in EPP; it is not the accumulated intermediate in AIP.

questions.topicName: Porphyrins and Iron Homeostasis (2 of 2)

questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman with genetically confirmed acute intermittent porphyria and frequent disabling attacks undergoes liver transplantation from an unaffected donor. After transplantation her attacks cease entirely, even though her red blood cells still carry the mutation. Which of the following best explains why replacing the liver cures her disease?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The erythroid PBGD isoform in bone marrow is replaced by donor cells

choices.label: B
choices.text: The donor liver clears accumulated uroporphyrin from the skin

choices.label: C
choices.text: The donor liver restores hepcidin production and normalizes iron stores

choices.label: D
choices.text: Symptoms arise from hepatocytes being unable to make heme for cytochrome P450s

choices.label: E
choices.text: The donor liver supplies ferrochelatase to insert iron into protoporphyrin IX

explanation.summary: AIP symptoms come from the non-erythroid PBGD isoform in hepatocytes failing to make heme for cytochrome P450s, so a liver transplant cures the disease.
explanation.whyCorrect: The PBGD gene gives rise to two isoforms by alternative splicing: an erythroid isoform in red blood cells and a non-erythroid isoform in all other cells, including hepatocytes.
