The symptoms of AIP are due to the inability of hepatocytes to make heme for cytochrome P450s, which drives ALA and PBG accumulation. This is evidenced by patients being cured after receiving a liver transplant from an unaffected donor, even though their erythroid cells are unchanged.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A liver transplant does not replace bone marrow; the erythroid isoform is unaffected, which is exactly why the cure points to the liver as the source of disease.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Uroporphyrin accumulation in skin is the mechanism of porphyria cutanea tarda, not AIP.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hepcidin and iron stores are not the driver of AIP; hepcidin dysregulation is relevant to PCT and hemochromatosis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Ferrochelatase is the enzyme deficient in erythropoietic protoporphyria, not the enzyme at fault in AIP.

questions.topicName: Porphyrins and Iron Homeostasis (2 of 2)

questions.stem: A 29-year-old woman with known acute intermittent porphyria is admitted with severe abdominal pain and peripheral neuropathy two days after a weekend of heavy alcohol consumption. Which of the following best explains how alcohol precipitated her attack?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Alcohol stimulates CYP2E1, increasing hepatic heme demand

choices.label: C
choices.text: Alcohol oxidizes uroporphomethene to a UROD inhibitor

choices.label: D
choices.text: Alcohol suppresses hepcidin and raises hepatic iron

choices.label: E
choices.text: Alcohol blocks ferrochelatase in the mitochondria

explanation.summary: Alcohol triggers AIP attacks because it stimulates CYP2E1, raising heme demand and worsening ALA and PBG buildup.
explanation.whyCorrect: AIP attacks are precipitated by factors that increase heme demand, especially medications that induce cytochrome P450 enzymes, fasting, infections, and hormonal changes. Because alcohol consumption stimulates CYP2E1, it can be a major trigger: the liver attempts to make more heme for the induced P450, and the block at PBGD causes the neurotoxic intermediates ALA and PBG to accumulate further.

whyWrongByChoice.B: The PBGD deficiency is genetic; alcohol acts by raising heme demand upstream, not by inhibiting the enzyme directly.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Iron-mediated oxidation of uroporphomethene inhibiting UROD is the mechanism described for porphyria cutanea tarda, not AIP.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Decreased hepcidin with increased hepatic iron is a feature of PCT; it does not explain an acute neurovisceral attack.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Ferrochelatase is the enzyme deficient in EPP and is not the target of alcohol in AIP.

questions.topicName: Porphyrins and Iron Homeostasis (2 of 2)

questions.stem: A patient with recurrent acute intermittent porphyria attacks is being considered for givosiran, though the cost is prohibitive. Which of the following best describes the mechanism of this therapy?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Chelation of accumulated ALA and PBG in plasma

choices.label: C
choices.text: siRNA directed against the ALAS1 transcript

choices.label: D
choices.text: Competitive inhibition of cytochrome P450 enzymes

explanation.summary: Givosiran is an siRNA against the ALAS1 transcript that eliminates the ALAS1 enzyme and dampens heme synthesis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Treatment of an AIP attack aims to dampen heme synthesis by negatively inhibiting ALAS-1 with glucose or hemin. Givosiran is a newer siRNA-based therapy against the ALAS1 transcript; by eliminating the ALAS1 enzyme it impedes heme synthesis and the production of ALA and PBG, but at this stage it is cost prohibitive for many AIP patients.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Givosiran does not replace the deficient PBGD enzyme; it lowers flux into the pathway upstream.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Givosiran does not bind or chelate ALA and PBG; chelation is a strategy for iron overload, not porphyria.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Givosiran does not act on cytochrome P450 enzymes; avoiding P450 inducers is a trigger-avoidance strategy, not the drug's mechanism.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Givosiran reduces production of PBG rather than increasing its excretion.

questions.topicName: Porphyrins and Iron Homeostasis (2 of 2)

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man with porphyria cutanea tarda is found to have markedly increased hepatic iron. His physician explains that the excess iron worsens his porphyria by reducing uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase activity. Which of the following best describes how iron does this?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Iron displaces zinc from the active site of the enzyme

choices.label: B
choices.text: Iron raises hepcidin, which targets the enzyme for degradation

choices.label: C
choices.text: Iron induces cytochrome P450, increasing flux past the enzyme

choices.label: D
choices.text: Iron binds uroporphyrinogen III and blocks substrate access

choices.label: E
choices.text: Iron oxidizes uroporphomethene, which inhibits the enzyme

explanation.summary: In PCT, hepatic iron oxidizes uroporphomethene, and the oxidized compound inhibits uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase.
explanation.whyCorrect: Increased hepatic iron is seen in porphyria cutanea tarda, possibly due to decreased hepcidin production, which increases gut iron uptake and liver storage. This increased iron is thought to oxidize a compound called uroporphomethene in the liver, which then inhibits uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase in its oxidized form. This is why iron plays a particularly important role in PCT and why phlebotomy to reduce iron stores is a treatment.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Displacement of a metal cofactor is not the described mechanism; iron acts by generating an inhibitor of UROD.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Hepcidin is decreased in PCT, not increased, and hepcidin degrades ferroportin, not UROD.
whyWrongByChoice.C: PCT is not exacerbated by upregulation of the heme synthesis pathway or P450 inducers, unlike AIP.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Iron does not act by binding the substrate; it oxidizes uroporphomethene into an enzyme inhibitor.

questions.topicName: Porphyrins and Iron Homeostasis (2 of 2)

questions.stem: A 50-year-old man with porphyria cutanea tarda develops a seizure disorder and is started on a barbiturate, a strong inducer of cytochrome P450 enzymes. Which of the following is the most likely effect of this medication on his porphyria?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Precipitation of an acute neurovisceral attack

choices.label: B
choices.text: No significant exacerbation of his cutaneous disease

choices.label: D
choices.text: Urine turning port-wine colored on standing

choices.label: E
choices.text: New onset of painful non-blistering photosensitivity

explanation.summary: Unlike AIP, PCT is not exacerbated by upregulation of the heme synthesis pathway, including P450 inducers.
explanation.whyCorrect: AIP attacks are precipitated by drugs that induce cytochrome P450 because they increase heme demand and worsen ALA and PBG buildup. PCT behaves differently: it is not exacerbated by upregulation of the heme synthesis pathway, including the activity of P450 inducers. PCT is instead driven by triggers such as alcohol, smoking, iron overload, estrogens, and hepatitis B or C or HIV infection.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Neurovisceral attacks are the hallmark of AIP; PCT is a cutaneous porphyria and P450 inducers do not precipitate attacks in it.
whyWrongByChoice.C: PCT is not worsened by P450 induction, so no increase in blistering is expected from this medication.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Port-wine urine reflects PBG and ALA accumulation in AIP; PCT urine is tea-colored from uroporphyrins and does not change with P450 induction.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Painful non-blistering photosensitivity characterizes erythropoietic protoporphyria, not a drug effect in PCT.

questions.topicName: Porphyrins and Iron Homeostasis (2 of 2)

questions.stem: A 52-year-old man is diagnosed with porphyria cutanea tarda after urinary uroporphyrin and heptacarboxylporphyrin are found to be elevated. He is counseled to stop drinking and to protect his skin from the sun. Which of the following is an appropriate additional treatment to reduce his porphyrin burden?

explanation.summary: PCT is treated with phlebotomy to reduce iron stores or low-dose hydroxychloroquine to enhance porphyrin excretion.
explanation.whyCorrect: Management of porphyria cutanea tarda often includes phlebotomy to reduce iron stores or low-dose hydroxychloroquine to enhance porphyrin excretion, along with avoiding alcohol and protecting the skin from sun exposure. Reducing iron is important because hepatic iron oxidizes uroporphomethene into an inhibitor of uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Hemin infusion downregulates ALA synthase to abort acute AIP attacks; PCT is not driven by pathway upregulation.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Glucose infusion is a treatment for acute AIP attacks, not for the cutaneous disease of PCT.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Givosiran is an siRNA against ALAS1 for AIP; it is not a PCT therapy.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Iron overload is a trigger of PCT and directly impairs UROD activity, so iron supplementation would worsen the disease.

questions.topicName: Porphyrins and Iron Homeostasis (2 of 2)

questions.stem: A 58-year-old woman develops fragile skin and blisters on the backs of her hands and face over several months, without preceding sunburn. Her urine is tea-colored, and urinary uroporphyrin and heptacarboxylporphyrin are elevated. Which of the following elements of her history is most likely to have precipitated this disorder?

explanation.summary: PCT can be inherited or acquired and is triggered by liver conditions such as hepatitis C, alcohol use, and iron overload.
explanation.whyCorrect: The tea-colored urine and elevated urinary uroporphyrin and heptacarboxylporphyrin confirm porphyria cutanea tarda. The UROD defect can be inherited or acquired and is often triggered by liver conditions such as hepatitis C, alcohol use, or iron overload. Other recognized triggers include smoking, estrogens, hepatitis B, and HIV infection, all of which increase uroporphyrin production.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Fasting increases heme demand and triggers acute intermittent porphyria attacks; it is not a PCT trigger.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Barbiturates induce cytochrome P450 and precipitate AIP attacks, but PCT is not exacerbated by P450 inducers.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Iron overload, not iron deficiency, triggers PCT because iron directly impairs UROD function.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Infections are listed as triggers of acute AIP attacks; the infections relevant to PCT are hepatitis B or C and HIV.

questions.topicName: Porphyrins and Iron Homeostasis (2 of 2)

questions.stem: A 47-year-old man with porphyria cutanea tarda is seen for follow-up. In addition to the blistering and skin fragility on his hands, which of the following additional findings is characteristically associated with his disorder?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Hook-like osteophytes of the hand joints

explanation.summary: Onycholysis, painless detachment of the nail from the nailbed, is an associated symptom of porphyria cutanea tarda.
explanation.whyCorrect: PCT causes photosensitivity with blistering, skin fragility, and hyperpigmentation on sun-exposed areas like the hands and face; over time the skin may scar or change texture. Another symptom associated with porphyria cutanea tarda is onycholysis, the painless detachment of the nail from the nailbed.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Hook-like osteophytes from the radial ends of the hand joints are a feature of hemochromatosis arthropathy, not PCT.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Gallstones are common in erythropoietic protoporphyria because protoporphyrin accumulates in bile.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Peripheral neuropathy and muscle weakness are neurovisceral features of acute intermittent porphyria.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Testicular atrophy and gynecomastia reflect hypogonadism from iron deposition in hemochromatosis.

questions.topicName: Porphyrins and Iron Homeostasis (2 of 2)

questions.stem: A 15-year-old boy with lifelong painful burning of the skin after brief sun exposure presents with right upper quadrant pain and is found to have gallstones. His red blood cell protoporphyrin level is markedly elevated. Which of the following best explains the development of his gallstones?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Uroporphyrin deposition in the gallbladder wall

choices.label: D
choices.text: Neurotoxic ALA and PBG impairing biliary motility

explanation.summary: Gallstones are common in EPP because water-insoluble protoporphyrin accumulates in bile.
explanation.whyCorrect: Painful photosensitivity from childhood with elevated red blood cell protoporphyrin indicates erythropoietic protoporphyria. Excess protoporphyrin accumulates in red blood cells, skin, and liver, and because it is insoluble in water it is excreted through the bile into stool. Gallstones are common in EPP due to protoporphyrin accumulation in the bile, leading to biliary complications.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Uroporphyrin is the photosensitive intermediate of porphyria cutanea tarda and is not the compound accumulating in EPP.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Hemosiderin deposition reflects iron overload, which is not the mechanism of biliary disease in EPP.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Ineffective erythropoiesis causes secondary hemochromatosis; EPP is a ferrochelatase defect, not an iron overload state.
whyWrongByChoice.D: ALA and PBG neurotoxicity underlies the neurovisceral attacks of AIP, not gallstone formation in EPP.

questions.topicName: Porphyrins and Iron Homeostasis (2 of 2)

questions.stem: The parents of an 8-year-old girl with erythropoietic protoporphyria ask why her urine has always looked normal even though her doctor said porphyrias cause discolored urine. Which of the following best explains this observation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Protoporphyrin is fully converted to heme before it can be excreted

choices.label: B
choices.text: Protoporphyrin is retained entirely within circulating red blood cells

choices.label: C
choices.text: Protoporphyrin is metabolized by the liver into a colorless product

choices.label: D
choices.text: Protoporphyrin is water-insoluble and is excreted in the stool

choices.label: E
choices.text: Protoporphyrin is destroyed by sunlight before reaching the kidneys

explanation.summary: In EPP, water-insoluble protoporphyrin is excreted in stool, so urine changes are mild or absent while stool is dark.
explanation.whyCorrect: Protoporphyrin is insoluble in water and thus is excreted in the stool, giving it a dark color. Urine color changes in EPP may be mild or absent, which makes stool color and photosensitivity the key diagnostic clues; the diagnosis is confirmed by measuring elevated protoporphyrin in red blood cells. This contrasts with AIP (port-wine urine from PBG and ALA) and PCT (tea-colored urine from uroporphyrins).

whyWrongByChoice.A: The ferrochelatase deficiency prevents iron insertion, so excess protoporphyrin is not converted to heme.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Protoporphyrin accumulates in red blood cells, skin, and liver and is excreted via bile into stool; it is not confined to red cells.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Protoporphyrin is not metabolized to a colorless compound; it is eliminated intact through the biliary route.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Sunlight causes protoporphyrin to generate reactive oxygen species in skin; it does not destroy the compound before excretion.

questions.topicName: Porphyrins and Iron Homeostasis (2 of 2)

questions.stem: A 62-year-old woman is diagnosed with hereditary hemochromatosis. Her brother, who carries the same HFE genotype, was diagnosed with the same disease at age 44. Which of the following best explains why she developed clinical disease later than her brother?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Estrogen enhances hepcidin production in premenopausal women

choices.label: B
choices.text: Menstrual blood loss offset her excess iron absorption for decades

choices.label: C
choices.text: Women absorb a smaller fraction of dietary iron than men

choices.label: D
choices.text: Women store excess iron preferentially as hemosiderin

choices.label: E
choices.text: Transferrin receptor expression is lower in female tissues

explanation.summary: Menstrual iron loss balances the excess absorption of hemochromatosis, so women present in their 50s-60s rather than 40s-50s.
explanation.whyCorrect: Hereditary hemochromatosis is classically seen in middle-aged men (40s-50s) but manifests in women at slightly older ages (50s-60s). A person homozygous for the HFE mutation absorbs two to four times more iron than normal, so over 20 years a man can store up to 20 g. In women, menstruation adds a balancing variable: from their early teens to mid-to-late 50s they lose up to 60-100 mL of blood per cycle, so it takes 30-40 years to store 20 g of iron because iron lost through menstruation balances the excess absorbed.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The brick attributes the delay to menstrual blood loss, not to a sex-hormone effect on hepcidin; HFE dysfunction lowers hepcidin activity in both sexes.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The HFE mutation increases absorption two to four times in homozygotes regardless of sex; the difference lies in iron loss, not uptake.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Hemosiderin forms in iron excess in both sexes and does not protect against organ damage or delay disease.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Transferrin receptor expression depends on tissue iron need, not on sex, and is not the reason for later presentation.

questions.topicName: Porphyrins and Iron Homeostasis (2 of 2)

questions.stem: A healthy adult contains roughly 3-4 grams of total body iron. Which of the following compartments holds the largest share of this iron?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Ferritin and hemosiderin in the liver

explanation.summary: About 70% of all bodily iron is contained in hemoglobin.
explanation.whyCorrect: Adults contain 3-4 grams of iron in total, and 70% of all bodily iron is contained in hemoglobin (about 1800 mg in red blood cells). The liver holds roughly 1000 mg as ferritin and hemosiderin, reticuloendothelial cells about 600 mg, and muscle myoglobin and bone erythropoiesis about 300 mg each. Predominant non-heme bound iron sits in iron-sulfur clusters within electron transport chain enzymes, and only about 3 mg circulates bound to transferrin at any time.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The liver is the major storage organ at about 1000 mg, but that is well under the hemoglobin pool.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Muscle myoglobin, cytochromes, and iron enzymes hold only about 300 mg.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Reticuloendothelial macrophage stores are about 600 mg, a third of the hemoglobin pool.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Plasma transferrin carries only about 3 mg of iron at any time, the smallest pool despite its transport importance.

questions.topicName: Porphyrins and Iron Homeostasis (2 of 2)

questions.stem: A 31-year-old woman in her second trimester of pregnancy asks how her iron needs compare with before she was pregnant, when she had regular menstrual cycles. Which of the following best describes her change in daily iron requirement?

choices.label: A
choices.text: About 2-3 mg/day more than a non-pregnant woman

choices.label: B
choices.text: About 8-18 mg/day more than a non-pregnant woman

choices.label: C
choices.text: About 1 mg/day less, because menstruation has stopped

choices.label: D
choices.text: No net change, because fetal demand equals menstrual loss

choices.label: E
choices.text: About 5 times higher, the same as with menorrhagia

explanation.summary: Pregnancy costs about 650 mg of iron, an additional 2-3 mg/day above baseline loss.
explanation.whyCorrect: Estimated daily iron loss is about 1 mg/day in non-menstruating females and males; menstruating females lose an additional 1 mg per cycle, and menorrhagia causes roughly 5 times higher loss. Pregnancy requires about 650 mg of iron per pregnancy, which works out to an additional 2-3 mg/day to supply iron to the growing fetus. This is why premenopausal and pregnant women are more likely than men to suffer iron deficiency.

whyWrongByChoice.B: 8-18 mg is the total adult RDA for dietary iron, not the added daily requirement of pregnancy; only 10-20% of dietary iron is absorbed.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Although menstruation stops, the fetal iron demand far exceeds the roughly 1 mg per cycle that menstruation costs.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Menstrual loss is only about 1 mg per cycle, whereas pregnancy adds 2-3 mg every day, so there is a large net increase.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The 5-fold increase in loss describes menorrhagia, not pregnancy.

questions.topicName: Porphyrins and Iron Homeostasis (2 of 2)

questions.stem: A 61-year-old man who eats a typical Western diet including red meat is found to have a microcytic anemia with low serum iron, low ferritin, and elevated TIBC. He takes no medications and has no known inflammatory disease. Which of the following is the most appropriate next consideration?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Inadequate dietary intake of heme iron

choices.label: C
choices.text: Inherited deficiency of duodenal cytochrome B

choices.label: D
choices.text: Occult bleeding from a gastrointestinal ulcer or colon cancer

choices.label: E
choices.text: Homozygous HFE mutation lowering hepcidin activity

explanation.summary: A man on a Western diet with iron deficiency anemia should be evaluated for gastrointestinal blood loss.
explanation.whyCorrect: The iron lost by adult men (about 1 mg/day) through desquamation of skin and losses in bile, feces, urine, and sweat is readily replaced by dietary iron, so men are not as likely to suffer iron deficiency as premenopausal women, who also lose iron through menstruation and pregnancy. If a man eating a Western diet has iron deficiency anemia, his physician should suspect bleeding from the gastrointestinal tract as a result of ulcers or colon cancer. His low ferritin and high TIBC confirm true iron deficiency.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A Western diet with red meat supplies ample heme iron, which is absorbed as Fe2+ via the heme transporter; dietary lack is unlikely.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Hepcidin excess in anemia of chronic disease produces low serum iron with low TIBC and normal or high ferritin, not the low ferritin and high TIBC seen here.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Duodenal cytochrome B deficiency is not a described cause of adult-onset iron deficiency; the first suspicion in a man is blood loss.
whyWrongByChoice.E: An HFE mutation causes iron overload with high ferritin and low TIBC, the opposite of this pattern.

questions.topicName: Porphyrins and Iron Homeostasis (2 of 2)

questions.stem: A biochemistry student notes that iron in the body is essentially always bound to proteins such as transferrin, ferritin, hemoglobin, and iron-sulfur clusters, with almost no free iron. Which of the following best explains why free iron must be avoided?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Free iron is rapidly lost in the urine before tissues can use it

choices.label: B
choices.text: Free iron precipitates in plasma and occludes small vessels

choices.label: C
choices.text: Free iron binds and inactivates hepcidin in the circulation

choices.label: D
choices.text: Free iron competes with copper for hephaestin binding

choices.label: E
choices.text: Free iron generates hydroxyl radical, a reactive oxygen species

explanation.summary: Free iron is highly toxic because it produces hydroxyl radical, so iron is normally bound to proteins.
explanation.whyCorrect: Free iron is highly toxic due to its production of hydroxyl radical, a reactive oxygen species. For this reason iron is normally bound to a variety of proteins: transferrin in plasma, ferritin for intracellular storage, hemoglobin, myoglobin, cytochromes, and iron-sulfur clusters in electron transport chain enzymes. Because there is no regulated pathway for iron excretion, overload and poisoning are also a concern.

whyWrongByChoice.A: There is no regulated excretory pathway for iron; the hazard of free iron is its chemical reactivity, not its loss.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Precipitation in vessels is not the described toxicity; oxidative damage from hydroxyl radical is.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Iron does not inactivate hepcidin; high iron actually induces hepcidin production.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Hephaestin is a copper-dependent ferroxidase that acts on iron as its substrate; competition with copper is not the toxicity mechanism.

questions.topicName: Porphyrins and Iron Homeostasis (2 of 2)

questions.stem: A pathologist examines the spleen of a patient who had a large intra-abdominal hemorrhage several weeks before death. Macrophage lysosomes are packed with an insoluble, iron-rich, golden-brown material. Which of the following best characterizes this material?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Soluble ferritin that releases iron rapidly on cellular demand

choices.label: B
choices.text: Denatured ferritin that is not a readily accessible source of iron

choices.label: C
choices.text: Ferric iron bound to transferrin awaiting receptor uptake

choices.label: D
choices.text: Free ferrous iron released from lysed red blood cells

explanation.summary: Hemosiderin is an insoluble complex of denatured ferritin that forms in iron excess and after hemorrhage and is not readily mobilized.
explanation.whyCorrect: Intracellular iron is predominantly stored bound to ferritin until needed. In contrast, hemosiderin is an insoluble iron-rich storage complex typically formed when there is an excess of iron; it contains denatured ferritin and is not a readily accessible source of iron. It is typically found in macrophage lysosomes, especially in the liver, spleen, and bone marrow, and readily forms after bleeding or hemorrhage in a variety of tissues.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Soluble, readily mobilizable storage describes ferritin, not the insoluble hemosiderin that accumulates after hemorrhage.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Transferrin-bound iron is the plasma transport form, not an intracellular lysosomal deposit.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Free iron is highly toxic via hydroxyl radical and is not left unbound; it is sequestered into ferritin and hemosiderin.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Uroporphyrin accumulates in skin and urine in porphyria cutanea tarda; it is not an iron storage product.

questions.topicName: Porphyrins and Iron Homeostasis (2 of 2)

questions.stem: A 68-year-old man with long-standing lower-extremity edema from cardiovascular disease notices a gradually darkening brown discoloration of the skin around both ankles. He is otherwise well, and his iron studies are normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Serial phlebotomy to reduce total body iron

choices.label: C
choices.text: Identify and address the underlying cause of the deposition

choices.label: E
choices.text: Genetic testing for an HFE mutation

explanation.summary: Localized hemosiderosis rarely needs treatment itself, but its underlying cause merits identification.
explanation.whyCorrect: Overaccumulation from bleeding into a tissue area or abnormal red blood cell turnover causes hemosiderosis, which appears as a darkened area usually localized to the lower leg near the ankles or feet. While this does not usually require treatment, the underlying causes, such as trauma, cardiovascular disease, edema, or diabetes, merit identification. His normal iron studies argue against systemic iron overload.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Phlebotomy is first-line for hemochromatosis with systemic iron overload; localized hemosiderosis with normal iron studies does not warrant it.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Chelating drugs bind free iron in severe overload or in anemic patients who cannot undergo phlebotomy; they are not indicated for local deposition.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Hydroxychloroquine enhances porphyrin excretion in porphyria cutanea tarda and has no role in hemosiderosis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Normal iron studies and a localized lesion with an obvious cause make hereditary hemochromatosis unlikely.

questions.topicName: Porphyrins and Iron Homeostasis (2 of 2)

questions.stem: A researcher measures transferrin receptor (TfR) protein in erythroid precursors from a patient with severe iron deficiency and finds it markedly increased compared with an iron-replete control. The TfR mRNA carries iron response elements in its 3' untranslated region. Which of the following best explains the increase?

choices.label: A
choices.text: IRP binds the 3' IREs and stabilizes the TfR mRNA against degradation

choices.label: B
choices.text: IRP dissociates from the 3' IREs, freeing the mRNA for translation

choices.label: C
choices.text: IRP binds the 5' IRE and physically blocks ribosome scanning

choices.label: D
choices.text: Hepcidin binds the 3' IREs and enhances transcription of the gene

choices.label: E
choices.text: Low iron denatures ferritin, releasing stored TfR protein

explanation.summary: In low iron, IRP binds the 3' IREs of TfR mRNA, stabilizing the transcript so more transferrin receptor is made.
explanation.whyCorrect: Iron regulatory protein (IRP) binds IRE-containing mRNA transcripts in times of low iron and dissociates when iron is high. Whether IRP occupancy activates or prevents expression depends solely on the role of the protein encoded: for TfR, the IREs sit in the 3' untranslated region, so IRP binding stabilizes the mRNA and it is used in protein synthesis, increasing TfR. This fits the physiology that TfR is upregulated in iron deficiency and high erythropoietic demand and downregulated by high intracellular iron.

whyWrongByChoice.B: IRP dissociates from IREs when iron is high, not low; in the low-iron state described, IRP is bound.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A 5' IRE that blocks translation when IRP is bound is the ferritin mechanism, which decreases, not increases, protein in low iron.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Hepcidin is a hormone that degrades ferroportin; it does not bind iron response elements or regulate TfR transcription.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Ferritin stores iron, not receptor protein; hemosiderin (denatured ferritin) forms in iron excess, not deficiency.

questions.topicName: Porphyrins and Iron Homeostasis (2 of 2)

questions.stem: Serum hepcidin is measured in several patients. In which of the following clinical states would hepcidin production be expected to be suppressed?

explanation.summary: Hepcidin is induced by high iron and inflammation (IL-6) but suppressed in anemia and hypoxia.
explanation.whyCorrect: Hepcidin is a liver-produced hormone that regulates iron homeostasis by degrading ferroportin, reducing iron export from enterocytes and macrophages. Its production is induced by high iron levels and inflammation, classically via IL-6, and is suppressed in anemia and hypoxia, states in which the body needs more iron delivered to the marrow for erythropoiesis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: High iron levels induce hepcidin so that ferroportin is degraded and further absorption is limited.
whyWrongByChoice.B: IL-6-driven inflammation induces hepcidin, which is the basis of anemia of chronic disease.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Infection is an inflammatory state that raises hepcidin as a protective measure, since many pathogens require iron.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Transfusions load the body with iron, a high-iron state that induces rather than suppresses hepcidin.

questions.topicName: Porphyrins and Iron Homeostasis (2 of 2)

questions.stem: A 22-year-old man with a chronic anemia caused by ineffective erythropoiesis has received monthly red blood cell transfusions for 10 years. He now has markedly elevated serum ferritin and transferrin saturation, and testing shows he does not carry an HFE mutation. Which of the following best explains his iron overload?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Transfused red cells induce DMT-1 on duodenal enterocytes

choices.label: B
choices.text: The body has no pathway to increase iron excretion to offset the transfused iron

choices.label: C
choices.text: Transfused blood suppresses hepatic transferrin synthesis

choices.label: D
choices.text: Chronic anemia upregulates hephaestin in the colon and spleen

choices.label: E
choices.text: Transfused hemoglobin iron bypasses ferritin and deposits directly as hemosiderin

explanation.summary: Secondary hemochromatosis from transfusions occurs because the body cannot increase iron excretion to compensate.
explanation.whyCorrect: Secondary hemochromatosis is iron overload from causes other than an HFE mutation: excessive iron supplementation, multiple and frequent blood transfusions, and ineffective erythropoiesis. Transfusions introduce significant amounts of iron, and because there is no regulated mechanism or pathway for iron excretion, the body cannot compensate and iron accumulates. His underlying ineffective erythropoiesis is itself an additional contributor to overload.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Transfused iron enters directly into the circulation; the problem is not increased apical uptake by DMT-1.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Transferrin synthesis is inversely related to iron stores, but reduced transferrin is a consequence of overload, not its cause.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Hephaestin is upregulated in iron deficiency and downregulated when stores are high; it does not drive transfusional overload.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Hemosiderin forms from denatured ferritin in iron excess; it is a result of overload rather than a bypass mechanism.

questions.topicName: Porphyrins and Iron Homeostasis (2 of 2)

questions.stem: A 24-year-old woman with a transfusion-dependent anemia has developed iron overload with a serum ferritin far above normal and a transferrin saturation of 90%. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment to reduce her iron burden?

explanation.summary: Patients with anemia and iron overload receive chelating drugs alone because they cannot spare the red cell loss of phlebotomy.
explanation.whyCorrect: Iron-chelating drugs such as deferasirox, deferoxamine, and deferiprone have a high affinity for iron and, like a sponge cleaning a spill, bind up free iron. In severe hemochromatosis they are used alongside phlebotomy, but in patients with anemia only chelating drugs are used because these patients cannot spare the loss of red blood cells by phlebotomy. Response is monitored with ferritin, serum iron, and transferrin saturation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Phlebotomy is first-line for hemochromatosis in general, but an anemic, transfusion-dependent patient cannot tolerate removing red cells.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Routine blood donation is a strategy for mild hemochromatosis and is not possible for a patient who is anemic and receiving transfusions.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Liver transplant is reserved for hemochromatosis with end-stage liver disease, decided similarly to other cirrhosis patients; it is not a treatment for iron burden itself.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Combining chelation with phlebotomy is reserved for severe cases in patients who can tolerate red cell loss, which an anemic patient cannot.

questions.topicName: Porphyrins and Iron Homeostasis (2 of 2)

questions.stem: A 49-year-old man with hereditary hemochromatosis begins a program of regular therapeutic phlebotomy. Which of the following sets of laboratory values is used to monitor his response to treatment?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Ferritin, serum iron, and transferrin saturation

choices.label: C
choices.text: Red blood cell protoporphyrin and stool color

explanation.summary: Response to hemochromatosis treatment is monitored with ferritin, serum iron, and transferrin saturation.
explanation.whyCorrect: Phlebotomy is the first-line treatment for hemochromatosis, removing excess iron by removing red blood cells. Throughout the treatment process, responsiveness is monitored with ferritin, serum iron, and transferrin saturation, the same iron studies that are elevated in iron overload and should fall as stores are depleted.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Urinary PBG and ALA are the diagnostic markers of acute intermittent porphyria, not of iron overload.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Red cell protoporphyrin and dark stool are diagnostic clues in erythropoietic protoporphyria.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Hepcidin and hephaestin are regulatory proteins of iron handling, but they are not the parameters used to track treatment response.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Urinary uroporphyrin and heptacarboxylporphyrin confirm porphyria cutanea tarda, not hemochromatosis.

questions.topicName: Porphyrins and Iron Homeostasis (2 of 2)

questions.stem: A 46-year-old man with newly diagnosed hereditary hemochromatosis reports several months of pain in the joints of both hands. Radiographs show hook-like, beak-shaped osteophytes projecting from the radial ends of the joints. Which of the following best explains his joint disease?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Uroporphyrin deposition in the synovium after sun exposure

choices.label: B
choices.text: Hemosiderin from repeated bleeding into the joint spaces

choices.label: C
choices.text: Iron deposition in the synovial fluid

explanation.summary: Hemochromatosis arthropathy results from iron deposition in the synovial fluid, most commonly affecting the hands.
explanation.whyCorrect: Joint pain in hemochromatosis is known as hemochromatosis arthropathy. Iron deposition in the synovial fluid leads to joint pain most commonly in the hands, although larger joints can also be affected, and hook-like osteophytes (beak-like projections) from the radial ends of the joints of the hands can occur. Other findings of iron overload include hypogonadism with testicular atrophy and gynecomastia, and hepatomegaly from the space the iron takes up.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Uroporphyrin deposits in the skin in porphyria cutanea tarda, causing blistering, not joint disease.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Hemosiderin from hemorrhage causes localized hemosiderosis in tissues; the arthropathy of hemochromatosis reflects systemic iron deposition, not bleeding.
whyWrongByChoice.D: IL-6 raises hepcidin and causes anemia of chronic disease; it is not the mechanism of hemochromatosis arthropathy.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Insulin resistance from cirrhosis contributes to bronze diabetes, not to joint pain or osteophytes.

questions.topicName: Porphyrins and Iron Homeostasis (2 of 2)

questions.stem: A 6-month-old infant is brought in for poor growth and a protuberant abdomen. He has doll-like facial features with fat cheeks. After a brief fast he develops a seizure; labs show severe hypoglycemia, elevated lactate, hypertriglyceridemia, and hyperuricemia. Exam reveals marked hepatomegaly. Deficiency of which of the following enzymes is the most likely cause?

explanation.summary: von Gierke disease (GSD type I) is glucose-6-phosphatase deficiency causing severe fasting hypoglycemia with lactic acidosis, hyperlipidemia, and hyperuricemia.
explanation.whyCorrect: Without glucose-6-phosphatase the liver cannot convert glucose-6-phosphate to free exportable glucose, so both gluconeogenesis and glycogenolysis are impaired. Accumulating glucose-6-phosphate spills into other pathways, producing lactic acidosis (impaired Cori cycle), hypertriglyceridemia, and hyperuricemia, along with hepatomegaly and doll-like facies.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Acid alpha-glucosidase deficiency causes Pompe disease, which spares the liver's glucose output (normal glucose and pH) and presents with cardiomyopathy and hypotonia.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Muscle glycogen phosphorylase deficiency causes McArdle disease, an exercise-related muscle disorder without infantile hepatomegaly or fasting hypoglycemia.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Debranching enzyme deficiency causes Cori disease, which is milder with only mild hypoglycemia and characteristically no lactic acidosis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Branching enzyme deficiency causes Andersen disease, marked by abnormal amylopectin-like glycogen and early cirrhosis rather than this metabolic picture.

questions.topicName: Inborn Errors of Carbohydrate Metabolism

questions.stem: A 4-month-old boy has a large protruding tongue, profound hypotonia, and difficulty feeding. Exam reveals a markedly enlarged heart, and echocardiography demonstrates hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. Fasting glucose and blood pH are normal, but serum creatine kinase is elevated. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanation.summary: Macroglossia, hypotonia, and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy with normal glucose and pH point to Pompe disease (lysosomal acid alpha-glucosidase deficiency).
explanation.whyCorrect: Pompe disease is a lysosomal storage disease in which glycogen accumulates in lysosomes and damages muscle fibers. The classic infantile form presents with macroglossia, weakness, hypotonia, and rapidly progressive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy; because the liver functions normally there is no hypoglycemia or lactic acidosis, and creatine kinase is elevated from muscle damage.

whyWrongByChoice.A: von Gierke disease affects the liver and would produce severe fasting hypoglycemia and lactic acidosis, not normal glucose and pH.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Cori disease causes hepatomegaly with mild hypoglycemia, not the hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and macroglossia seen here.
whyWrongByChoice.D: McArdle disease affects skeletal muscle and presents in adolescence or young adulthood with exercise intolerance, not in infancy with cardiomegaly.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Hers disease is a milder hepatic phosphorylase deficiency presenting with hypoglycemia and ketosis, not cardiomyopathy.

questions.topicName: Inborn Errors of Carbohydrate Metabolism

questions.stem: A 14-year-old boy reports muscle cramps and weakness within minutes of starting to run, but if he pushes through and slows down he can then continue comfortably for the rest of a race. After intense training his urine turns reddish-brown. Serum creatine kinase is elevated at rest. Deficiency of which of the following enzymes best explains his presentation?

explanation.summary: Exercise-induced cramps with a second-wind phenomenon and myoglobinuria indicate McArdle disease (muscle glycogen phosphorylase deficiency).
explanation.whyCorrect: McArdle disease presents in adolescence with muscle cramps early in exercise and a pathognomonic second-wind phenomenon, in which increased blood flow delivers circulating glucose so activity can continue after the initial fatigue. Muscle breakdown produces rhabdomyolysis and myoglobinuria (dark urine) with elevated creatine kinase.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Hepatic glycogen phosphorylase deficiency (Hers disease) affects the liver with hypoglycemia and ketosis, not exertional muscle symptoms.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Acid alpha-glucosidase deficiency (Pompe) presents in infancy with cardiomyopathy and hypotonia, not adolescent exercise intolerance.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Glucose-6-phosphatase deficiency (von Gierke) causes hepatic hypoglycemia, not exercise-triggered myoglobinuria.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Muscle phosphofructokinase deficiency (Tarui) causes similar exertional myopathy but characteristically LACKS the second-wind phenomenon this patient shows.

questions.topicName: Inborn Errors of Carbohydrate Metabolism

questions.stem: A 2-year-old has mild fasting hypoglycemia, hepatomegaly, and short stature. Unlike a related glycogen storage disease, her blood lactate is normal and she has no lactic acidosis. Liver biopsy shows glycogen with a normal branching pattern but abnormally short outer branches (limit dextrin). Which of the following best explains the absence of lactic acidosis in this patient?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Gluconeogenesis remains intact, keeping the Cori cycle functional

choices.label: B
choices.text: Glucose-6-phosphatase activity is preserved and exports glucose normally

choices.label: D
choices.text: Lysosomal glycogen degradation is selectively impaired

choices.label: E
choices.text: Skeletal muscle is entirely spared from the enzyme defect

explanation.summary: In Cori disease (debranching enzyme deficiency), gluconeogenesis is unaffected, so the Cori cycle clears lactate and no lactic acidosis develops.
explanation.whyCorrect: Cori disease results from deficiency of the debranching enzyme (alpha-1,6-glucosidase), producing limit dextrin accumulation. Because the defect does not impede gluconeogenesis, lactate can still be converted to glucose in the liver, so unlike von Gierke disease these patients do not develop lactic acidosis and have only mild fasting hypoglycemia.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Glucose-6-phosphatase is normal in Cori disease, but that is not the reason lactic acidosis is absent; the key is that gluconeogenesis and the Cori cycle stay intact.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Absent glycogen synthesis describes GSD type 0 (glycogen synthase deficiency), a different disorder that actually causes fasting lactic acidosis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Impaired lysosomal glycogen degradation describes Pompe disease, which is not the mechanism here.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Muscle is not spared in Cori disease; debranching enzyme deficiency can cause muscle weakness and cardiomyopathy, and this does not explain the lactate finding.

questions.topicName: Inborn Errors of Carbohydrate Metabolism

questions.stem: A 7-year-old boy develops fatigue, scleral icterus, and dark urine two days after starting an antibiotic; he had also recently eaten fava beans. A peripheral blood smear shows Heinz bodies and bite cells. The underlying enzyme deficiency most directly leads to which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Inadequate NADPH, leading to oxidative injury of hemoglobin

choices.label: C
choices.text: Inability to reduce ferric iron within hemoglobin

choices.label: D
choices.text: Accumulation of limit dextrin within erythrocytes

choices.label: E
choices.text: Reduced synthesis of the glutathione reductase protein itself

explanation.summary: G6PD deficiency reduces NADPH production, leaving red cells unable to neutralize reactive oxygen species, which oxidizes and damages hemoglobin.
explanation.whyCorrect: G6PD generates NADPH in the pentose phosphate pathway. Without adequate NADPH, glutathione cannot be kept reduced, so reactive oxygen species accumulate and oxidize hemoglobin. This produces Heinz bodies (oxidized Hb polymers) and bite cells, culminating in episodic hemolysis triggered by oxidative stressors such as drugs, infection, or fava beans.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Impaired glycolytic ATP production describes pyruvate kinase deficiency, which causes chronic hemolysis without an oxidative trigger, not Heinz bodies and bite cells.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Inability to reduce ferric iron describes methemoglobinemia (cytochrome b5 reductase deficiency), which causes cyanosis rather than oxidative hemolysis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Limit dextrin accumulation is a feature of Cori disease in liver and muscle, not a red-cell process.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Glutathione reductase function is lost because of missing NADPH cofactor, not because the reductase protein itself is deficient or under-synthesized.

questions.topicName: Inborn Errors of Carbohydrate Metabolism

questions.stem: A newborn is found to have chronic hemolytic anemia present since birth with no identifiable oxidative trigger. The peripheral smear shows spiculated (echinocyte) red cells, and 2,3-BPG is elevated. Which of the following best characterizes this disorder compared with G6PD deficiency?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Hemolysis is chronic rather than episodic, and 2,3-BPG is increased

choices.label: B
choices.text: Hemolysis requires exposure to oxidant drugs or fava beans

choices.label: C
choices.text: Heinz bodies and bite cells are the characteristic smear finding

choices.label: D
choices.text: NADPH production through the pentose phosphate pathway is deficient

choices.label: E
choices.text: Red cells rely on mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation for ATP

explanation.summary: Pyruvate kinase deficiency causes chronic hemolysis from birth (no trigger needed) and elevated 2,3-BPG, distinguishing it from the episodic, trigger-dependent hemolysis of G6PD deficiency.
explanation.whyCorrect: Because mature red cells rely solely on glycolysis for ATP, pyruvate kinase deficiency impairs ATP generation, producing rigid spiculated cells that undergo chronic hemolysis diagnosed early in life. The upstream glycolytic block redistributes intermediates through the shunt that generates 2,3-BPG, so 2,3-BPG is elevated.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Requiring an oxidant trigger describes G6PD deficiency; pyruvate kinase deficiency causes hemolysis without such triggers.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Heinz bodies and bite cells are hallmarks of oxidative hemolysis in G6PD deficiency, not pyruvate kinase deficiency.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Deficient NADPH from the pentose phosphate pathway is the defect in G6PD deficiency, not pyruvate kinase deficiency.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Mature red cells lack mitochondria and depend on glycolysis for ATP, so they cannot use oxidative phosphorylation.

questions.topicName: Inborn Errors of Carbohydrate Metabolism

questions.stem: A cyanotic infant has an oxygen saturation that does not improve with supplemental oxygen, and arterial blood is described as chocolate-brown. Cyanosis resolves promptly after intravenous methylene blue. Deficiency of which of the following enzymes is the most likely underlying cause?

explanation.summary: Congenital methemoglobinemia results from cytochrome b5 reductase deficiency, leaving hemoglobin iron in the ferric (Fe3+) state.
explanation.whyCorrect: Cytochrome b5 reductase normally reconverts methemoglobin (ferric, Fe3+) back to functional hemoglobin (ferrous, Fe2+). When it is deficient, methemoglobin accumulates and cannot bind oxygen, producing cyanosis and chocolate-brown blood that does not respond to oxygen. Methylene blue reduces met-Hb to Hb in an NADPH-dependent manner, reversing the cyanosis.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Pyruvate kinase deficiency causes chronic hemolytic anemia, not methemoglobinemia or chocolate-brown blood.
whyWrongByChoice.C: G6PD deficiency causes episodic oxidative hemolysis; although severe oxidative stress can transiently form met-Hb, it is not the classic congenital cause described here.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Acid alpha-glucosidase deficiency causes Pompe disease with cardiomyopathy, unrelated to cyanosis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: PEPCK deficiency impairs gluconeogenesis and causes fasting hypoglycemia, not methemoglobinemia.

questions.topicName: Inborn Errors of Carbohydrate Metabolism

questions.stem: A neonate has failure to thrive, severe lactic acidosis, hypotonia, and ataxia, with abnormalities on neuroimaging. A high-fat, low-carbohydrate (ketogenic) diet along with thiamine supplementation is initiated. Which of the following best explains why the ketogenic diet is beneficial in this disorder?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Fatty acids stimulate residual glucose-6-phosphatase activity

choices.label: C
choices.text: Ketone bodies inhibit lactate production by pyruvate carboxylase

choices.label: D
choices.text: Dietary fat provides substrate for hepatic glycogen synthesis

choices.label: E
choices.text: Ketosis restores debranching enzyme function in muscle

explanation.summary: In pyruvate dehydrogenase (PDH) complex deficiency, a ketogenic diet supplies acetyl-CoA from ketone bodies, bypassing the blocked pyruvate-to-acetyl-CoA step.
explanation.whyCorrect: PDH deficiency prevents pyruvate from being converted to acetyl-CoA, so glycolysis cannot be linked to the citric acid cycle and lactate builds up, severely affecting the brain. A ketogenic diet generates acetyl-CoA from ketone bodies instead of pyruvate, providing CNS fuel; vitamin cofactors like thiamine are tried to recover any residual enzyme activity.

whyWrongByChoice.B: The defect is in pyruvate dehydrogenase, not glucose-6-phosphatase, and fatty acids do not stimulate that enzyme.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The benefit comes from generating acetyl-CoA that bypasses PDH, not from inhibiting pyruvate carboxylase.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Providing substrate for glycogen synthesis would not address the block linking glycolysis to the TCA cycle.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Debranching enzyme is unrelated to PDH deficiency, and ketosis does not restore its function.

questions.topicName: Inborn Errors of Carbohydrate Metabolism

questions.stem: A 3-month-old presents with fasting hypoglycemia, lactic acidosis, hepatomegaly, and hypotonia. In addition, serum ammonia is markedly elevated. This hyperammonemia distinguishes the disorder from PEPCK deficiency and is best explained by a deficiency of which of the following enzymes?

explanation.summary: Pyruvate carboxylase deficiency causes fasting hypoglycemia and acidosis like PEPCK deficiency but is uniquely associated with hyperammonemia due to reduced oxaloacetate.
explanation.whyCorrect: Pyruvate carboxylase converts pyruvate to oxaloacetate, an anaplerotic reaction that supports gluconeogenesis, the TCA cycle, and the urea cycle. When it is deficient, dampened oxaloacetate formation deprives the urea cycle of needed intermediates, producing hyperammonemia in addition to the fasting hypoglycemia and acidosis shared with PEPCK deficiency.

whyWrongByChoice.B: PEPCK deficiency impairs gluconeogenesis and causes fasting hypoglycemia, but it does not produce hyperammonemia, which is the distinguishing feature here.
whyWrongByChoice.C: PDH complex deficiency causes lactic acidosis with prominent neurologic disease, not the hyperammonemia that specifically defines this case.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Glucose-6-phosphatase deficiency (von Gierke) causes hepatomegaly and hyperuricemia but is not characterized by hyperammonemia.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Hepatic glycogen phosphorylase deficiency (Hers) causes mild hypoglycemia and ketosis, not hyperammonemia.

questions.topicName: Inborn Errors of Carbohydrate Metabolism

questions.stem: A child with confirmed glucose-6-phosphatase deficiency is noted to have persistently elevated serum uric acid and later develops gout, for which allopurinol is started. Which of the following mechanisms best accounts for the hyperuricemia in this disorder?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Excess glucose-6-phosphate is shunted into the pentose phosphate pathway to overproduce purines

choices.label: B
choices.text: Impaired purine salvage increases renal reabsorption of hypoxanthine

choices.label: C
choices.text: Chronic hemolysis releases purines that raise uric acid

choices.label: D
choices.text: Ketone bodies directly stimulate xanthine oxidase activity

choices.label: E
choices.text: Deficient renal gluconeogenesis increases tubular secretion of urate

explanation.summary: In von Gierke disease, hyperuricemia arises from purine overproduction via the pentose phosphate pathway plus reduced renal urate clearance because lactate competes for the same transporter.
explanation.whyCorrect: Accumulated glucose-6-phosphate is diverted into the pentose phosphate pathway, driving overproduction of purines and thus uric acid. At the same time, elevated lactate competes with urate for the shared renal transporter, impairing uric acid clearance. Both mechanisms raise serum uric acid, and allopurinol is used to manage resulting gout.

whyWrongByChoice.B: The problem is purine overproduction and impaired excretion, not enhanced renal reabsorption of hypoxanthine.
whyWrongByChoice.C: von Gierke disease is not a hemolytic disorder, so hemolysis-derived purines do not explain the hyperuricemia.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Ketone bodies do not directly stimulate xanthine oxidase; the mechanism involves purine flux and lactate competition.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Renal handling is impaired (reduced clearance), and there is no increase in tubular urate secretion in this disease.

questions.topicName: Inborn Errors of Carbohydrate Metabolism

questions.stem: A 15-month-old has failure to thrive and progressive hepatomegaly with early cirrhosis. Liver biopsy shows abnormal, poorly branched glycogen resembling amylopectin, accompanied by an inflammatory reaction thought to reflect an immune response against the abnormal glycogen. The child dies before age 2. Deficiency of which of the following enzymes is most likely?

explanation.summary: Andersen disease (GSD type IV) is branching enzyme deficiency, producing amylopectin-like glycogen, early cirrhosis, and death by about 2 years.
explanation.whyCorrect: The branching enzyme forms alpha-1,6 glycosidic branches. Its deficiency yields abnormal, long-chain, poorly branched glycogen resembling amylopectin. This abnormal glycogen triggers an inflammatory immune response leading to early liver cirrhosis and death by roughly 2 years of age.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Debranching enzyme deficiency causes Cori disease, which produces limit dextrin (short branches), not long amylopectin-like polymers, and is comparatively milder.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Glucose-6-phosphatase deficiency (von Gierke) causes severe hypoglycemia with normal glycogen structure, not abnormal branching.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Hepatic glycogen phosphorylase deficiency (Hers) is a milder disorder with normal glycogen structure.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Glycogen synthase deficiency (GSD type 0) results in essentially absent glycogen, not abnormally structured amylopectin-like glycogen.

questions.topicName: Inborn Errors of Carbohydrate Metabolism

questions.stem: A 5-year-old with a hereditary hemolytic anemia is admitted during an active hemolytic crisis. Which of the following laboratory findings is expected as a shared consequence of both G6PD deficiency and pyruvate kinase deficiency during ongoing hemolysis?

explanation.summary: Active hemolysis from either enzyme deficiency consumes haptoglobin as it binds released free hemoglobin, so serum haptoglobin falls.
explanation.whyCorrect: Haptoglobin binds cell-free hemoglobin released during hemolysis, and the complex is cleared by macrophages. During a hemolytic crisis the surplus of free hemoglobin depletes haptoglobin, so levels are low regardless of whether the hemolysis is oxidative (G6PD) or from impaired glycolytic ATP (pyruvate kinase).

whyWrongByChoice.B: Haptoglobin decreases, not increases, because it is consumed binding free hemoglobin during hemolysis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hemolysis produces hyperbilirubinemia and jaundice, so total bilirubin rises rather than falls.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Serum LDH is elevated in hemolysis because it is released from lysed red cells, not decreased.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The reticulocyte count increases as the marrow compensates for red-cell loss, so it is not decreased.

questions.topicName: Inborn Errors of Carbohydrate Metabolism

questions.stem: A 4-year-old girl has recurrent early-morning episodes of lethargy and irritability that resolve after breakfast. Laboratory studies drawn on waking show hypoglycemia with ketosis and mild lactic acidosis. On examination the abdomen is flat and the liver is not enlarged. Liver biopsy demonstrates essentially no glycogen. Deficiency of which of the following enzymes is the most likely cause?

explanation.summary: GSD type 0 is hepatic glycogen synthase deficiency: glycogen is nonexistent, the liver is small, and patients have ketotic hypoglycemia especially after waking with fasting lactic acidosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Without hepatic glycogen synthase the liver cannot build glycogen at all, so there is nothing to mobilize during an overnight fast. The result is ketotic hypoglycemia that is worst on waking and fasting lactic acidosis. Because no glycogen accumulates, the liver is small rather than enlarged, which separates GSD 0 from the other hepatic glycogen storage diseases.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Glucose-6-phosphatase deficiency (von Gierke) causes marked hepatomegaly from glycogen accumulation, the opposite of a small liver with absent glycogen.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Hepatic glycogen phosphorylase deficiency (Hers) produces hypoglycemia with ketosis but with glycogen accumulation and hepatomegaly.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Debranching enzyme deficiency (Cori) leaves glycogen with shortened outer branches (limit dextrin) and mild hepatomegaly, not absent glycogen.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Branching enzyme deficiency (Andersen) produces abnormal amylopectin-like glycogen with early cirrhosis, not a glycogen-free liver.

questions.topicName: Inborn Errors of Carbohydrate Metabolism

questions.stem: A 3-year-old boy with mild hepatomegaly and slowed growth has mild fasting hypoglycemia with ketosis; blood lactate is normal. Liver biopsy shows increased glycogen with a normal branching pattern and normal-length outer branches. Assays show normal debranching enzyme and glucose-6-phosphatase activity in the liver. Deficiency of which of the following enzymes is most likely?

explanation.summary: Hers disease (GSD type 6) is hepatic glycogen phosphorylase deficiency, a milder form of type I with hypoglycemia, ketosis, and structurally normal glycogen.
explanation.whyCorrect: Hepatic glycogen phosphorylase removes glucose units from the outer branches of liver glycogen. Its deficiency means glucose cannot be mobilized from glycogen stores, producing hypoglycemia and ketosis with hepatic glycogen accumulation. Glycogen structure is normal and debranching and glucose-6-phosphatase activities are intact, which excludes Cori and von Gierke disease.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Muscle glycogen phosphorylase deficiency (McArdle) causes exercise intolerance and myoglobinuria in adolescents, not hepatic hypoglycemia in a toddler.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Acid alpha-glucosidase deficiency (Pompe) causes lysosomal glycogen storage with cardiomyopathy and hypotonia, and there is no hypoglycemia.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Branching enzyme deficiency (Andersen) produces abnormal, poorly branched amylopectin-like glycogen, not a normal branching pattern.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Muscle phosphofructokinase deficiency (Tarui) causes exertional myopathy and rhabdomyolysis, not fasting hypoglycemia.

questions.topicName: Inborn Errors of Carbohydrate Metabolism

questions.stem: A 19-year-old man reports muscle cramps and exercise intolerance with dark urine after strenuous activity. Unlike a classmate with a similar muscle disorder, he never experiences relief if he pushes through the initial fatigue. He also has a mild chronic hemolytic anemia with an elevated reticulocyte count. Deficiency of which of the following enzymes is the most likely cause?

explanation.summary: Tarui disease (GSD type 7) is muscle phosphofructokinase deficiency: exertional myopathy with rhabdomyolysis, no second-wind phenomenon, and hemolytic anemia in select cases.
explanation.whyCorrect: Muscle PFK converts fructose 6-phosphate to fructose 1,6-bisphosphate in glycolysis. Its deficiency produces exertional myopathy, muscle cramps, exercise intolerance, and rhabdomyolysis, but characteristically without the second-wind phenomenon seen in McArdle disease. Because red blood cells carry a partial PFK deficiency, select patients also develop hemolytic anemia.

whyWrongByChoice.A: McArdle disease (muscle glycogen phosphorylase) shares the cramps and myoglobinuria but is defined by a second-wind phenomenon and is not associated with hemolytic anemia.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Debranching enzyme deficiency (Cori) presents in childhood with hepatomegaly and mild hypoglycemia, not adult exertional rhabdomyolysis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Pyruvate kinase deficiency causes chronic hemolytic anemia from birth but no exercise-induced muscle cramps or myoglobinuria.
whyWrongByChoice.E: G6PD deficiency causes episodic oxidative hemolysis triggered by drugs, infection, or fava beans, not exertional myopathy.

questions.topicName: Inborn Errors of Carbohydrate Metabolism

questions.stem: The parents of a 2-year-old with von Gierke disease are instructed to give cornstarch before bedtime. They ask whether they can cook it into a pudding so their child will accept it more readily. Which of the following best explains why the cornstarch should be given uncooked?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Heating disrupts the starch's branching structure and shortens its slow glucose release

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cooking converts the starch into fructose, which worsens glucose-6-phosphate buildup

choices.label: C
choices.text: Cooked starch resists digestion entirely and passes unchanged into the stool

choices.label: D
choices.text: Heating generates lactate within the starch and aggravates the lactic acidosis

choices.label: E
choices.text: Cooking destroys the enzyme inside the starch granule that liberates glucose

explanation.summary: Uncooked cornstarch provides a slow, steady glucose release over roughly 4-8 hours; heating compromises its branching structure and decreases its efficacy.
explanation.whyCorrect: Uncooked cornstarch is a complex carbohydrate whose intact branching structure is digested slowly, releasing glucose over about 4-8 hours and circumventing the need to liberate glycogen stores. This is especially effective before sleeping to prevent severe morning hypoglycemia. Cooking heats the starch and damages that branching structure, so the glucose is released too quickly and the protective effect is lost. Glycosade is a specially processed starch that can be prescribed for the same purpose.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Cooking does not convert starch to fructose; the issue is structural damage to the starch, not sugar conversion.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Cooked starch is digested, in fact too rapidly; the problem is loss of the slow-release property, not failure of absorption.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Heating starch does not generate lactate; lactic acidosis in von Gierke comes from impaired hepatic gluconeogenesis and the Cori cycle.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Starch contains no glucose-liberating enzyme; digestion of starch depends on the patient's own enzymes and on the starch's physical structure.

questions.topicName: Inborn Errors of Carbohydrate Metabolism

questions.stem: A 5-year-old with Cori disease is treated with cornstarch supplementation. His cousin with von Gierke disease has been told to strictly avoid milk, fruit, and table sugar. The parents ask whether their son must follow the same restriction. Which of the following is the most appropriate response?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Yes, because lactose and fructose worsen limit dextrin accumulation in the cytosol

choices.label: B
choices.text: No, because gluconeogenesis is intact so these sugars can be safely converted to glucose

choices.label: C
choices.text: Yes, because these sugars compete with lactate for the shared renal urate transporter

choices.label: D
choices.text: No, because debranching enzyme deficiency spares the liver and affects only muscle

choices.label: E
choices.text: Yes, because these sugars bypass glucose-6-phosphatase and raise blood lactate

explanation.summary: In Cori disease there is no need to avoid sucrose, fructose, or lactose because gluconeogenesis is not affected, unlike von Gierke disease.
explanation.whyCorrect: Treatment of Cori disease mirrors von Gierke disease in using cornstarch to avoid hypoglycemia, but the key difference is that the debranching enzyme defect does not impede gluconeogenesis. Lactose, fructose, and sucrose therefore do not cause the glucose-6-phosphate accumulation that makes them harmful in von Gierke disease, so the dietary restriction is unnecessary.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Limit dextrin accumulates because of the debranching defect itself; dietary sugars do not worsen it and are not restricted in Cori disease.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Competition between lactate and urate for a renal transporter explains hyperuricemia in von Gierke disease; it is not a reason to restrict sugars in Cori disease.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Debranching enzyme is important in both liver and muscle, and Cori disease clearly involves the liver with hepatomegaly and hypoglycemia.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Sugars worsening glucose-6-phosphate accumulation and lactate is the von Gierke rationale; glucose-6-phosphatase is normal in Cori disease.

questions.topicName: Inborn Errors of Carbohydrate Metabolism

questions.stem: A 24-year-old woman with von Gierke disease managed since infancy with uncooked cornstarch presents for routine follow-up. Abdominal imaging shows multiple well-circumscribed masses within the liver. Which of the following best describes these lesions and the principal concern they raise?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Amylopectin deposits with progression to cirrhosis

choices.label: B
choices.text: Lysosomal glycogen engorgement with heart failure

choices.label: C
choices.text: Fatty infiltration with progression to pancreatitis

choices.label: D
choices.text: Hepatic adenomas with increased risk of liver cancer

choices.label: E
choices.text: Metastatic deposits from an enlarged kidney

explanation.summary: Hepatic adenomas develop in the second or third decade of life in von Gierke disease and carry an increased risk of liver cancer.
explanation.whyCorrect: Long-standing glycogen accumulation and damage to the liver in glucose-6-phosphatase deficiency lead to hepatic adenomas that appear in the second or third decade. These adenomas increase the risk of liver cancer, so patients require ongoing surveillance even when hypoglycemia is well controlled with dietary therapy.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Amylopectin-like glycogen with early cirrhosis is the pathology of Andersen disease (branching enzyme deficiency), which is lethal by about 2 years.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Lysosomal glycogen engorgement with heart failure describes Pompe disease, not von Gierke disease.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Pancreatitis risk in von Gierke disease arises from elevated triglycerides, not from focal fatty liver masses.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Kidney enlargement in von Gierke disease is from glycogen accumulation, not a tumor that metastasizes to the liver.

questions.topicName: Inborn Errors of Carbohydrate Metabolism

questions.stem: A 3-year-old with glucose-6-phosphatase deficiency is found on ultrasound to have bilaterally enlarged kidneys, and laboratory studies show early kidney disease. Which of the following best explains the renal involvement in this disorder?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The kidney performs some gluconeogenesis and accumulates glycogen when the enzyme is absent

choices.label: B
choices.text: Myoglobin released from exercise-damaged muscle deposits within the renal tubules

choices.label: C
choices.text: Ammonia accumulating from a failing urea cycle directly injures the tubular epithelium

choices.label: D
choices.text: Amylopectin-like glycogen provokes an immune reaction within the glomeruli

choices.label: E
choices.text: Glycogen stored in lysosomes of tubular cells engorges and enlarges the organ

explanation.summary: Because the kidney carries out a small amount of gluconeogenesis and can produce glycogen, glucose-6-phosphatase deficiency manifests in the kidney as glycogen accumulation with enlargement and kidney disease.
explanation.whyCorrect: The liver and muscle are the main glycogen-using organs, but the kidney also produces glycogen to some extent and performs a small amount of gluconeogenesis. Glucose-6-phosphatase is therefore needed in the kidney as well, and its absence in von Gierke disease leads to renal glycogen accumulation, kidney enlargement, and kidney disease.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Myoglobin-related kidney stress occurs with rhabdomyolysis in McArdle disease; von Gierke disease is not a muscle disorder.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hyperammonemia is a feature of pyruvate carboxylase deficiency, not von Gierke disease.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Immune reaction against amylopectin-like glycogen describes the liver injury of Andersen disease, not renal disease in von Gierke.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Lysosomal glycogen storage is the mechanism of Pompe disease; in von Gierke disease glycogen accumulates because glucose-6-phosphate cannot be converted to free glucose.

questions.topicName: Inborn Errors of Carbohydrate Metabolism

questions.stem: A 28-year-old man has 3 years of slowly progressive weakness of the hips and thighs with difficulty climbing stairs. He denies cramps with exertion or dark urine. Echocardiography is normal. Serum creatine kinase is elevated, and muscle biopsy shows glycogen accumulated within membrane-bound lysosomes. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanation.summary: The adult (late-onset) form of Pompe disease presents from after infancy up to the 2nd-3rd decade with lower-extremity muscle weakness as lysosomes slowly fill with glycogen, and it lacks the cardiac involvement of the pediatric form.
explanation.whyCorrect: Pompe disease is unique among GSDs in having two forms by age of presentation. The adult form has less of an acid alpha-glucosidase deficiency, is largely asymptomatic until lysosomes gradually fill with glycogen, and then manifests as muscle weakness, particularly of the lower extremities. Importantly it lacks the cardiac issues that define the pediatric form, matching the normal echocardiogram here; lysosomal glycogen on biopsy confirms the lysosomal storage nature of the disease.

whyWrongByChoice.A: McArdle disease produces exercise-induced cramps, myoglobinuria, and a second-wind phenomenon rather than fixed progressive weakness, and glycogen is not lysosomal.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Cori disease presents in childhood with hepatomegaly and hypoglycemia; its glycogen (limit dextrin) accumulates in the cytosol, not lysosomes.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Tarui disease causes exertional myopathy with cramps and rhabdomyolysis, not slowly progressive proximal weakness without exercise symptoms.
whyWrongByChoice.D: von Gierke disease is a hepatic disorder presenting in infancy with severe hypoglycemia and lactic acidosis, not adult muscle weakness.

questions.topicName: Inborn Errors of Carbohydrate Metabolism

questions.stem: A 5-month-old with hypotonia, macroglossia, and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is diagnosed with acid alpha-glucosidase deficiency. Fasting glucose and blood pH are normal, yet examination reveals a clearly enlarged liver. Which of the following best explains the hepatomegaly in this patient?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cytosolic accumulation of limit dextrin within hepatocytes

choices.label: B
choices.text: Congestion from fluid overload caused by heart failure

choices.label: C
choices.text: Glycogen accumulation that blocks glucose export from hepatocytes

choices.label: D
choices.text: Fatty infiltration secondary to elevated triglycerides

choices.label: E
choices.text: Inflammatory reaction against abnormally branched glycogen

explanation.summary: In Pompe disease the liver functions properly, and the hepatomegaly reflects extra fluid from heart failure rather than a primary hepatic defect.
explanation.whyCorrect: Pompe disease damages muscle fibers, including the heart, producing rapidly progressive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. The liver itself functions normally, which is why there is no hypoglycemia or lactic acidosis, but it is often enlarged because of the extra fluid that accumulates with heart failure. Most untreated infants die around 1 year of age from that heart failure.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Limit dextrin accumulation in the cytosol is the hepatic pathology of Cori disease, not Pompe.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Blocked glucose export from glycogen-laden hepatocytes describes von Gierke disease, which would produce hypoglycemia and lactic acidosis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Elevated triglycerides with hepatic consequences belong to von Gierke disease; Pompe does not disturb lipid metabolism.
whyWrongByChoice.E: An immune response against abnormal glycogen causing liver damage is the mechanism in Andersen disease.

questions.topicName: Inborn Errors of Carbohydrate Metabolism

questions.stem: A 4-month-old girl is diagnosed with classic infantile Pompe disease after enzyme assay confirms deficient acid alpha-glucosidase. Her parents are told that without treatment most affected infants die around 1 year of age from heart failure. Which of the following is the most appropriate disease-specific therapy?

explanation.summary: Enzyme replacement therapy for acid alpha-glucosidase, approved in 2006, improves cardiac and skeletal muscle function in Pompe disease.
explanation.whyCorrect: Classic Pompe disease has a very poor prognosis, but enzyme replacement therapy with acid alpha-glucosidase was approved in 2006 and has been shown to improve cardiac and skeletal muscle function. Without enzyme replacement the life expectancy of the pediatric form is about 1-2 years, so it is the treatment of choice.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Uncooked cornstarch prevents hypoglycemia in hepatic GSDs (types 0, I, III, VI); Pompe disease has normal glucose and the problem is lysosomal storage in muscle.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A ketogenic diet is the strategy for pyruvate dehydrogenase deficiency, supplying acetyl-CoA from ketones; it does not address lysosomal glycogen.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Methylene blue reduces methemoglobin in methemoglobinemia and has no role in Pompe disease.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Allopurinol for gout and sugar restriction are components of von Gierke disease management, not Pompe.

questions.topicName: Inborn Errors of Carbohydrate Metabolism

questions.stem: A child is diagnosed with Cori disease. In a healthy individual, glycogen phosphorylase liberates glucose 1-phosphate from a glycogen branch until only about 3-4 glucose residues remain. Which of the following best describes the subsequent action of the enzyme that is deficient in this patient?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Sequentially removes the remaining residues as glucose 1-phosphate units

choices.label: B
choices.text: Adds a new alpha-1,6 branch point so phosphorylase can continue working

choices.label: C
choices.text: Moves the residual residues to another chain and cleaves the alpha-1,6 glucose

choices.label: D
choices.text: Hydrolyzes the whole residual branch within the lysosome to free glucose

choices.label: E
choices.text: Converts the released glucose 1-phosphate into glucose 6-phosphate

explanation.summary: Debranching enzyme transfers the short residual branch onto another chain, exposing the single alpha-1,6-linked glucose, which it then cleaves; without it, glucose liberation is limited but not prevented.
explanation.whyCorrect: Glycogen phosphorylase stops when about 3-4 residues remain on a branch. The debranching enzyme (alpha-1,6 glucosidase) transfers this portion onto another branch, creating more substrate for phosphorylase, and this transfer exposes the final glucose unit directly at the alpha-1,6 branch point, which is then cleaved. In Cori disease the truncated polymer (limit dextrin) accumulates; the lack of this enzyme does not prevent glucose liberation but does limit the amount that can be liberated compared to an unaffected individual.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Releasing glucose 1-phosphate residue by residue is the job of glycogen phosphorylase, which cannot proceed past the last 3-4 residues near a branch point.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Creating alpha-1,6 branches is the function of branching enzyme during glycogen synthesis (deficient in Andersen disease), not glycogenolysis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Lysosomal hydrolysis of glycogen is performed by acid alpha-glucosidase (acid maltase), the enzyme deficient in Pompe disease.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Interconversion of glucose 1-phosphate and glucose 6-phosphate is a separate step downstream of debranching.

questions.topicName: Inborn Errors of Carbohydrate Metabolism
