questions.stem: A 7-year-old with confirmed debranching enzyme deficiency, previously followed only for hepatomegaly and mild fasting hypoglycemia, develops progressive muscle weakness, and echocardiography now shows cardiomyopathy. Which of the following best explains these new findings?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Glycogen has accumulated within the lysosomes of cardiac muscle

choices.label: B
choices.text: Recurrent hypoglycemia has caused chronic ischemic injury to muscle

choices.label: C
choices.text: Progressive lactic acidosis has impaired cardiac contractility

choices.label: D
choices.text: The deficient enzyme is required in muscle as well as the liver

choices.label: E
choices.text: Amylopectin-like glycogen has triggered an immune attack on muscle

explanation.summary: Because debranching enzyme is important in muscle as well as the liver, Cori patients may present with muscle weakness and cardiomyopathy.
explanation.whyCorrect: Unlike glucose-6-phosphatase, which is a hepatic (and renal) enzyme, the debranching enzyme is needed wherever glycogen is degraded, including skeletal and cardiac muscle. Its deficiency therefore causes limit dextrin accumulation in muscle too, so Cori disease can produce muscle symptoms such as weakness and cardiomyopathy in addition to its hepatic features.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Lysosomal glycogen storage in cardiac muscle is the mechanism of Pompe disease; in Cori disease the abnormal glycogen (limit dextrin) accumulates in the cytosol.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Hypoglycemia in Cori disease is mild, and hypoglycemia causes neurologic rather than muscular injury.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Cori patients have an intact Cori cycle and do not have lactic acidosis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Immune reaction against amylopectin-like glycogen describes Andersen disease (branching enzyme deficiency).

questions.topicName: Inborn Errors of Carbohydrate Metabolism

questions.stem: A 16-year-old boy with exercise-induced cramps and dark urine is being evaluated for McArdle disease. After an overnight fast, a blood pressure cuff is inflated on his upper arm while he repeatedly opens and closes his fist, and blood is drawn from the exercised arm. Compared with a resting sample, which of the following results most supports the diagnosis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Lactate rises markedly above the resting level

choices.label: B
choices.text: Lactate fails to rise above the resting level

choices.label: C
choices.text: Creatine kinase falls below the resting level

choices.label: D
choices.text: Glucose rises markedly above the resting level

choices.label: E
choices.text: Myoglobin falls below the resting level

explanation.summary: In the ischemic forearm exercise test, a patient with McArdle disease shows no increase in lactate compared with rest, provided they have fasted.
explanation.whyCorrect: The ischemic forearm exercise test, developed by Dr. McArdle, forces the forearm muscle to rely on anaerobic glycogen breakdown. Because muscle glycogen phosphorylase is deficient, glycogen cannot be broken down to fuel glycolysis, so no lactate is produced and the level does not rise above the resting state as long as the patient has fasted. Enzyme assay and gene analysis then confirm the diagnosis; a 15-minute cycling test to reproduce the second wind is another initial approach.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A marked rise in lactate is the normal response, since a healthy muscle breaks down glycogen and produces lactate during ischemic exercise.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Creatine kinase is persistently elevated in McArdle disease, even at rest, from ongoing muscle damage; it does not fall with exercise.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The test measures lactate production from muscle glycogen, not glucose; a fasted state is required precisely to prevent circulating glucose from masking the defect.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Myoglobin is released, not consumed, when muscle is damaged; a falling myoglobin level is not a feature of the test.

questions.topicName: Inborn Errors of Carbohydrate Metabolism

questions.stem: A 15-year-old runner is newly diagnosed with muscle glycogen phosphorylase deficiency. He asks how he should manage his diet and training. Which of the following is the most appropriate advice?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Adopt a high-fat, low-carbohydrate diet and rest from all physical activity

choices.label: B
choices.text: Restrict simple sugars and perform brief high-intensity intervals to build tolerance

choices.label: C
choices.text: Consume simple sugars before exertion and favor dynamic aerobic activity like walking

choices.label: D
choices.text: Eat uncooked cornstarch at bedtime and strictly avoid fructose, sucrose, and lactose

choices.label: E
choices.text: Increase protein intake and perform heavy resistance training several times weekly

explanation.summary: McArdle treatment is diet-based: plenty of complex carbohydrates, simple sugars before strenuous activity, avoidance of very intense exercise, and beneficial dynamic aerobic exercise such as cycling or walking.
explanation.whyCorrect: Because muscle cannot mobilize its own glycogen, McArdle patients depend on circulating glucose. They should eat a lot of complex carbohydrates and increase simple sugar (glucose, fructose, or sucrose) intake before strenuous activity. Very intense exercise should be avoided because it precipitates cramps and rhabdomyolysis, whereas dynamic aerobic exercise like cycling or walking is actually beneficial.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Carbohydrates are the needed fuel in McArdle disease, and complete rest is not recommended since dynamic aerobic exercise is beneficial.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Simple sugars should be increased before exertion, not restricted, and very intense exercise should be avoided.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Bedtime cornstarch and avoidance of fructose, sucrose, and lactose is the regimen for von Gierke disease, a hepatic disorder, not McArdle.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Heavy resistance training is the kind of very intense exercise McArdle patients must avoid, and protein does not replace the needed carbohydrate.

questions.topicName: Inborn Errors of Carbohydrate Metabolism

questions.stem: A 20-year-old man with known G6PD deficiency is started on a new medication. Two days later he develops headache, fatigue on exertion, and bluish lips. Pulse oximetry is low and does not improve with supplemental oxygen, and arterial blood is dark chocolate-brown. Cytochrome b5 reductase activity is normal. Which of the following best explains his presentation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Oxidative stress from the drug transiently oxidized hemoglobin iron to the ferric state

choices.label: B
choices.text: The drug irreversibly inactivated cytochrome b5 reductase within his red cells

choices.label: C
choices.text: Hemolysis released free hemoglobin that cannot bind oxygen in the plasma

choices.label: D
choices.text: Accumulated Heinz bodies physically obstruct hemoglobin's oxygen-binding sites

choices.label: E
choices.text: Elevated 2,3-BPG shifted the oxygen dissociation curve far to the right

explanation.summary: Methemoglobinemia has many causes: beyond the genetic form, oxidative stress such as that associated with G6PD deficiency or medications can prompt transient met-Hb formation.
explanation.whyCorrect: Met-Hb forms naturally under oxidative stress and is normally reconverted by cytochrome b5 reductase. In a G6PD-deficient patient, inadequate NADPH leaves the red cell unable to neutralize reactive oxygen species, so an oxidant medication can oxidize hemoglobin iron to the ferric (Fe3+) state faster than it can be reduced. The resulting transient methemoglobinemia causes cyanosis, chocolate-colored blood, fatigue upon exertion, and headache, and can potentiate oxygen delivery problems requiring medical attention even though cytochrome b5 reductase itself is normal.

whyWrongByChoice.B: The enzyme activity is normal; the met-Hb is generated by oxidative stress overwhelming the pathway, not by loss of the reductase.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Free hemoglobin from hemolysis lowers haptoglobin but does not produce chocolate-brown blood or oxygen-unresponsive cyanosis; the problem is ferric iron within hemoglobin.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Heinz bodies are precipitated oxidized hemoglobin that lead to hemolysis; they do not block oxygen binding on functional hemoglobin.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A rightward shift from 2,3-BPG improves oxygen unloading and is a feature of pyruvate kinase deficiency, not a cause of cyanosis with brown blood.

questions.topicName: Inborn Errors of Carbohydrate Metabolism

questions.stem: A 4-month-old with chronic hemolytic anemia is diagnosed with pyruvate kinase deficiency by enzymatic activity assay. The parents ask why only the red blood cells are affected when pyruvate kinase is needed for glycolysis in every cell of the body. Which of the following is the best explanation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Other tissues bypass the blocked step by running PEPCK in the reverse direction

choices.label: B
choices.text: Red cells alone depend on glycolysis; other tissues rely on the pentose phosphate pathway

choices.label: C
choices.text: The defect lies in a glucose transporter that is expressed only on red cells

choices.label: D
choices.text: Tissue-specific isoforms exist; a total deficiency would be incompatible with life

choices.label: E
choices.text: Hemoglobin binds and inactivates the mutant enzyme only inside red cells

explanation.summary: Pyruvate kinase exists as tissue isoforms; clinical deficiency involves the red cell isoform because a total tissue deficiency of pyruvate kinase would not be compatible with life.
explanation.whyCorrect: The concept of isoforms is central to pyruvate kinase deficiency. Because pyruvate kinase catalyzes the final control point of glycolysis in all cells, a mutation that eliminated the enzyme in every tissue would be lethal. The disease therefore reflects deficiency of the erythrocyte isoform, and because mature red cells are fully reliant on glycolysis for ATP production, the consequence is devastating specifically to red cell function.

whyWrongByChoice.A: PEPCK converts oxaloacetate to phosphoenolpyruvate to bypass pyruvate kinase during gluconeogenesis; it does not rescue glycolytic ATP production in other tissues.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Glycolysis operates in all tissues; the pentose phosphate pathway generates NADPH and ribose, not a substitute for glycolytic ATP.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The defect is in the pyruvate kinase enzyme, not in glucose uptake.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Hemoglobin does not bind or inactivate pyruvate kinase; tissue specificity comes from separate isoforms.

questions.topicName: Inborn Errors of Carbohydrate Metabolism

questions.stem: A 2-year-old with pyruvate kinase deficiency and chronic hemolysis is found to have a markedly elevated red-cell 2,3-BPG concentration. Which of the following best describes the effect of this finding on hemoglobin?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Increases oxygen affinity, shifting the dissociation curve to the left

choices.label: B
choices.text: Decreases oxygen affinity, shifting the dissociation curve to the right

choices.label: C
choices.text: Oxidizes the heme iron from the ferrous to the ferric state

choices.label: D
choices.text: Promotes binding of free hemoglobin tetramers to haptoglobin

choices.label: E
choices.text: Stabilizes oxidized hemoglobin polymers into Heinz bodies

explanation.summary: Elevated 2,3-BPG in pyruvate kinase deficiency decreases hemoglobin's affinity for oxygen, shifting the dissociation curve to the right and potentially aiding tissue oxygen delivery.
explanation.whyCorrect: The block at the final control point of glycolysis redistributes glycolytic intermediates and increases flux through the Rapoport-Luebering shunt that generates 2,3-BPG. While not a clinical diagnostic, this elevated 2,3-BPG is postulated to make the condition slightly more manageable, because 2,3-BPG decreases hemoglobin's affinity for oxygen (shifting the dissociation curve to the right) and so increases oxygen delivery to tissues.

whyWrongByChoice.A: 2,3-BPG lowers, not raises, oxygen affinity; a leftward shift would worsen tissue oxygen delivery.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Oxidation of heme iron to the ferric state produces methemoglobin and is driven by oxidative stress, not by 2,3-BPG.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Haptoglobin binding of free hemoglobin occurs during hemolysis and is unrelated to 2,3-BPG levels.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Heinz bodies are oxidized hemoglobin polymers from oxidative stress in G6PD deficiency; 2,3-BPG does not form them.

questions.topicName: Inborn Errors of Carbohydrate Metabolism

questions.stem: A peripheral blood smear from an infant with pyruvate kinase deficiency shows spiculated, fragile red cells prone to lysis. Which of the following best explains this change in red cell shape and integrity?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Oxidative cross-linking of membrane proteins by reactive oxygen species

choices.label: B
choices.text: Loss of NADPH leaving membrane lipids unprotected from peroxidation

choices.label: C
choices.text: ATP depletion compromising the Na+/K+ pump and other energy-dependent functions

choices.label: D
choices.text: Accumulation of limit dextrin glycogen within the red cell cytosol

choices.label: E
choices.text: Precipitation of ferric methemoglobin against the inner membrane

explanation.summary: Red cells lack mitochondria and rely solely on glycolysis for ATP; pyruvate kinase deficiency causes ATP loss that compromises the Na/K pump, producing spiculated, fragile cells prone to lysis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Mature erythrocytes have no mitochondria and depend entirely on substrate-level phosphorylation in glycolysis for ATP. When pyruvate kinase is absent, glycolysis is compromised and no lactate is formed from pyruvate to regenerate NAD+, so ATP production collapses. ATP loss impairs energy-dependent cellular functions such as the Na/K pump, and the cells become spiculated, fragile, and prone to lysis or turnover.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Oxidative damage from reactive oxygen species is the mechanism of G6PD deficiency, not pyruvate kinase deficiency.
whyWrongByChoice.B: NADPH is generated by the pentose phosphate pathway via G6PD; it is not the deficiency in pyruvate kinase disease.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Limit dextrin accumulates in liver and muscle in Cori disease; red cells do not store glycogen in this way.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Methemoglobin accumulation causes cyanosis and hypoxia without hemolysis, and is not the cause of spiculated cells.

questions.topicName: Inborn Errors of Carbohydrate Metabolism

questions.stem: Three infants are evaluated: one with G6PD deficiency during an acute crisis, one with pyruvate kinase deficiency, and one with congenital methemoglobinemia from cytochrome b5 reductase deficiency. Which of the following laboratory findings would be expected in the infant with methemoglobinemia but not in the other two?

explanation.summary: Met-Hb with ferric iron cannot bind oxygen, causing cyanosis and tissue hypoxia, but methemoglobinemia does not lead to hemolysis, so hemolysis markers such as haptoglobin remain normal.
explanation.whyCorrect: Both G6PD deficiency (oxidative stress) and pyruvate kinase deficiency (ATP loss) cause hemolytic anemia, with the typical findings of hyperbilirubinemia, elevated LDH, decreased haptoglobin, and increased reticulocytes. Methemoglobinemia is different: the ferric iron makes hemoglobin unable to bind and transport oxygen, producing cyanosis and tissue hypoxia, but the red cells are not destroyed. Without hemolysis, no surplus free hemoglobin consumes haptoglobin, so its level stays normal.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Elevated LDH is a hemolysis marker seen in both G6PD and pyruvate kinase deficiency, not in methemoglobinemia.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Reticulocytosis reflects marrow compensation for hemolysis, present in the two hemolytic disorders but not in methemoglobinemia.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hyperbilirubinemia results from hemoglobin breakdown during hemolysis and is expected in G6PD and pyruvate kinase deficiency.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Decreased haptoglobin is the shared finding of the two hemolytic disorders; it is the opposite of what methemoglobinemia shows.

questions.topicName: Inborn Errors of Carbohydrate Metabolism

questions.stem: A 5-month-old has fasting hypoglycemia, mild lactic acidosis, hepatomegaly, and hypotonia. Serum ammonia is normal. After several years of misdiagnosis, phosphoenolpyruvate carboxykinase deficiency is confirmed. Which of the following reactions is directly impaired in this patient?

explanation.summary: PEPCK converts oxaloacetate to phosphoenolpyruvate, a step required for gluconeogenesis because it bypasses the control point catalyzed by pyruvate kinase.
explanation.whyCorrect: Phosphoenolpyruvate carboxykinase (PEPCK) catalyzes oxaloacetate to phosphoenolpyruvate, allowing gluconeogenesis to circumvent the irreversible pyruvate kinase step of glycolysis. PEPCK deficiency is a rare inborn error that adversely impacts hepatic gluconeogenesis, so glucose cannot be made once glycogen stores are depleted, producing fasting hypoglycemia, mild lactic acidosis, hepatomegaly, and hypotonia. Symptoms begin in the neonatal period or a few months after birth, yet the average time to accurate diagnosis is 6 years because it is routinely misdiagnosed.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Pyruvate to oxaloacetate is catalyzed by pyruvate carboxylase; that deficiency would additionally cause hyperammonemia, which is absent here.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Pyruvate to acetyl-CoA is the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex reaction, whose deficiency causes prominent lactic acidosis with severe CNS dysfunction rather than a primarily gluconeogenic defect.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Glucose 6-phosphate to glucose is catalyzed by glucose-6-phosphatase, deficient in von Gierke disease.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Phosphoenolpyruvate to pyruvate is the pyruvate kinase reaction of glycolysis, the control point that PEPCK bypasses.

questions.topicName: Inborn Errors of Carbohydrate Metabolism

questions.stem: A 6-year-old is finally diagnosed with PEPCK deficiency after years of evaluation for recurrent fasting hypoglycemia and hepatomegaly. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

choices.label: A
choices.text: High-fat, low-carbohydrate diet so ketone bodies supply the brain

choices.label: B
choices.text: Enzyme replacement therapy to restore hepatic enzyme activity

choices.label: C
choices.text: Strict avoidance of sucrose, fructose, and lactose in the diet

choices.label: D
choices.text: Avoidance of fasting plus extra carbohydrate during illness and exercise

choices.label: E
choices.text: Thiamin and lipoic acid supplementation to recover enzyme activity

explanation.summary: PEPCK deficiency is treated by avoiding fasting and increasing intake of carbohydrate-rich sources, especially during exercise and illness when the body needs additional energy.
explanation.whyCorrect: Because hepatic gluconeogenesis is impaired, patients with PEPCK deficiency become hypoglycemic whenever they must rely on making new glucose, particularly once glycogen stores are depleted. Treatment therefore focuses on avoiding fasting and increasing carbohydrate-rich intake, which is especially important in times of exercise and illness when the body needs additional sources of energy.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A ketogenic diet is the strategy for pyruvate dehydrogenase deficiency; restricting carbohydrate would worsen hypoglycemia in a gluconeogenic defect.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Enzyme replacement therapy is available for Pompe disease (acid alpha-glucosidase), not for PEPCK deficiency.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Avoiding sucrose, fructose, and lactose is a von Gierke disease measure to limit glucose-6-phosphate accumulation; it is not part of PEPCK management.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Thiamin and lipoic acid are coenzymes tried in pyruvate dehydrogenase deficiency, not PEPCK deficiency.

questions.topicName: Inborn Errors of Carbohydrate Metabolism

questions.stem: A neonate with failure to thrive, prominent lactic acidosis, hypotonia, and ataxia is diagnosed with pyruvate dehydrogenase complex deficiency. Before committing to a dietary strategy, the team attempts a trial of supplementation to determine whether enzyme activity can be recovered in the presence of excess coenzymes. Which of the following is the most appropriate supplementation?

explanation.summary: Vitamin supplementation with PDH coenzymes such as thiamin and lipoic acid is routinely attempted to see whether PDH activity is recovered in the presence of excess coenzymes.
explanation.whyCorrect: The pyruvate dehydrogenase complex requires coenzymes including thiamin and lipoic acid. In PDH deficiency, supplementation with these coenzymes is routinely attempted to determine if residual enzyme activity can be recovered when they are present in excess. If that fails, patients are placed on a high-fat, low-carbohydrate diet so that ketone bodies become the predominant CNS fuel.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Vitamin B12 and folate are not coenzymes of the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Vitamin C and vitamin E are antioxidants and play no role in the PDH reaction.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Vitamin D and calcium relate to bone metabolism, not to pyruvate dehydrogenase activity.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Vitamin K and iron are not PDH coenzymes and would not recover enzyme activity.

questions.topicName: Inborn Errors of Carbohydrate Metabolism

questions.stem: Two infants present with fasting hypoglycemia and acidosis. Enzyme studies show PEPCK deficiency in the first and pyruvate carboxylase deficiency in the second. Beyond gluconeogenesis, which of the following pathways is compromised in the second infant but remains intact in the first?

explanation.summary: Pyruvate carboxylase supports the TCA cycle through an anaplerotic reaction converting pyruvate to oxaloacetate, so its deficiency compromises the TCA cycle (and urea cycle) in addition to gluconeogenesis, whereas PEPCK deficiency affects gluconeogenesis alone.
explanation.whyCorrect: Both enzymes act in the gluconeogenic pathway, but pyruvate carboxylase also plays a critical role in aiding the TCA cycle to run efficiently by replenishing oxaloacetate through an anaplerotic reaction. When it is deficient, dampened oxaloacetate formation deprives the cycle of intermediates needed for ATP formation and also starves the urea cycle, producing hyperammonemia. PEPCK, by contrast, acts downstream on oxaloacetate and its deficiency does not compromise the TCA cycle.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Glycolysis proceeds normally in both disorders; neither enzyme is part of the glycolytic pathway.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Glycogenolysis depends on glycogen phosphorylase and debranching enzyme and is unaffected in both gluconeogenic defects.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The pentose phosphate pathway runs from glucose 6-phosphate and is not dependent on pyruvate carboxylase or PEPCK.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Glycogen synthesis requires glycogen synthase and branching enzyme and is not compromised by either deficiency.

questions.topicName: Inborn Errors of Carbohydrate Metabolism

questions.stem: A 3-week-old infant fed a standard milk-based formula develops hypoglycemia and is found to have bilateral cataracts. An inborn error of monosaccharide metabolism is suspected, in which accumulation of a phosphorylated sugar intermediate inhibits glycogen breakdown and gluconeogenesis and depletes ATP. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanation.summary: Inborn errors of fructose and galactose metabolism share a mechanism of phosphorylated monosaccharide intermediate accumulation, but cataracts are unique to galactosemia.
explanation.whyCorrect: Both fructose and galactose disorders range from mild to severe depending on accumulation of the phosphorylated monosaccharide intermediate, which inhibits glycogen breakdown and gluconeogenesis and causes ATP depletion, explaining the hypoglycemia. What distinguishes galactosemia is that cataracts are unique to it, so hypoglycemia plus cataracts in a milk-fed infant points to galactosemia.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Hereditary fructose intolerance shares the phosphorylated-intermediate mechanism and hypoglycemia, but cataracts are not a feature and fructose, not milk sugar, is the trigger.
whyWrongByChoice.B: von Gierke disease is a glycogen storage disease from glucose-6-phosphatase deficiency; it does not involve a monosaccharide intermediate or cataracts.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Cori disease is a debranching enzyme defect with limit dextrin accumulation and mild hypoglycemia, not cataracts.
whyWrongByChoice.D: PEPCK deficiency impairs gluconeogenesis directly at the oxaloacetate step and is not associated with cataracts.

questions.topicName: Inborn Errors of Carbohydrate Metabolism

questions.stem: A 12-year-old boy is evaluated for tonsils that appear strikingly orange-yellow on examination with no evidence of infection. A fasting lipid panel shows total cholesterol 100 mg/dL, HDL 5 mg/dL, LDL 50 mg/dL, and triglycerides 250 mg/dL. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanation.summary: Enlarged orange-yellow tonsils with low HDL and low total cholesterol is the classic presentation of Tangier disease.
explanation.whyCorrect: Tangier disease results from a deficiency of the ABC1 transporter, which normally promotes cholesterol efflux from peripheral tissue onto HDL. The failure of efflux causes intracellular cholesterol accumulation, producing low HDL and low overall cholesterol, and the characteristic orange-yellow discoloration and enlargement of the tonsils.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Familial hypercholesterolemia causes very high LDL cholesterol, not the low cholesterol and low HDL seen here.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Familial hyperchylomicronemia produces triglycerides often exceeding 1,000 mg/dL, far higher than this panel.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Familial hypertriglyceridemia shows high VLDL/triglycerides with low HDL but does not cause orange tonsils or low total cholesterol.
whyWrongByChoice.E: MCAD deficiency disrupts fatty acid oxidation and causes hypoketotic hypoglycemia, not orange tonsils or an abnormal lipid panel.

questions.topicName: Dyslipidemias, Lipid Storage Disorders, and other defects in Lipid Metabolism

questions.stem: A patient with confirmed Tangier disease has intracellular accumulation of cholesterol within peripheral tissues. A defect in which of the following is most directly responsible for this abnormality?

explanation.summary: Tangier disease is caused by a deficiency of the ABC1 transporter that mediates cholesterol efflux from peripheral tissue.
explanation.whyCorrect: ABC1 is the transporter that promotes cholesterol release from extra-hepatic tissue so it can be picked up by HDL via LCAT activity. When ABC1 is absent, cholesterol cannot leave the cell and accumulates intracellularly, and the serum shows low HDL and low total cholesterol.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Defective LDL receptors cause familial hypercholesterolemia with high LDL, not intracellular cholesterol accumulation with low HDL.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Lipoprotein lipase deficiency impairs triglyceride clearance and causes familial hyperchylomicronemia.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Apolipoprotein E defects cause familial dysbetalipoproteinemia with retained IDL and chylomicron remnants.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The OCTN2 transporter handles carnitine reabsorption and its defect causes primary carnitine deficiency, not Tangier disease.

questions.topicName: Dyslipidemias, Lipid Storage Disorders, and other defects in Lipid Metabolism

questions.stem: A 38-year-old woman presents with an increasing number of large, bumpy growths over her knees and buttocks as well as distinctive yellow-orange streaks in the creases of her palms. Both her mother and father developed heart disease before age 40. Her serum cholesterol and triglycerides are both elevated. Which of the following primary lipid disorders is most likely?

explanation.summary: Palmar xanthomas plus tuberoeruptive xanthomas with elevated cholesterol and triglycerides point to familial dysbetalipoproteinemia (type III).
explanation.whyCorrect: Palmar xanthomas along the palmar creases are pathognomonic for familial dysbetalipoproteinemia, which also commonly causes tuberoeruptive xanthomas on the knees and elbows. The disorder stems from an apolipoprotein E defect that impairs clearance of chylomicron and VLDL remnants, producing moderate elevations in both cholesterol and triglycerides and premature atherosclerotic heart disease, consistent with the family history.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Familial combined hyperlipidemia causes elevated cholesterol and triglycerides but does not produce pathognomonic palmar xanthomas.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Familial hypercholesterolemia raises cholesterol with near-normal triglycerides and does not cause palmar xanthomas.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Familial hyperchylomicronemia presents with markedly high triglycerides and near-normal cholesterol, without palmar xanthomas.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Familial hypertriglyceridemia shows high triglycerides with relatively normal cholesterol and lacks palmar xanthomas.

questions.topicName: Dyslipidemias, Lipid Storage Disorders, and other defects in Lipid Metabolism

questions.stem: A newborn from a family with a known lipid disorder is found to have very high LDL cholesterol at birth with normal triglycerides. The child's affected relatives suffered myocardial infarctions in early adulthood. Which of the following best explains the underlying defect?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Overproduction of VLDL by the liver

choices.label: C
choices.text: Too few or absent LDL receptors

explanation.summary: Familial hypercholesterolemia results from too few or absent LDL receptors, producing very high LDL with normal triglycerides.
explanation.whyCorrect: Familial hypercholesterolemia (type IIa) is an autosomal dominant disorder caused by mutations that reduce or eliminate functional LDL receptors, most often in the LDL receptor gene itself. Without adequate receptors, LDL cannot be cleared, so LDL cholesterol is very high even at birth while triglycerides remain near normal, driving early atherosclerosis and myocardial infarction.

whyWrongByChoice.A: VLDL overproduction underlies familial hypertriglyceridemia, which elevates triglycerides rather than LDL.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Lipoprotein lipase deficiency causes familial hyperchylomicronemia with very high triglycerides, not isolated high LDL.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A defective apolipoprotein E causes familial dysbetalipoproteinemia with elevated remnants and both cholesterol and triglycerides.
whyWrongByChoice.E: ABC1 transporter deficiency causes Tangier disease with low HDL and low total cholesterol.

questions.topicName: Dyslipidemias, Lipid Storage Disorders, and other defects in Lipid Metabolism

questions.stem: A 9-month-old infant is admitted with severe abdominal pain, and a fasting lipid panel reveals triglycerides of 1,400 mg/dL with cholesterol near the reference range. Genetic testing confirms a deficiency of lipoprotein lipase. This patient is at greatest risk for which of the following complications?

explanation.summary: Familial hyperchylomicronemia causes markedly high triglycerides that place patients primarily at risk for pancreatitis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Lipoprotein lipase (or apo C-II) deficiency impairs degradation and clearance of triglyceride-rich chylomicrons, so triglycerides often exceed 1,000 mg/dL. These patients are primarily at risk for acute pancreatitis. Because cholesterol stays within or near reference ranges, the risk for ischemic heart disease is not increased.

whyWrongByChoice.B: The risk for ischemic heart disease is not increased in familial hyperchylomicronemia because cholesterol is near normal.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Stroke is an atherosclerotic complication tied to elevated LDL, which is not the abnormality here.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The brick does not attribute hepatic cirrhosis to this disorder; pancreatitis is the primary risk.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Peripheral arterial disease reflects atherosclerosis, which is not the main risk given near-normal cholesterol.

questions.topicName: Dyslipidemias, Lipid Storage Disorders, and other defects in Lipid Metabolism

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man has a lipid panel showing moderately elevated VLDL and triglycerides with a total cholesterol near the reference range and low HDL. He has no palmar xanthomas, and the disorder is attributed to hepatic overproduction of a single lipoprotein class. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanation.summary: Familial hypertriglyceridemia (type IV) is driven by hepatic overproduction of VLDL, elevating VLDL and triglycerides with near-normal cholesterol.
explanation.whyCorrect: Familial hypertriglyceridemia results from hepatic overproduction of VLDL, so the lipid panel shows elevated VLDL and triglycerides while total cholesterol stays relatively normal and HDL is often low. Because LDL is not increased, a strong association with atherosclerotic heart disease has not been found, though high triglycerides raise the risk for acute pancreatitis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Familial hypercholesterolemia produces very high LDL cholesterol with normal triglycerides, not the reverse.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Familial dysbetalipoproteinemia elevates IDL and chylomicron remnants and typically causes palmar xanthomas.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Tangier disease causes low HDL and low total cholesterol from an ABC1 transporter defect, not VLDL overproduction.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Familial hyperchylomicronemia elevates chylomicrons from LPL deficiency rather than VLDL overproduction by the liver.

questions.topicName: Dyslipidemias, Lipid Storage Disorders, and other defects in Lipid Metabolism

questions.stem: A 30-year-old man with a strong family history of early heart disease has a lipid panel showing elevated LDL, elevated VLDL, elevated triglycerides, and low HDL. Analysis reveals increased apolipoprotein B-100 with hepatic overproduction of small VLDL and dense LDL particles. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanation.summary: Combined elevation of LDL, VLDL, and triglycerides with increased apo B-100 is characteristic of familial combined hyperlipidemia (type IIb).
explanation.whyCorrect: Familial combined hyperlipidemia is the most common primary lipid disorder overall and is polygenic. Mutations that increase apolipoprotein B-100 drive hepatic overproduction of small VLDL and small dense LDL particles, and decreased hepatic LDL clearance from increased PCSK9 activity contributes as well. Patients show combined elevations of LDL, VLDL, and triglycerides with low HDL and accelerated atherosclerosis.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Familial hypercholesterolemia raises LDL alone with normal triglycerides, not a combined pattern.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Familial hyperchylomicronemia elevates chylomicrons and triglycerides from LPL deficiency, without high LDL.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Familial hypertriglyceridemia elevates VLDL and triglycerides but does not increase LDL.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Tangier disease shows low HDL and low total cholesterol rather than combined elevations.

questions.topicName: Dyslipidemias, Lipid Storage Disorders, and other defects in Lipid Metabolism

questions.stem: A researcher is studying a monoclonal antibody that inhibits PCSK9 as a therapy for dyslipidemia. Inhibiting PCSK9 lowers circulating LDL by which of the following mechanisms?

choices.label: C
choices.text: Blocking lipoprotein lipase on endothelial cells

choices.label: D
choices.text: Enhancing cholesterol efflux through the ABC1 transporter

explanation.summary: PCSK9 normally targets LDL receptors for lysosomal degradation, so inhibiting it preserves receptors and lowers LDL.
explanation.whyCorrect: PCSK9 binds LDL receptors on hepatocytes; the complex is internalized and directed to lysosomes for degradation, preventing the receptor from recycling back to the cell surface. Inhibiting PCSK9 with a monoclonal antibody spares the receptors so they return to the surface and continue clearing LDL, lowering circulating LDL levels.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Increasing cholesterol synthesis would raise, not lower, circulating lipids and is not how PCSK9 inhibition works.
whyWrongByChoice.C: PCSK9 does not act on lipoprotein lipase; blocking LPL would impair triglyceride clearance.
whyWrongByChoice.D: ABC1-mediated efflux is the pathway defective in Tangier disease and is unrelated to PCSK9's action on LDL receptors.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Stimulating VLDL overproduction would worsen dyslipidemia and is not the mechanism of PCSK9 inhibitors.

questions.topicName: Dyslipidemias, Lipid Storage Disorders, and other defects in Lipid Metabolism

questions.stem: In the early atherosclerotic lesion of a patient with familial hypercholesterolemia, macrophages within the arterial wall become engorged with lipid and transform into foam cells. Which of the following best describes the process that generates these foam cells?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Macrophages take up oxidized LDL through scavenger receptors

choices.label: B
choices.text: Macrophages clear chylomicron remnants through apolipoprotein E receptors

choices.label: C
choices.text: Macrophages accumulate carnitine because of an OCTN2 defect

choices.label: D
choices.text: Macrophages overproduce VLDL and store it internally

choices.label: E
choices.text: Macrophages fail to efflux cholesterol because of an ABC1 defect

explanation.summary: Foam cells form when macrophages take up oxidized LDL via low-affinity, nonregulated scavenger receptors.
explanation.whyCorrect: When LDL is abundant it becomes more susceptible to oxidative damage, generating the pro-atherogenic oxLDL particle. Monocytes adhere to injured endothelium and become macrophages, which take up modified (oxidized) LDL through nonspecific scavenger receptors that are not downregulated by intracellular cholesterol. This unchecked uptake fills the macrophage with lipid, transforming it into a foam cell.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Apolipoprotein E-mediated remnant clearance occurs in the liver and is not the mechanism of foam cell formation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Carnitine accumulation from an OCTN2 defect relates to fatty acid oxidation, not foam cell formation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Foam cells form by taking up oxidized LDL, not by internally overproducing VLDL.
whyWrongByChoice.E: An ABC1 efflux defect describes Tangier disease; foam cells here form from oxLDL uptake via scavenger receptors.

questions.topicName: Dyslipidemias, Lipid Storage Disorders, and other defects in Lipid Metabolism

questions.stem: A patient's lipid panel is described as demonstrating reverse cholesterol transport in which a lipoprotein carries cholesterol from peripheral tissues back to the liver and donates apolipoproteins to other particles. Blood levels of this lipoprotein are inversely related to cardiac disease. Which lipoprotein is being described?

explanation.summary: HDL performs reverse cholesterol transport and donates apolipoproteins, and its levels are inversely related to cardiac disease.
explanation.whyCorrect: HDL delivers cholesterol from the tissues back to the liver, a process known as reverse cholesterol transport. It also acts as a 'helper,' donating important apolipoproteins to other lipoproteins so they can be recognized and taken up by the appropriate tissues. HDL blood levels are inversely related to cardiac disease.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Chylomicrons deliver dietary triglycerides and cholesterol from the intestines to peripheral tissues.
whyWrongByChoice.B: VLDL delivers liver-synthesized triglycerides to tissues, not cholesterol back to the liver.
whyWrongByChoice.C: IDL is a transitional particle between VLDL and LDL and does not carry out reverse cholesterol transport.
whyWrongByChoice.D: LDL delivers cholesterol from the liver to the tissues and its elevation is directly linked to cardiac disease.

questions.topicName: Dyslipidemias, Lipid Storage Disorders, and other defects in Lipid Metabolism

questions.stem: A 10-month-old infant develops lethargy and hypoglycemia during a viral illness with poor oral intake. Laboratory studies show low glucose with inappropriately low ketones. The child is subsequently diagnosed with medium-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase (MCAD) deficiency. The hypoketotic hypoglycemia in this disorder is best explained by which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Excess acetyl-CoA overwhelming the citric acid cycle

choices.label: B
choices.text: Failure to produce acetyl-CoA from beta-oxidation

choices.label: C
choices.text: Increased urinary loss of carnitine through OCTN2

choices.label: D
choices.text: Overproduction of ketone bodies by the liver

choices.label: E
choices.text: Deficient LDL receptor recycling in hepatocytes

explanation.summary: Both MCAD and carnitine deficiency cause hypoketotic hypoglycemia because impaired beta-oxidation fails to generate acetyl-CoA.
explanation.whyCorrect: Hypoketotic hypoglycemia results from a failure to produce acetyl-CoA through beta-oxidation. Acetyl-CoA is the required substrate for ketogenesis, its generation supplies ATP needed for gluconeogenesis, and it is an allosteric activator of pyruvate carboxylase. When beta-oxidation is blocked, ketones cannot be made and glucose cannot be maintained, a state worsened by fasting or illness.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The problem is too little acetyl-CoA from blocked beta-oxidation, not an excess.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Urinary carnitine wasting is the mechanism in primary carnitine deficiency, not the direct cause of hypoketotic hypoglycemia in MCAD deficiency.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Ketone production is decreased, not overproduced, which is why the hypoglycemia is hypoketotic.
whyWrongByChoice.E: LDL receptor recycling relates to cholesterol handling and has no role in this fatty acid oxidation defect.

questions.topicName: Dyslipidemias, Lipid Storage Disorders, and other defects in Lipid Metabolism

questions.stem: A dietitian is planning nutritional supplementation for two patients: one with systemic primary carnitine deficiency and one with MCAD deficiency. Which dietary supplement could be considered for the patient with carnitine deficiency but would not be appropriate for the patient with MCAD deficiency?

explanation.summary: Medium-chain fatty acids bypass carnitine transport and are useful in carnitine deficiency but cannot be metabolized in MCAD deficiency.
explanation.whyCorrect: Medium-chain fatty acids freely diffuse into the cell and mitochondria, bypassing the need for carnitine, so they can be metabolized in primary carnitine deficiency. In MCAD deficiency, however, the enzyme needed to catabolize these very substrates is missing, so MCFAs would only accumulate. MCFA supplementation is therefore considered only for carnitine deficiency, not MCAD.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Long-chain fatty acids should be avoided in both deficiencies because neither can properly catabolize them.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Short-chain fatty acids can be strategically provided in both deficiencies.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Carnitine supplementation is considered in both conditions and is routine in primary carnitine deficiency.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Glucose supports both patients by preventing catabolic states and is not contraindicated in either.

questions.topicName: Dyslipidemias, Lipid Storage Disorders, and other defects in Lipid Metabolism

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man with poorly controlled type 2 diabetes mellitus, untreated hypothyroidism, and heavy alcohol use is found on routine bloodwork to have elevated cholesterol and triglycerides. He has no family history of early cardiovascular disease. Which of the following best characterizes his lipid disorder?

explanation.summary: Elevated cholesterol and triglycerides driven by conditions such as diabetes, hypothyroidism, and heavy alcohol use represent a secondary lipid disorder, by far the most common category.
explanation.whyCorrect: Hyperlipidemias with a known cause are divided into primary and secondary disorders, and the secondary disorders are by far the most common. They are elevations of cholesterol and triglycerides caused by conditions like diabetes mellitus, chronic kidney disease, liver disease, hypothyroidism, obesity, smoking, heavy alcohol consumption, and medications. This patient has several of these drivers and no family history of early cardiovascular disease.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Primary dyslipidemias are inherited defects in lipid metabolism, typically with a family history of early-onset cardiovascular disease, which this patient lacks.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Fredrickson type I is familial hyperchylomicronemia, an inherited LPL or apo C-2 deficiency, not an acquired disorder from diabetes and alcohol.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Tangier disease is an inherited ABC1 transporter deficiency producing low HDL and low cholesterol, not elevated lipids from systemic illness.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Familial combined hyperlipidemia is a polygenic primary disorder; this patient's elevations are explained by his acquired conditions.

questions.topicName: Dyslipidemias, Lipid Storage Disorders, and other defects in Lipid Metabolism

questions.stem: A registry of patients diagnosed with primary lipid disorders is reviewed. Which of the following groups of Fredrickson phenotypes together account for more than 95% of these patients?

explanation.summary: Fredrickson types IIa, IIb, and IV are the most common primary lipid disorders, accounting for more than 95% of diagnosed patients.
explanation.whyCorrect: Familial hypercholesterolemia (IIa), familial combined hyperlipidemia (IIb), and familial hypertriglyceridemia (IV) are the most common primary lipid disorders. Together they account for more than 95% of patients diagnosed with a primary lipid disorder, whereas type I (hyperchylomicronemia) and type III (dysbetalipoproteinemia) are uncommon.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Type I and type III are uncommon disorders and are not among the three most common phenotypes.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Type I and type III are both uncommon; only type IV in this group is among the most common phenotypes.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Type III (familial dysbetalipoproteinemia) is uncommon; type IIb belongs in the common group instead.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Type III is uncommon; type IIa (familial hypercholesterolemia) belongs in the common group instead.

questions.topicName: Dyslipidemias, Lipid Storage Disorders, and other defects in Lipid Metabolism

questions.stem: A 52-year-old woman is found to have an LDL cholesterol of 210 mg/dL on routine screening bloodwork. She feels well and asks why she has never noticed any symptoms of her condition. Which of the following is the best explanation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Her lipid disorder must be secondary rather than primary

choices.label: B
choices.text: Elevated lipid levels are asymptomatic until complications develop

choices.label: C
choices.text: Her LDL particles have not yet been oxidized to oxLDL

choices.label: D
choices.text: Symptoms of dyslipidemia occur only in homozygous patients

choices.label: E
choices.text: Her HDL level is high enough to prevent any symptoms

explanation.summary: Elevated lipid levels themselves are asymptomatic; symptoms, when present, come from complications such as coronary artery disease or pancreatitis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Elevated lipid levels are asymptomatic, so patients are often unaware of the condition, which is commonly discovered on routine screening bloodwork or when evaluating a stroke or heart attack. When symptoms do occur, they are due to complications rather than the lipid disorder itself, such as chest pain from coronary artery disease or abdominal pain from pancreatitis secondary to high triglycerides.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Both primary and secondary dyslipidemias are asymptomatic; the absence of symptoms does not distinguish between them.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Oxidation of LDL drives foam cell formation and atherosclerosis, but the absence of symptoms is not explained by a lack of oxLDL.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Homozygous familial hypercholesterolemia is more severe, but heterozygotes and other dyslipidemias also produce complications; lipid elevation itself is silent in everyone.
whyWrongByChoice.E: HDL is inversely related to cardiac disease, but it does not suppress symptoms; elevated lipids are silent regardless of HDL.

questions.topicName: Dyslipidemias, Lipid Storage Disorders, and other defects in Lipid Metabolism

questions.stem: A biochemistry lecture reviews why patients with primary dyslipidemias develop high circulating levels of cholesterol or triglycerides. Which of the following is the most common underlying mechanism across these disorders?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Increased intestinal absorption of dietary cholesterol

choices.label: C
choices.text: Increased lipolysis of triglyceride in adipose tissue

choices.label: D
choices.text: Decreased LCAT activity on circulating HDL

choices.label: E
choices.text: Abnormal lipoproteins or receptors reducing lipid clearance

explanation.summary: Primary dyslipidemias are more often caused by abnormalities of lipoprotein structure or lipoprotein receptors that decrease lipid clearance, rather than by increased synthesis.
explanation.whyCorrect: One might expect primary dyslipidemias to arise from abnormally increased synthesis of cholesterol or triglycerides. Instead, they are more often abnormalities of lipoprotein structure or of lipoprotein receptors, leading to decreased lipid clearance. The specific way clearance is disrupted differs among the disorders (LPL deficiency, too few LDL receptors, defective apo E), and the resulting high circulating lipid levels increase atherosclerosis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Increased de novo synthesis through HMG-CoA reductase is not the usual basis of the primary dyslipidemias; clearance defects are.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Enhanced dietary absorption is not the mechanism described for the inherited disorders.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Adipose lipolysis releases free fatty acids but is not the mechanism underlying the primary lipoprotein disorders.
whyWrongByChoice.D: LCAT participates in HDL cholesterol transport, but decreased LCAT activity is not the common mechanism of the Fredrickson dyslipidemias.

questions.topicName: Dyslipidemias, Lipid Storage Disorders, and other defects in Lipid Metabolism

questions.stem: A 3-year-old girl with recurrent episodes of severe abdominal pain has a fasting triglyceride level of 2,200 mg/dL, and an enzyme assay demonstrates absent lipoprotein lipase activity. In a healthy child, this enzyme on the surface of endothelial cells primarily degrades the triglycerides carried in which of the following?

explanation.summary: Lipoprotein lipase on endothelial cells degrades circulating triglycerides carried mainly in VLDL and chylomicrons to free fatty acids.
explanation.whyCorrect: Lipoprotein lipase sits mainly on the surface of endothelial cells and degrades circulating triglycerides, mainly those in VLDL and chylomicrons, to free fatty acids. When LPL (or its cofactor apo C-2) is deficient, triglyceride degradation and clearance fall, producing the very high triglyceride levels (often above 1,000 mg/dL) of familial hyperchylomicronemia.

whyWrongByChoice.A: LDL and HDL are cholesterol-carrying particles; LDL is cleared by the LDL receptor rather than by LPL-mediated triglyceride hydrolysis.
whyWrongByChoice.B: IDL is a transitional particle between VLDL and LDL; the triglyceride-rich substrates of LPL are chylomicrons and VLDL.
whyWrongByChoice.C: HDL performs reverse cholesterol transport and donates apolipoproteins; it is not the triglyceride-rich substrate of LPL.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Remnants and IDL are what remain after LPL has acted on chylomicrons and VLDL and are cleared by the liver via apo E.

questions.topicName: Dyslipidemias, Lipid Storage Disorders, and other defects in Lipid Metabolism

questions.stem: A laboratory technician centrifuges blood samples from two patients with primary dyslipidemias. The supernatant from the first sample is creamy and milky, while the supernatant from the second is only turbid and faintly opaque. Which of the following best explains the difference in appearance?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Higher cholesterol content of the lipoproteins in the milky sample

choices.label: B
choices.text: Greater overall triglyceride content of the lipoproteins in the milky sample

choices.label: C
choices.text: Higher apolipoprotein content of the lipoproteins in the milky sample

choices.label: D
choices.text: Presence of oxidized LDL particles in the milky sample

choices.label: E
choices.text: Predominance of small, dense LDL particles in the milky sample

explanation.summary: A creamy or milky supernatant reflects excess triglycerides, whereas an increase in VLDL produces only a turbid, faintly opaque sample; the difference is the triglyceride content of the lipoproteins.
explanation.whyCorrect: The supernatant of spun blood in hypertriglyceridemia and hyperchylomicronemia is creamy or milky because of the excess triglycerides. By contrast, an increase in VLDL is often described as turbid or faintly opaque. The difference has to do with the overall triglyceride content within the respective lipoproteins.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cholesterol-rich particles such as LDL do not produce a milky supernatant; the milky appearance is a triglyceride effect.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Apolipoprotein content is not what distinguishes a milky from a turbid supernatant.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Oxidized LDL drives foam cell formation in the arterial wall but does not account for the appearance of spun plasma.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Small, dense LDL particles are a feature of familial combined hyperlipidemia and do not create a creamy supernatant.

questions.topicName: Dyslipidemias, Lipid Storage Disorders, and other defects in Lipid Metabolism

questions.stem: A genetics lecture describes familial hypercholesterolemia as the most common autosomal dominant disorder in humans. Approximately how frequently is this disorder seen in the population?

explanation.summary: Familial hypercholesterolemia (Fredrickson type IIa) is seen in about 1 in 300 patients and is the most common autosomal dominant disorder in humans.
explanation.whyCorrect: Fredrickson type IIa, familial hypercholesterolemia, is an autosomal dominant disorder seen in about 1:300 patients, making it the most common autosomal dominant disorder in humans. It is caused by mutations, most often within the LDL receptor gene itself, that lead to too few or absent LDL receptors.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A frequency of 1 in 30 is far higher than stated; even familial combined hyperlipidemia, the most common primary lipid disorder overall, affects only 1% to 2% of the population.
whyWrongByChoice.B: 1 in 3,000 is ten times rarer than the stated prevalence for familial hypercholesterolemia.
whyWrongByChoice.C: 1 in 30,000 would describe a rare disorder, not the most common autosomal dominant condition in humans.
whyWrongByChoice.D: 1 in 300,000 is far too rare for a disorder described as the most common autosomal dominant disorder in humans.

questions.topicName: Dyslipidemias, Lipid Storage Disorders, and other defects in Lipid Metabolism

questions.stem: A 5-year-old boy has an LDL cholesterol of 750 mg/dL with cutaneous and tendon xanthomas. Both parents have elevated LDL and a history of early myocardial infarction, and genetic testing shows the boy carries two mutant copies of the LDL receptor gene. If untreated, which of the following is the most likely outcome?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Death from cardiac disease before age 20

choices.label: E
choices.text: Normal life expectancy with dietary changes alone

explanation.summary: Homozygous familial hypercholesterolemia is uncommon but severe; affected patients often die of cardiac disease before age 20.
explanation.whyCorrect: In familial hypercholesterolemia, homozygous patients (uncommon) often die of cardiac disease before age 20, whereas heterozygotes have an increased risk of atherosclerotic disease. The very high LDL present even at birth causes severe atherosclerosis via foam cell formation, and myocardial infarction can occur within the first two decades of life.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Pancreatitis is the complication of very high triglycerides (typically above 1,000 mg/dL); triglycerides are near normal in familial hypercholesterolemia.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hepatomegaly with orange-yellow tonsils describes Tangier disease, an ABC1 transporter deficiency with low HDL and low cholesterol.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Hypoketotic hypoglycemia results from defects in beta-oxidation such as MCAD or carnitine deficiency, not from LDL receptor loss.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Untreated homozygous disease carries a high risk of early cardiac death; diet alone would not be expected to normalize the outcome.

questions.topicName: Dyslipidemias, Lipid Storage Disorders, and other defects in Lipid Metabolism

questions.stem: A 34-year-old man is diagnosed with familial hypercholesterolemia after a myocardial infarction. He is the first person in his family to receive this diagnosis. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step regarding his relatives?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Genetic testing only for relatives who develop chest pain

choices.label: B
choices.text: Lipid screening of his immediate family members

choices.label: C
choices.text: Reassurance that heterozygous relatives are unaffected

choices.label: D
choices.text: Screening limited to his male relatives

choices.label: E
choices.text: Deferral of screening until relatives reach age 40

explanation.summary: Identification of the first case of familial hypercholesterolemia in a family necessitates screening of the immediate family members.
explanation.whyCorrect: Familial hypercholesterolemia is an autosomal dominant disorder in which LDL is very high even at birth and heart disease commonly develops in young adulthood. Because elevated lipid levels are asymptomatic, identification of the first case in a family necessitates screening of immediate family members so that affected relatives can be found before complications occur.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Waiting for chest pain defeats the purpose of screening, since lipid elevations are silent until a complication such as myocardial infarction occurs.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Heterozygotes have an increased risk of atherosclerotic disease and are not unaffected.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Although heart disease in young adulthood is especially common in men, the disorder is autosomal dominant and affects both sexes; screening is for immediate family members.
whyWrongByChoice.E: LDL is elevated from birth and myocardial infarction can occur within the first two decades, so screening should not be deferred to age 40.

questions.topicName: Dyslipidemias, Lipid Storage Disorders, and other defects in Lipid Metabolism

questions.stem: A 42-year-old man has a lipid panel showing markedly elevated VLDL and triglycerides with a normal LDL, relatively normal total cholesterol, and low HDL; his evaluation is consistent with familial hypertriglyceridemia. His brother has familial combined hyperlipidemia. Compared with his brother, this patient's risk for atherosclerotic heart disease is best described as which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Equivalent, because both disorders involve hepatic VLDL overproduction

choices.label: B
choices.text: Greater, because his triglycerides are more elevated

choices.label: C
choices.text: Not strongly associated, because his LDL is not increased

choices.label: D
choices.text: Greater, because his HDL is low

choices.label: E
choices.text: Equivalent, because both disorders increase apolipoprotein B-100

explanation.summary: Familial hypertriglyceridemia can resemble familial combined hyperlipidemia, but because LDL is not increased, a strong association with atherosclerotic heart disease has not been found.
explanation.whyCorrect: Patients with familial hypertriglyceridemia (type IV) can look a lot like those with familial combined hyperlipidemia (type IIb), since both have elevated VLDL and triglycerides with low HDL. However, in type IV the LDL is not increased, and a strong association between this disease and atherosclerotic heart disease has not been found. In contrast, familial combined hyperlipidemia raises LDL, VLDL, and triglycerides and carries an elevated risk of accelerated atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease. The main risk in type IV is acute pancreatitis when triglycerides exceed 1,000 mg/dL.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Both involve hepatic VLDL overproduction, but the atherosclerotic risk differs because only familial combined hyperlipidemia raises LDL.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Very high triglycerides raise the risk of acute pancreatitis, not atherosclerotic heart disease.
whyWrongByChoice.D: HDL is often low in both disorders, so it does not make his risk greater than his brother's.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Increased apolipoprotein B-100 with small dense LDL is a feature of familial combined hyperlipidemia, not familial hypertriglyceridemia.

questions.topicName: Dyslipidemias, Lipid Storage Disorders, and other defects in Lipid Metabolism

questions.stem: A 50-year-old man with tuberoeruptive xanthomas on his elbows and yellow-orange plaques along his palmar creases is found to have a defective apolipoprotein E. In a healthy individual, the apolipoprotein E present on the surface of chylomicrons and VLDL is normally donated by which of the following lipoproteins?

explanation.summary: ApoE is donated from HDL to the surface of chylomicrons and VLDL and is required for these particles or their derivatives to enter the liver for clearance.
explanation.whyCorrect: HDL serves as the "helper" lipoprotein, donating important apolipoproteins to other lipoproteins so they can be recognized and taken up by the appropriate tissues. ApoE specifically is donated from HDL to the surface of chylomicrons and VLDL and is needed for entry of these particles or their derivatives into the liver. In familial dysbetalipoproteinemia the ApoE is defective, so chylomicrons, VLDLs, and IDLs have a prolonged presence in the circulation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Chylomicron remnants are recipients of ApoE that depend on it for hepatic uptake; they do not donate it.
whyWrongByChoice.B: IDL is a transitional particle whose clearance is impaired when ApoE is defective; it is not the source of ApoE.
whyWrongByChoice.C: LDL delivers cholesterol to tissues and is cleared through the LDL receptor; it does not donate apolipoproteins to other particles.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Oxidized LDL is the pro-atherogenic particle taken up by macrophage scavenger receptors; it plays no role in apolipoprotein donation.

questions.topicName: Dyslipidemias, Lipid Storage Disorders, and other defects in Lipid Metabolism

questions.stem: A 41-year-old man is noted to have firm yellow-white nodules along both Achilles tendons. Which of the following is the most accurate interpretation of this finding?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It commonly occurs in individuals with normal lipid levels

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is always indicative of a familial lipid disorder

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is pathognomonic for familial dysbetalipoproteinemia

choices.label: D
choices.text: It indicates triglyceride levels above 1,000 mg/dL

choices.label: E
choices.text: It reflects lipid deposition within the cornea

explanation.summary: Unlike xanthelasma, xanthoma deposits in the tendons are always indicative of a familial lipid disorder.
explanation.whyCorrect: Xanthomas are yellow-white masses of lipid-laden macrophages in the subepithelial connective tissue of skin or tendons, and can appear on the tendons of the hands, the Achilles, the knees, and the eyelids. Xanthelasma around the eyes can also occur in individuals with normal lipid levels, but deposits in the tendons are always indicative of a familial lipid disorder.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Occurrence with normal lipid levels is a feature of xanthelasma around the eyes, not of tendon deposits.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Palmar xanthomas along the palmar creases are the lesion pathognomonic for familial dysbetalipoproteinemia; tendon xanthomas occur in familial hypercholesterolemia and other familial disorders.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Triglycerides above 1,000 mg/dL are associated with pancreatitis and eruptive xanthomas, not specifically with tendon xanthomas.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Lipid deposition within the eye itself produces a corneal arcus, a separate finding from tendon xanthomas.

questions.topicName: Dyslipidemias, Lipid Storage Disorders, and other defects in Lipid Metabolism

questions.stem: A 38-year-old man with a triglyceride level of 2,400 mg/dL develops crops of small yellow-red papules over his buttocks and extensor surfaces. The lesions are itchy and tender, and several have become inflamed and oozed. Which of the following best describes these lesions?

explanation.summary: Eruptive xanthomas are inflamed, oozing skin lesions from excessive fat accumulation under the skin and may be itchy, tender, or painful.
explanation.whyCorrect: Eruptive xanthomas become inflamed and ooze because of the excessive accumulation of fats under the skin, and the lesions may be itchy, tender, or painful. They are one of the observable manifestations of hyperlipidemia, seen with very high triglyceride levels.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Xanthelasma are xanthomas of the skin around the eyes and can occur even with normal lipid levels; they are not inflamed, oozing papules.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A corneal arcus is a faint white ring of lipid deposited within the eye itself, not a skin lesion.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Palmar xanthomas are yellow-orange plaques along the creases of the palms, pathognomonic for familial dysbetalipoproteinemia.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Tendon xanthomas are firm deposits in tendons such as the Achilles and are not itchy, oozing papules.

questions.topicName: Dyslipidemias, Lipid Storage Disorders, and other defects in Lipid Metabolism

questions.stem: In a patient with familial hypercholesterolemia, the abundant circulating LDL is prone to oxidative modification into the pro-atherogenic oxLDL particle. Which of the following would be expected to inhibit this modification?

explanation.summary: Dietary antioxidants such as vitamin E, ascorbic acid, and beta-carotene inhibit the oxidation of LDL to oxLDL, whereas oxidants such as superoxide promote it.
explanation.whyCorrect: When LDL is increased in abundance it becomes more susceptible to oxidative damage, generating the pro-atherogenic oxLDL particle that macrophages take up through scavenger receptors to become foam cells. Oxidants including superoxide, nitric oxide, and hydrogen peroxide drive this conversion, while vitamin E, ascorbic acid, beta-carotene, and other antioxidants from the diet inhibit it.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Superoxide is one of the oxidants that promotes, rather than inhibits, the formation of oxLDL.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Nitric oxide is listed among the oxidants that promote LDL oxidation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Hydrogen peroxide is an oxidant that drives the conversion of LDL to oxLDL.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Lipoprotein lipase hydrolyzes triglycerides in chylomicrons and VLDL and has no role in preventing LDL oxidation.

questions.topicName: Dyslipidemias, Lipid Storage Disorders, and other defects in Lipid Metabolism

questions.stem: In an early atherosclerotic lesion, foam cells accumulate within the intima and release growth factors and cytokines. Which of the following is the most direct consequence of this release?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Downregulation of scavenger receptors on macrophages

choices.label: B
choices.text: Efflux of cholesterol from foam cells through the ABC1 transporter

choices.label: C
choices.text: Reversion of foam cells into circulating monocytes

choices.label: D
choices.text: Migration of smooth muscle cells from the media into the intima

choices.label: E
choices.text: Lysosomal degradation of hepatic LDL receptors

explanation.summary: Growth factors and cytokines released by accumulating foam cells stimulate smooth muscle cells to migrate from the media into the intima, where they proliferate, produce collagen, and take up lipid.
explanation.whyCorrect: After monocytes adhere to injured endothelium, enter the subendothelium (intima), and become macrophages that consume oxidized LDL, the resulting foam cells accumulate and release growth factors and cytokines. These signals stimulate the migration of smooth muscle cells from the media to the intima, where the smooth muscle cells proliferate, produce collagen, and take up lipid, potentially becoming foam cells themselves.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Scavenger receptors are low-affinity, nonspecific, and nonregulated; it is the high-affinity LDL receptor that is downregulated when the cell has sufficient cholesterol.
whyWrongByChoice.B: ABC1-mediated cholesterol efflux is the pathway defective in Tangier disease; it is not the response to foam cell cytokine release.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Foam cells do not revert to monocytes; the lesion progresses as more foam cells accumulate.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Lysosomal degradation of hepatic LDL receptors is the action of PCSK9 in the liver, unrelated to events within the arterial wall.

questions.topicName: Dyslipidemias, Lipid Storage Disorders, and other defects in Lipid Metabolism

questions.stem: A 28-year-old woman has an LDL cholesterol of 320 mg/dL, a corneal arcus, and a father who died of a myocardial infarction at age 38. Sequencing of her LDL receptor gene is normal. Which of the following genetic changes would best account for her phenotype?

choices.label: D
choices.text: Loss-of-function mutation in the ABC1 transporter

explanation.summary: Gain-of-function PCSK9 mutations cause familial hypercholesterolemia by increasing degradation of LDL receptors, even when the LDL receptor gene itself is normal.
explanation.whyCorrect: PCSK9 binds LDL receptors on hepatocytes; the complex is internalized and directed to lysosomes for degradation, preventing the receptor from recycling to the cell surface. Gain-of-function PCSK9 mutants are known to cause dyslipidemias such as familial hypercholesterolemia, which is depicted as a loss of the ability to inhibit or suppress PCSK9 function. The result is too few LDL receptors and very high LDL, producing the familial hypercholesterolemia phenotype with corneal arcus and early myocardial infarction despite a normal LDL receptor gene.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Loss of PCSK9 function would preserve LDL receptors and lower LDL, the opposite of this patient's phenotype.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A defective apolipoprotein E causes familial dysbetalipoproteinemia with elevated remnants, both cholesterol and triglycerides, and palmar xanthomas.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Increased lipoprotein lipase activity would enhance triglyceride clearance; it does not raise LDL.
whyWrongByChoice.D: ABC1 transporter loss causes Tangier disease with low HDL and low total cholesterol, not an isolated very high LDL.

questions.topicName: Dyslipidemias, Lipid Storage Disorders, and other defects in Lipid Metabolism

questions.stem: Cholesterol released from peripheral tissue through the ABC1 transporter is loaded onto HDL for return to the liver. Which of the following activities is required for HDL to transport this cholesterol?

explanation.summary: ABC1 promotes cholesterol release from extra-hepatic tissue, and that cholesterol is transported by HDL via LCAT activity.
explanation.whyCorrect: ABC1 is the specific transporter that promotes cholesterol release by extra-hepatic tissue so it can be transported by HDL via LCAT activity as part of reverse cholesterol transport. In Tangier disease, ABC1 is deficient, intracellular cholesterol accumulates, and the lipid panel shows low HDL and low overall cholesterol.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Lipoprotein lipase degrades triglycerides in chylomicrons and VLDL on endothelial cells; it does not load cholesterol onto HDL.
whyWrongByChoice.B: HMG-CoA reductase catalyzes hepatic cholesterol synthesis from HMG-CoA to mevalonate and is unrelated to HDL cholesterol transport.
whyWrongByChoice.C: PCSK9 targets hepatic LDL receptors for lysosomal degradation and has no role in HDL cholesterol loading.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Carnitine acyltransferase-1 forms fatty acyl-carnitine for mitochondrial import of long-chain fatty acids, a step in beta-oxidation rather than cholesterol transport.

questions.topicName: Dyslipidemias, Lipid Storage Disorders, and other defects in Lipid Metabolism

questions.stem: During catabolism of a long-chain fatty acid, fatty acyl-carnitine is transported into the mitochondrial matrix. Which of the following then regenerates fatty acyl-CoA from fatty acyl-carnitine within the matrix?

explanation.summary: Carnitine acyltransferase-2 replaces carnitine with CoA inside the mitochondrial matrix, regenerating fatty acyl-CoA for beta-oxidation.
explanation.whyCorrect: A fatty acyl-CoA is first converted to fatty acyl-carnitine by carnitine acyltransferase-1, and the fatty acyl-carnitine is transported into the mitochondrial matrix by the carnitine acyl-carnitine translocase. Once within the matrix, carnitine acyltransferase-2 replaces the carnitine with CoA to regenerate the fatty acyl-CoA, the liberated carnitine is recycled for more transport, and the fatty acyl-CoA becomes a substrate for beta-oxidation.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Carnitine acyltransferase-1 performs the earlier step, converting fatty acyl-CoA to fatty acyl-carnitine before transport.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The translocase moves fatty acyl-carnitine across the inner mitochondrial membrane but does not regenerate acyl-CoA.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Medium-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase catalyzes the first oxidative step of beta-oxidation for medium-chain substrates, after acyl-CoA has been regenerated.
whyWrongByChoice.E: OCTN2 is the plasma membrane and renal transporter for carnitine itself, not a matrix enzyme.

questions.topicName: Dyslipidemias, Lipid Storage Disorders, and other defects in Lipid Metabolism

questions.stem: Approximately 25% of the body's carnitine is produced by endogenous synthesis, with the remainder obtained from food. The multi-step synthesis of carnitine begins with which of the following pairs of amino acids?

explanation.summary: Carnitine is derived from lysine and methionine through a multi-step enzymatic synthesis cascade.
explanation.whyCorrect: Carnitine is synthesized from lysine and methionine through a multi-step enzymatic cascade. This endogenous production provides roughly 25% of bodily needs, and the rest is derived from a variety of food sources. Once synthesized or absorbed, carnitine requires the OCTN2 transporter for cellular uptake and renal reabsorption.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Glycine and arginine are not the amino acid precursors of carnitine described.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The branched-chain amino acids leucine and isoleucine are not precursors of carnitine.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Glutamine and aspartate are not the source amino acids for carnitine synthesis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Serine and cysteine are not involved in the carnitine synthesis cascade.

questions.topicName: Dyslipidemias, Lipid Storage Disorders, and other defects in Lipid Metabolism

questions.stem: A 14-month-old boy develops lethargy and hypoketotic hypoglycemia during a febrile illness. Plasma carnitine is very low, and genetic testing identifies a mutation in SLC22A5. Which of the following best explains his low circulating carnitine level?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Impaired synthesis of carnitine from lysine and methionine

choices.label: B
choices.text: Consumption of carnitine by excess medium-chain acyl-carnitine formation

choices.label: C
choices.text: Failure of renal reabsorption with urinary carnitine wasting

choices.label: D
choices.text: Sequestration of carnitine within the mitochondrial matrix

explanation.summary: SLC22A5 encodes the OCTN2 transporter, which normally reabsorbs more than 90% of filtered carnitine; without it, carnitine is readily excreted in the urine.
explanation.whyCorrect: Primary systemic carnitine deficiency is caused by defective OCTN2 transporters, encoded by the SLC22A5 gene. Carnitine is readily excreted in the urine, and OCTN2 typically reabsorbs more than 90% of it. In the absence of this transporter there is significant carnitine wasting, so circulating carnitine is low and too little is available to import long-chain fatty acids into the mitochondria for beta-oxidation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Synthesis from lysine and methionine is intact in primary carnitine deficiency; the defect is in the transporter, not the synthetic cascade.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Medium-chain acyl-carnitine formation is a rescue mechanism seen in MCAD deficiency and does not explain carnitine loss from an OCTN2 defect.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Carnitine is not trapped in mitochondria; it is lost from the body through the urine.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Dietary intake normally supplies most carnitine, but the low level here is due to renal wasting from the transporter mutation, not poor intake.

questions.topicName: Dyslipidemias, Lipid Storage Disorders, and other defects in Lipid Metabolism

questions.stem: A child with MCAD deficiency is found to have markedly elevated medium-chain acyl-carnitines in plasma. Given that medium-chain fatty acids do not normally require carnitine to enter mitochondria, which of the following best explains the formation of these acyl-carnitines?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A rescue mechanism that conserves CoA for other critical processes

choices.label: B
choices.text: Compensatory upregulation of carnitine acyltransferase-1 for transport

choices.label: C
choices.text: Loss of the passive diffusion pathway for medium-chain fatty acids

choices.label: D
choices.text: Direct conversion of long-chain acyl-carnitines by residual MCAD activity

choices.label: E
choices.text: Increased renal reabsorption of carnitine through OCTN2

explanation.summary: In MCAD deficiency, medium-chain acyl-carnitine formation is a rescue mechanism that conserves CoA and creates a more soluble derivative that cannot be properly metabolized.
explanation.whyCorrect: Attachment of carnitine to medium-chain fatty acids is not normally necessary in hepatocytes because MCFAs can passively diffuse from the intestine to the mitochondrial matrix. However, an acyl-CoA group is always added to fatty acids in the mitochondria regardless of SCAD, MCAD, or LCAD activity. When MCAD is deficient, the medium-chain acyl-CoAs accumulate rapidly from two sources (pre-existing MCFAs and MCFAs generated as LCFA catabolism shortens the chain), and forming medium-chain acyl-carnitines is a rescue mechanism whereby the body conserves CoA for other critical processes and creates a more soluble derivative that cannot be metabolized.

whyWrongByChoice.B: The acyl-carnitines arise from the need to free CoA, not from upregulated carnitine acyltransferase-1 transport.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Passive diffusion of MCFAs is preserved in MCAD deficiency; the block is at the first oxidative step, not at entry.
