whyWrongByChoice.D: MCAD activity is deficient; the acyl-carnitines form because accumulating medium-chain acyl-CoAs cannot be oxidized, not from residual enzyme action on long-chain species.
whyWrongByChoice.E: OCTN2 renal handling of carnitine is not what generates medium-chain acyl-carnitines.

questions.topicName: Dyslipidemias, Lipid Storage Disorders, and other defects in Lipid Metabolism

questions.stem: A 2-year-old girl with known MCAD deficiency presents with profound hypoglycemia after 14 hours without food during viral gastroenteritis. In addition to the failure to generate acetyl-CoA, which of the following further worsens her hypoglycemia?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Excess ketone bodies suppressing hepatic glucose output

choices.label: B
choices.text: Depletion of hepatic glycogen by carnitine wasting

choices.label: C
choices.text: Unoxidized fatty acid metabolites inhibiting gluconeogenic enzymes

choices.label: D
choices.text: Insulin release stimulated by circulating medium-chain fatty acids

choices.label: E
choices.text: Loss of pyruvate carboxylase activation by carnitine

explanation.summary: Hypoketotic hypoglycemia in MCAD and carnitine deficiency is exacerbated by fasting or illness, and accumulated unoxidized fatty acid metabolites inhibit gluconeogenic enzymes, worsening the hypoglycemia.
explanation.whyCorrect: Hypoketotic hypoglycemia is a shared symptom of MCAD deficiency and primary carnitine deficiency and is greatly exacerbated by fasting or catabolic states such as illness. Beyond the failure to produce acetyl-CoA (needed as a ketogenesis substrate, as an ATP source for gluconeogenesis, and as an allosteric activator of pyruvate carboxylase), the accumulation of unoxidized fatty acid metabolites also inhibits gluconeogenic enzymes, worsening the associated hypoglycemia.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Ketone production is decreased, not increased; the hypoglycemia is hypoketotic.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Carnitine wasting is the mechanism of primary carnitine deficiency and is not a cause of glycogen depletion in MCAD deficiency.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Insulin release from medium-chain fatty acids is not a mechanism described for the hypoglycemia in these disorders.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Pyruvate carboxylase is allosterically activated by acetyl-CoA, not by carnitine.

questions.topicName: Dyslipidemias, Lipid Storage Disorders, and other defects in Lipid Metabolism

questions.stem: The parents of an infant with systemic primary carnitine deficiency meet with a dietitian. They are instructed to avoid fasting, feed the infant frequently, and limit dietary fatty acid intake. Which of the following becomes necessary as a direct consequence of limiting dietary fatty acids?

explanation.summary: Limiting dietary fatty acids is always encouraged in MCAD and carnitine deficiency, but it creates a need to supplement essential fatty acids.
explanation.whyCorrect: Common treatment strategies for MCAD and primary carnitine deficiency entail avoidance of fasting, frequent feeding, and to some extent supplementing specific fatty acids. Limiting dietary fatty acid intake is always encouraged, but this restriction creates a need to supplement essential fatty acids so that biological requirements are still met.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Long-chain fatty acid supplementation should be avoided in both carnitine deficiency and MCAD deficiency, since neither can properly catabolize them.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Glucose is not restricted; avoiding fasting and feeding frequently are central to preventing the catabolic state that triggers hypoglycemia.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Lengthening feeding intervals would promote fasting, which greatly exacerbates hypoketotic hypoglycemia.
whyWrongByChoice.E: High-dose carnitine supplementation is routine in systemic primary carnitine deficiency and is not discontinued because of fat restriction.

questions.topicName: Dyslipidemias, Lipid Storage Disorders, and other defects in Lipid Metabolism

questions.stem: Two infants are evaluated in a metabolic clinic. The first has systemic primary carnitine deficiency caused by an OCTN2 variant that retains some function; the second has MCAD deficiency. Regarding high-dose carnitine supplementation, which of the following is most accurate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Routine in both conditions regardless of carnitine status

choices.label: B
choices.text: Avoided in both conditions because acyl-carnitines accumulate

choices.label: C
choices.text: Routine in carnitine deficiency; individualized by carnitine status in MCAD

choices.label: D
choices.text: Ineffective in carnitine deficiency because OCTN2 cannot transport it

choices.label: E
choices.text: Routine in MCAD deficiency; debated in carnitine deficiency

explanation.summary: High-dose carnitine is routine in systemic primary carnitine deficiency, especially with partially functional OCTN2 variants, whereas its universal use in MCAD deficiency is debated and depends on the individual's carnitine status.
explanation.whyCorrect: High-dose carnitine supplementation is routine in systemic primary carnitine deficiency, and select variants of the OCTN2 transporter that retain some functionality are the predominant target of this strategy. In contrast, there is debate over the universal use of carnitine in MCAD deficiency; the benefit is currently considered to depend on the carnitine status of the individual MCAD-deficient patient.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Carnitine is not routinely given to all MCAD-deficient patients; its use there is individualized rather than universal.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Carnitine is not avoided; it is routine in primary carnitine deficiency and considered case by case in MCAD deficiency.
whyWrongByChoice.D: High-dose carnitine specifically targets OCTN2 variants that retain some function, so it is effective in this patient rather than useless.
whyWrongByChoice.E: This reverses the relationship: carnitine is routine in primary carnitine deficiency and debated in MCAD deficiency.

questions.topicName: Dyslipidemias, Lipid Storage Disorders, and other defects in Lipid Metabolism

questions.stem: A 6-month-old boy of Ashkenazi Jewish descent, who developed normally until now, is losing previously acquired motor skills and demonstrates an exaggerated startle response to loud sounds. Fundoscopic exam reveals a cherry-red spot on the macula. The liver and spleen are not enlarged. Which of the following enzyme deficiencies is most likely responsible?

explanation.summary: Tay-Sachs disease is caused by hexosaminidase A deficiency with GM2 ganglioside accumulation.
explanation.whyCorrect: The infantile cherry-red macula, exaggerated startle response reflecting abnormal brainstem function, progressive loss of motor skills, and absence of hepatosplenomegaly in an Ashkenazi Jewish infant are classic for Tay-Sachs disease. Hexosaminidase A deficiency leads to accumulation of GM2 ganglioside, which is critical for neuronal health.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Sphingomyelinase deficiency causes Niemann-Pick disease, which shares the cherry-red spot but characteristically presents with prominent hepatosplenomegaly, absent here.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Glucocerebrosidase deficiency causes Gaucher disease, marked by hepatosplenomegaly and bone disease rather than a cherry-red spot with a normal-sized liver and spleen.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Alpha-galactosidase A deficiency causes Fabry disease, an adult-onset X-linked disorder with angiokeratomas and acroparesthesia, not infantile neurodegeneration.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Galactocerebrosidase deficiency causes Krabbe disease, which features globoid cells and optic atrophy rather than a cherry-red macular spot with startle response.

questions.topicName: Dyslipidemias, Lipid Storage Disorders, and other defects in Lipid Metabolism (2 of 2)

questions.stem: A 5-month-old infant who was healthy at birth now has failure to thrive, spasticity, and rapidly progressing neurologic deterioration. On exam there is massive hepatosplenomegaly, and fundoscopy shows a cherry-red spot on the macula. The infant dies at 30 months of age. Which enzyme deficiency best explains this presentation?

explanation.summary: Niemann-Pick disease type A results from sphingomyelinase deficiency and accumulation of sphingomyelin.
explanation.whyCorrect: The combination of a cherry-red macular spot AND massive hepatosplenomegaly with rapidly progressive neurologic decline and death by about age 3 is characteristic of Niemann-Pick disease type A. It is caused by a deficiency of sphingomyelinase, leading to accumulation of sphingomyelin.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Hexosaminidase A deficiency (Tay-Sachs) also causes a cherry-red spot, but there is no hepatosplenomegaly, which is a prominent finding here.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Alpha-galactosidase A deficiency (Fabry) is an adult-onset X-linked disorder with angiokeratomas and renal/cardiac disease, not infantile hepatosplenomegaly with a cherry-red spot.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Glucocerebrosidase deficiency (Gaucher type 1) causes hepatosplenomegaly and bone disease but not a cherry-red macular spot or this fulminant infantile neurodegeneration.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Galactocerebrosidase deficiency (Krabbe) spares the liver and spleen and does not produce a cherry-red macular spot.

questions.topicName: Dyslipidemias, Lipid Storage Disorders, and other defects in Lipid Metabolism (2 of 2)

questions.stem: Two infants each present with progressive neurodegeneration and a cherry-red spot on the macula. Which of the following findings would most reliably distinguish Niemann-Pick disease from Tay-Sachs disease?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Presence of a cherry-red spot on the macula

explanation.summary: Hepatosplenomegaly is present in Niemann-Pick but absent in Tay-Sachs, distinguishing the two.
explanation.whyCorrect: Both diseases share a cherry-red macular spot and infantile progressive neurodegeneration, so those features cannot separate them. The brick specifically notes that the absence of hepatosplenomegaly helps distinguish Tay-Sachs from Niemann-Pick, in which hepatosplenomegaly is a prominent finding.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A cherry-red spot occurs in both conditions and therefore cannot distinguish them.
whyWrongByChoice.B: An increased startle response reflects brainstem dysfunction seen with progressive neurodegeneration and is not specific to one disease.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Both disorders present in infancy, so onset timing does not separate them.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Both are progressive, fatal neurodegenerative diseases, so this feature is shared.

questions.topicName: Dyslipidemias, Lipid Storage Disorders, and other defects in Lipid Metabolism (2 of 2)

questions.stem: A 22-year-old woman presents with chronic bone pain, anemia, easy bruising, and an abdomen distended by a massively enlarged spleen. A bone marrow biopsy shows lipid-laden macrophages with a 'crinkled paper' or 'wrinkled silk' cytoplasmic appearance. Which enzyme deficiency is most consistent with these findings?

explanation.summary: Gaucher disease is caused by glucocerebrosidase deficiency and features Gaucher cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: Hepatosplenomegaly with prominent splenomegaly, anemia, thrombocytopenia causing easy bruising, bone pain, and lipid-laden macrophages with a crinkled-paper appearance (Gaucher cells) define Gaucher disease, the most common lysosomal storage disease. It results from glucocerebrosidase deficiency and accumulation of glucocerebroside.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Sphingomyelinase deficiency (Niemann-Pick) causes hepatosplenomegaly but is associated with a cherry-red spot and, in type A, fatal infantile neurodegeneration rather than crinkled-paper macrophages.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Alpha-galactosidase A deficiency (Fabry) causes angiokeratomas, acroparesthesia, and renal/cardiac disease, not Gaucher cells.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Hexosaminidase A deficiency (Tay-Sachs) causes infantile neurodegeneration with a cherry-red spot and no hepatosplenomegaly.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Galactocerebrosidase deficiency (Krabbe) produces globoid cells and neurologic disease, sparing the spleen and liver.

questions.topicName: Dyslipidemias, Lipid Storage Disorders, and other defects in Lipid Metabolism (2 of 2)

questions.stem: A 28-year-old man with Gaucher disease is started on glucocerebrosidase enzyme replacement therapy. Compared with the untreated natural history of other lysosomal storage diseases discussed, which statement about his expected outcome is most accurate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Enzyme replacement therapy can allow him to live a long, normal life

choices.label: B
choices.text: Death is expected within 2 to 3 years regardless of therapy

choices.label: C
choices.text: Therapy will reverse an existing cherry-red macular spot

choices.label: D
choices.text: He will inevitably develop severe central nervous system degeneration

choices.label: E
choices.text: Therapy prevents accumulation of very-long-chain fatty acids

explanation.summary: Type 1 Gaucher disease is treatable, and enzyme replacement therapy supports a relatively normal lifespan.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick emphasizes that Gaucher disease is treatable: with glucocerebrosidase enzyme replacement therapy, patients can live relatively long, normal lives. This is a notable contrast to most other lysosomal storage diseases, which are fatal at a young age.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Death within 2 to 3 years describes untreated Tay-Sachs disease, not treated Gaucher disease.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A cherry-red spot is a feature of Tay-Sachs and Niemann-Pick disease, not Gaucher disease.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Type 1 (non-neuronopathic) Gaucher disease accounts for 99% of cases and does not involve the central nervous system.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Very-long-chain fatty acid accumulation is a feature of peroxisomal disorders, not Gaucher disease, and is unrelated to glucocerebrosidase therapy.

questions.topicName: Dyslipidemias, Lipid Storage Disorders, and other defects in Lipid Metabolism (2 of 2)

questions.stem: A 34-year-old man reports years of burning pain and tingling in his hands and feet, markedly decreased sweating, and intermittent abdominal cramping. Examination reveals clusters of small, raised reddish-purple skin lesions, and urinalysis shows proteinuria. His maternal uncle died of renal failure at a young age. Which enzyme is most likely deficient?

explanation.summary: Fabry disease is an X-linked deficiency of alpha-galactosidase A with ceramide trihexoside accumulation.
explanation.whyCorrect: Acroparesthesia (burning/tingling of the hands and feet), hypohidrosis, angiokeratomas (raised reddish-purple skin lesions), and renal disease in a male with an X-linked family pattern are classic for Fabry disease. It results from deficiency of alpha-galactosidase A, causing accumulation of ceramide trihexoside.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Glucocerebrosidase deficiency (Gaucher) causes splenomegaly, anemia, and bone disease, not angiokeratomas and acroparesthesia.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hexosaminidase A deficiency (Tay-Sachs) is a fatal infantile neurodegenerative disorder, not an adult-onset disease with skin and peripheral nerve findings.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Sphingomyelinase deficiency (Niemann-Pick) causes hepatosplenomegaly and a cherry-red spot, not this constellation of adult symptoms.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Galactocerebrosidase deficiency (Krabbe) is an infantile demyelinating disease, not an adult disorder with angiokeratomas.

questions.topicName: Dyslipidemias, Lipid Storage Disorders, and other defects in Lipid Metabolism (2 of 2)

questions.stem: A 38-year-old man with a long history of hypohidrosis, angiokeratomas, and acroparesthesia is found to have deficient alpha-galactosidase A activity. As his disease progresses, sphingolipid accumulates in the vascular endothelial lining. Which of the following complications is most characteristically associated with this process?

choices.label: C
choices.text: Globoid cell formation in nervous tissue

choices.label: D
choices.text: Massive hepatosplenomegaly with a huge spleen

explanation.summary: In Fabry disease, sphingolipid deposition in vascular endothelium promotes early stroke.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick notes that Fabry disease produces early stroke because of sphingolipid accumulation in the vascular endothelial lining, along with renal and cardiac complications that can lead to death in the third or fourth decade.

whyWrongByChoice.B: A cherry-red macular spot is a feature of Tay-Sachs and Niemann-Pick disease, not Fabry disease.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Globoid cells are pathognomonic of Krabbe disease, not Fabry disease.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Massive splenomegaly is characteristic of Gaucher disease; Fabry disease does not cause a hugely enlarged spleen.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Crinkled-paper macrophages are Gaucher cells, seen in Gaucher disease rather than Fabry disease.

questions.topicName: Dyslipidemias, Lipid Storage Disorders, and other defects in Lipid Metabolism (2 of 2)

questions.stem: A 5-month-old infant who was normal at birth now has failure to thrive, marked irritability, and progressive vision loss due to optic atrophy, along with seizure-like episodes that do not respond to anticonvulsant therapy. There is no hepatosplenomegaly. Nervous tissue shows multinucleated macrophages with abundant cytoplasm. Which enzyme deficiency is most likely?

explanation.summary: Krabbe disease results from galactocerebrosidase deficiency and produces globoid cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: Infantile onset at 4-6 months with failure to thrive, irritability, optic atrophy with vision loss, seizures unresponsive to anticonvulsants, absence of liver and spleen involvement, and multinucleated globoid cells are hallmarks of Krabbe disease. It is caused by galactocerebrosidase deficiency with accumulation of galactocerebroside, a major component of myelin.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Hexosaminidase A deficiency (Tay-Sachs) causes a cherry-red spot and startle response, not globoid cells.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Sphingomyelinase deficiency (Niemann-Pick) causes hepatosplenomegaly and a cherry-red spot, both absent here.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Glucocerebrosidase deficiency (Gaucher) causes splenomegaly and bone disease with Gaucher cells, not globoid cells or optic atrophy.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Alpha-galactosidase A deficiency (Fabry) is an adult-onset disorder with angiokeratomas, not an infantile demyelinating disease.

questions.topicName: Dyslipidemias, Lipid Storage Disorders, and other defects in Lipid Metabolism (2 of 2)

questions.stem: A neonate presents with severe hypotonia, seizures, jaundice, and hepatomegaly. Physical exam shows a high forehead, widely spaced eyes, and a broad nasal bridge. Laboratory testing reveals elevated very-long-chain fatty acids, and tissue analysis shows that peroxisomes are essentially absent. This disorder is inherited in an autosomal recessive fashion. Which underlying defect is most likely responsible?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Defective PEX proteins impairing peroxisome biogenesis

choices.label: C
choices.text: A defective ABC transporter for fatty acid import

choices.label: D
choices.text: Deficiency of a mitochondrial beta-oxidation enzyme

explanation.summary: Zellweger syndrome is caused by defective PEX proteins, leading to failed peroxisome biogenesis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Zellweger syndrome is an autosomal recessive disorder of the PEX gene causing faulty peroxisomal biogenesis. Without functional peroxins, peroxisomal enzymes cannot be imported, so peroxisomes are absent or nonfunctional, VLCFAs accumulate in liver and brain, and infants show craniofacial anomalies, hypotonia, seizures, jaundice, and hepatomegaly, usually dying before age 1.

whyWrongByChoice.B: A deficient lysosomal hydrolase would cause a lysosomal storage disease with substrate accumulation, not an absence of peroxisomes with elevated VLCFAs.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A defective ABC transporter underlies X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy, in which peroxisomes still form; here peroxisomes are essentially absent.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A mitochondrial beta-oxidation defect would not eliminate peroxisomes or produce this dysmorphic biogenesis phenotype.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Sphingomyelinase deficiency causes Niemann-Pick disease, a lysosomal disorder unrelated to peroxisome biogenesis.

questions.topicName: Dyslipidemias, Lipid Storage Disorders, and other defects in Lipid Metabolism (2 of 2)

questions.stem: An 8-year-old boy develops progressive neurologic decline together with signs of adrenal insufficiency, including fatigue and skin hyperpigmentation. Plasma very-long-chain fatty acids are elevated, but peroxisomes are present in his tissues. The condition is inherited in an X-linked pattern. Which molecular defect best explains this presentation?

explanation.summary: X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy is caused by a defective ABC transporter that imports VLCFA substrates into peroxisomes.
explanation.whyCorrect: X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy occurs when transport of VLCFA substrates into the peroxisome is defective due to a faulty ABC transporter that normally uses ATP hydrolysis. VLCFAs accumulate in blood and tissues, and the disease presents later in childhood with neurologic decline and adrenal insufficiency, with peroxisomes still present.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Absent peroxins causing failed peroxisome formation describes Zellweger syndrome, in which peroxisomes are absent; here they are present.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Glucocerebrosidase deficiency causes Gaucher disease, a lysosomal disorder with hepatosplenomegaly and bone disease.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Hexosaminidase A deficiency causes Tay-Sachs disease, an infantile neurodegenerative lysosomal storage disease.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Catalase reduces hydrogen peroxide to water; its deficiency does not explain elevated VLCFAs with adrenal and neurologic disease.

questions.topicName: Dyslipidemias, Lipid Storage Disorders, and other defects in Lipid Metabolism (2 of 2)

questions.stem: A researcher studies isolated peroxisomes and notes that their beta-oxidation reactions transfer electrons directly to oxygen, generating hydrogen peroxide rather than driving ATP synthesis. Which peroxisomal enzyme is chiefly responsible for protecting the cell from the toxic hydrogen peroxide produced?

explanation.summary: Catalase in peroxisomes reduces toxic hydrogen peroxide to water.
explanation.whyCorrect: Because hydrogen peroxide is toxic, it is sequestered within the peroxisome, which contains catalase to reduce hydrogen peroxide to water and protect the cell from damage.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Acyl-CoA oxidase catalyzes the first step of peroxisomal beta-oxidation and actually generates hydrogen peroxide rather than detoxifying it.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Carnitine acetyltransferase transports activated acyl groups out of the peroxisome toward the mitochondria; it does not neutralize hydrogen peroxide.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Glucocerebrosidase is a lysosomal enzyme deficient in Gaucher disease, not a peroxisomal antioxidant.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Sphingomyelinase is a lysosomal enzyme deficient in Niemann-Pick disease, unrelated to peroxisomal hydrogen peroxide handling.

questions.topicName: Dyslipidemias, Lipid Storage Disorders, and other defects in Lipid Metabolism (2 of 2)

questions.stem: A biochemistry student is asked to describe how peroxisomal beta-oxidation differs from mitochondrial beta-oxidation. Which of the following best characterizes the substrate handled specifically by peroxisomal beta-oxidation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Very-long-chain fatty acids greater than 22 carbons

choices.label: B
choices.text: Short-chain fatty acids that are fully oxidized to carbon dioxide within the peroxisome

choices.label: C
choices.text: Glycogen, which is degraded to glucose within the peroxisome

choices.label: D
choices.text: Glycosaminoglycans that are broken down into monosaccharides

choices.label: E
choices.text: Sphingolipids requiring a unique acid hydrolase active at pH 5

explanation.summary: Peroxisomal beta-oxidation shortens very-long-chain fatty acids too large for mitochondria into medium-chain products.
explanation.whyCorrect: Peroxisomal beta-oxidation breaks down very-long-chain fatty acids larger than 22 carbons, which are too big for transport into mitochondria. It produces medium-chain fatty acids that are then transported to mitochondria to complete beta-oxidation.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Peroxisomal beta-oxidation does not fully oxidize substrates to carbon dioxide; it shortens VLCFAs and hands medium-chain products to mitochondria.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Glycogen degradation defects (Pompe disease) involve lysosomes, not peroxisomal beta-oxidation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Glycosaminoglycan (mucopolysaccharide) degradation is impaired in Hunter and Hurler syndromes, which are lysosomal, not peroxisomal.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Enzymes active at pH 5 are lysosomal acid hydrolases used for sphingolipid turnover, not peroxisomal beta-oxidation of fatty acids.

questions.topicName: Dyslipidemias, Lipid Storage Disorders, and other defects in Lipid Metabolism (2 of 2)

questions.stem: A researcher isolates the hydrolytic enzymes from purified lysosomes and assays their activity against protein, lipid, carbohydrate, and nucleic acid substrates in a series of buffers. At which pH is maximal activity of these enzymes expected?

explanation.summary: Lysosomal hydrolytic enzymes are active only at the acidic pH of 5 found in the lysosomal lumen.
explanation.whyCorrect: Lysosomes are membrane-bound organelles that degrade proteins, lipids, carbohydrates, and nucleic acids from intracellular and extracellular debris. The digestive hydrolytic enzymes they house are active only at the acidic pH of 5 maintained inside the lysosomal lumen, which is why the lysosome is described as the cell's own personal stomach.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A pH of 2 is far more acidic than the lysosomal lumen; lysosomal hydrolases are tuned to the mildly acidic pH of 5.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Physiologic cytosolic pH of 7.4 keeps lysosomal hydrolases inactive, which protects the cell if small amounts leak from the organelle.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Alkaline conditions do not support activity of lysosomal acid hydrolases.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Strongly alkaline conditions are incompatible with lysosomal acid hydrolase activity.

questions.topicName: Dyslipidemias, Lipid Storage Disorders, and other defects in Lipid Metabolism (2 of 2)

questions.stem: A 2-year-old girl with a confirmed lysosomal storage disease has marked hepatosplenomegaly. Biopsy of the spleen shows large foam cells packed with undigested substrate. Which of the following best explains why the liver and spleen are preferentially enlarged in this group of diseases?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Hepatocytes are the only cells that synthesize the deficient enzyme

choices.label: B
choices.text: Dietary sphingolipids are delivered directly to the liver through the portal circulation

choices.label: C
choices.text: The spleen sequesters red blood cells whose membranes carry the accumulated lipid

choices.label: D
choices.text: Monocytes and macrophages that clear cellular debris contain many lysosomes and fill with substrate

choices.label: E
choices.text: Extramedullary hematopoiesis expands these organs in response to marrow failure

explanation.summary: Accumulated substrates collect in cells of the mononuclear phagocyte system, and diseased phagocytes settling in the liver and spleen produce hepatosplenomegaly.
explanation.whyCorrect: A common hallmark of lysosomal storage diseases is that the accumulated substrates end up in cells of the mononuclear phagocyte system (monocytes and macrophages), because these cells are active in removing cellular debris and contain many lysosomes. When diseased phagocytic cells such as foam cells accumulate in the liver and spleen, hepatosplenomegaly results.

whyWrongByChoice.A: All cells contain lysosomes and the deficient enzyme is not restricted to hepatocytes; the organ enlargement reflects phagocyte accumulation, not hepatocyte enzyme synthesis.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The stored substrates arise from normal turnover of the body's own macromolecules, not from dietary sphingolipids arriving through the portal vein.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The enlargement is caused by substrate-laden macrophages, not by splenic trapping of red blood cells.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Marrow infiltration can cause anemia in some lysosomal storage diseases, but organomegaly is explained by foam cell accumulation rather than extramedullary hematopoiesis.

questions.topicName: Dyslipidemias, Lipid Storage Disorders, and other defects in Lipid Metabolism (2 of 2)

questions.stem: A study of tissue from patients with lysosomal storage diseases finds that the degree of cellular dysfunction exceeds what would be predicted from the volume of stored material alone. Which of the following secondary processes is most likely contributing to the cellular damage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Macrophage activation with release of cytokines

choices.label: B
choices.text: Hydrogen peroxide generation by peroxisomal catalase

choices.label: D
choices.text: Autoantibody production against the stored lipid

choices.label: E
choices.text: Loss of ATP from uncoupled mitochondrial oxidation

explanation.summary: Cellular dysfunction in lysosomal storage diseases results from storage of undigested material plus a cascade of secondary events such as macrophage activation and cytokine release.
explanation.whyCorrect: Among the common hallmarks of lysosomal storage diseases is that cellular dysfunctions are caused not only by storage of undigested materials but also by a cascade of triggered secondary events, specifically macrophage activation and release of cytokines.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Catalase reduces hydrogen peroxide to water rather than generating it, and peroxisomal chemistry is not the secondary injury mechanism in lysosomal storage diseases.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Complement-mediated lysis is not the secondary mechanism described for lysosomal storage diseases.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Autoantibody formation against stored lipid is not part of the pathogenesis of lysosomal storage diseases.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Uncoupled oxidation and ATP loss relate to peroxisomal beta-oxidation chemistry, not to the secondary injury in lysosomal storage diseases.

questions.topicName: Dyslipidemias, Lipid Storage Disorders, and other defects in Lipid Metabolism (2 of 2)

questions.stem: A pediatrician reviews the lysosomal storage diseases with a group of students. She notes that most of the diseases under discussion involve accumulation of a sphingolipid, but two of them instead involve disrupted degradation of glycosaminoglycans (mucopolysaccharides). Which pair of diseases is she describing?

explanation.summary: Hunter and Hurler syndromes are carbohydrate-based lysosomal storage diseases with disrupted degradation of glycosaminoglycans (mucopolysaccharides).
explanation.whyCorrect: The lysosomal storage diseases that entail defective turnover of carbohydrate-based substrates include Pompe disease, a defect in glycogen turnover, and Hunter syndrome and Hurler syndrome, which involve disrupted degradation of glycosaminoglycans, also called mucopolysaccharides.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Tay-Sachs and Niemann-Pick are sphingolipidoses that accumulate GM2 ganglioside and sphingomyelin, respectively.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Gaucher and Fabry are sphingolipidoses that accumulate glucocerebroside and ceramide trihexoside, respectively.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Krabbe disease is a sphingolipidosis accumulating galactocerebroside, and Zellweger syndrome is a peroxisomal biogenesis disorder, not a lysosomal storage disease.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Pompe disease is a defect in glycogen turnover rather than glycosaminoglycan degradation, and I-cell disease is not the mucopolysaccharide disorder described.

questions.topicName: Dyslipidemias, Lipid Storage Disorders, and other defects in Lipid Metabolism (2 of 2)

questions.stem: A biochemistry student is asked to describe the sphingosine backbone that is common to all sphingolipids, including the substrates that accumulate in the sphingolipidoses. Which structural description is most accurate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A glycerol backbone esterified to three fatty acids

choices.label: B
choices.text: A glycerol backbone linked to a phosphate head group

choices.label: C
choices.text: Four fused hydrocarbon rings with a hydroxyl group

choices.label: D
choices.text: A long saturated hydrocarbon chain ending in a carboxylic acid

choices.label: E
choices.text: A long hydrocarbon chain bearing two hydroxyl groups and an amine

explanation.summary: Sphingosine resembles a fatty acid except that the hydrocarbon chain carries two hydroxyls and an amine instead of a carboxylic acid.
explanation.whyCorrect: All sphingolipids are membrane lipids built on a sphingosine backbone. The structure looks similar to a fatty acid, except that instead of a carboxylic acid, the long hydrocarbon chain contains two hydroxyls and an amine. A variety of structures attached to these groups yield the spectrum of sphingolipids, each of which requires its own lysosomal enzyme for degradation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A glycerol backbone with three fatty acids describes a triglyceride, not sphingosine.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A glycerol-phosphate backbone describes glycerophospholipids, whereas sphingolipids are built on sphingosine rather than glycerol.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A fused four-ring structure describes a sterol such as cholesterol, not sphingosine.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A hydrocarbon chain ending in a carboxylic acid is a fatty acid; sphingosine specifically replaces that carboxylic acid with hydroxyl and amine groups.

questions.topicName: Dyslipidemias, Lipid Storage Disorders, and other defects in Lipid Metabolism (2 of 2)

questions.stem: A laboratory report identifies the specific sphingolipid accumulating in a child's tissue biopsy, and the clinician states that this single finding is sufficient to name the exact lysosomal storage disease. Which of the following best explains why the identity of the accumulated sphingolipid is so diagnostic?

choices.label: A
choices.text: All sphingolipids are degraded by one shared lysosomal enzyme

choices.label: B
choices.text: Each sphingolipid requires its own unique lysosomal enzyme for turnover

choices.label: C
choices.text: Sphingolipids are synthesized exclusively within neurons

choices.label: D
choices.text: Sphingolipid accumulation is confined to the spleen in every disease

choices.label: E
choices.text: Sphingolipids share a glycerol backbone with glycerophospholipids

explanation.summary: Because each sphingolipid requires a unique lysosomal enzyme for degradation, the specific sphingolipid that accumulates is a tell-tale sign of the exact lysosomal storage disease.
explanation.whyCorrect: Each sphingolipid requires a unique lysosomal enzyme for turnover and degradation. Therefore the identity of the specific accumulating sphingolipid points directly to which enzyme is deficient and thus to the exact lysosomal storage disease. The names of these substrates usually end with the suffix '-side'.

whyWrongByChoice.A: If one enzyme degraded all sphingolipids, a single deficiency would cause every sphingolipid to accumulate and the substrate identity would not be discriminating.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Sphingolipids are membrane lipids present throughout the body, although many are important for nervous tissue function and myelination.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Sphingolipid accumulation is not confined to the spleen; distribution varies by disease, with some sparing the liver and spleen entirely.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Sphingolipids are built on a sphingosine backbone, not glycerol, and backbone chemistry does not explain the diagnostic specificity of the substrate.

questions.topicName: Dyslipidemias, Lipid Storage Disorders, and other defects in Lipid Metabolism (2 of 2)

questions.stem: A 5-month-old boy from a Cajun family in Louisiana is evaluated for loss of previously acquired motor skills and an exaggerated startle to sound. Fundoscopy reveals a cherry red spot on the macula, and the liver and spleen are of normal size. Which substance is accumulating within his neurons?

explanation.summary: Tay-Sachs disease, prevalent in Ashkenazi Jewish, Cajun, and French Canadian populations, involves accumulation of GM2 ganglioside.
explanation.whyCorrect: Infantile neurodegeneration with an increased startle response, a macular cherry red spot, and no hepatosplenomegaly is Tay-Sachs disease, which has a high prevalence in the Ashkenazi Jewish, Cajun, and French Canadian populations. Hexosaminidase A deficiency causes accumulation of GM2 ganglioside, a sphingolipid critical for neuronal health.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Sphingomyelin accumulates in Niemann-Pick disease, which would present with prominent hepatosplenomegaly.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Glucocerebroside accumulates in Gaucher disease, which causes splenomegaly and bone disease without a cherry red spot.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Ceramide trihexoside accumulates in Fabry disease, an adult-onset disorder with angiokeratomas and acroparesthesia.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Galactocerebroside accumulates in Krabbe disease, which produces globoid cells and optic atrophy rather than a cherry red spot.

questions.topicName: Dyslipidemias, Lipid Storage Disorders, and other defects in Lipid Metabolism (2 of 2)

questions.stem: During fundoscopic examination of an infant with hexosaminidase A deficiency, a medical student notes a red dot in the center of the macula surrounded by a pale, cloudy retina. Which of the following best explains the appearance of this finding?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Lipid accumulation makes the surrounding retina opaque, leaving the central red dot visible

choices.label: B
choices.text: Hemorrhage from fragile lipid-laden vessels pools at the center of the macula

choices.label: C
choices.text: New vessel growth at the fovea creates a focus of hyperemia

choices.label: D
choices.text: Stored ganglioside within the fovea itself is intrinsically red in color

choices.label: E
choices.text: Optic nerve atrophy causes pallor of the disc that contrasts with a normal macula

explanation.summary: The cherry red spot forms because lipid accumulation causes opaqueness of the retina, leaving a central red dot visible.
explanation.whyCorrect: The macular cherry red spot seen on fundoscopy in Tay-Sachs disease (and Niemann-Pick disease) occurs as the accumulation of lipids causes opaqueness of the surrounding tissue, leaving a central red dot visible in the middle of the illuminated eye.

whyWrongByChoice.B: The cherry red spot is not a hemorrhage; it is a contrast phenomenon created by lipid-induced opacity around the macula.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Neovascularization is not part of the pathology of the cherry red spot in sphingolipidoses.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The stored lipid produces opacity of the surrounding retina; the red dot is the central macula showing through, not colored ganglioside.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Optic atrophy with vision loss is a feature of Krabbe disease and does not create a cherry red macular spot.

questions.topicName: Dyslipidemias, Lipid Storage Disorders, and other defects in Lipid Metabolism (2 of 2)

questions.stem: The parents of a 7-month-old boy are told that enzymatic assays confirm a deficiency of hexosaminidase A. He appeared normal at birth but began losing motor skills at 4 months of age. The parents ask what to expect over the coming years. Which of the following is the most accurate description of the natural course of his disease?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Near-normal lifespan once enzyme replacement therapy is started

choices.label: B
choices.text: Survival into adolescence with progressive hepatosplenomegaly and cirrhosis

choices.label: C
choices.text: Progressive neurologic deterioration with death usually before 4 years of age

choices.label: D
choices.text: Slow progression with the most serious complications arising in adulthood

choices.label: E
choices.text: Death before the first birthday from hepatic failure and seizures

explanation.summary: Tay-Sachs disease is progressive and fatal, with seizures, blindness, paralysis, and a vegetative state; most children do not live past 4 years of age.
explanation.whyCorrect: Infants with Tay-Sachs disease appear normal at birth, show weakness and loss of motor skills at 3-6 months, and go on to suffer neurologic impairment, seizures, blindness, and paralysis. Death usually occurs within 2-3 years after the onset of a vegetative state, and most children do not live past 4 years of age.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A relatively long, normal life with enzyme replacement therapy describes Gaucher disease, not Tay-Sachs disease.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Survival into adolescence or early adulthood with progressive hepatosplenomegaly and cirrhosis describes Niemann-Pick type B; Tay-Sachs has no hepatosplenomegaly.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Slow progression with adult-onset complications describes Fabry disease, not the rapidly fatal infantile course of Tay-Sachs.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Death before 1 year of age with hepatomegaly and seizures describes Zellweger syndrome, a peroxisomal disorder.

questions.topicName: Dyslipidemias, Lipid Storage Disorders, and other defects in Lipid Metabolism (2 of 2)

questions.stem: A 9-year-old boy is referred for progressively enlarging liver and spleen first noted at age 5. He is performing well in school, and his neurologic examination is entirely normal. Enzyme testing shows markedly reduced sphingomyelinase activity. As his disease progresses, which of the following complications is he most likely to develop?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Rapidly progressive spasticity with death by age 3

choices.label: B
choices.text: Erlenmeyer flask deformity of the distal femur

choices.label: D
choices.text: Globoid cell infiltration of the brain with demyelination

choices.label: E
choices.text: Pulmonary disease and cirrhosis as the liver fills with foam cells

explanation.summary: Niemann-Pick type B has later onset, progressive hepatosplenomegaly without neurologic manifestations, and eventual pulmonary disease and cirrhosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Sphingomyelinase deficiency with later-onset, progressive hepatosplenomegaly and uniquely no neurological manifestations is Niemann-Pick type B, the most common subtype. These patients eventually develop pulmonary disease and cirrhosis as the liver fills with foam cells, with death usually in adolescence or early adulthood.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Rapidly progressing neurological deterioration, spasticity, and death around age 3 describe Niemann-Pick type A, which begins in the first 6 months of life; this child is neurologically normal at age 9.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Erlenmeyer flask deformity results from Gaucher cells filling the bone marrow in glucocerebrosidase deficiency, not sphingomyelinase deficiency.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Angiokeratomas and early stroke are complications of Fabry disease (alpha-galactosidase A deficiency).
whyWrongByChoice.D: Globoid cells and demyelination are pathognomonic of Krabbe disease (galactocerebrosidase deficiency).

questions.topicName: Dyslipidemias, Lipid Storage Disorders, and other defects in Lipid Metabolism (2 of 2)

questions.stem: A 4-year-old girl has hepatosplenomegaly and progressive neurologic decline that clinically resemble Niemann-Pick disease. However, an enzymatic assay demonstrates normal sphingomyelinase activity. Genetic testing identifies a defect in a protein other than sphingomyelinase. Which of the following mechanisms best explains her disease?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Deficient hexosaminidase A with ganglioside storage

choices.label: E
choices.text: Defective ABC transporter for very-long-chain fatty acids

explanation.summary: Niemann-Pick types C1 and C2 are caused by disrupted intracellular lipid trafficking due to alterations in proteins other than sphingomyelinase.
explanation.whyCorrect: Niemann-Pick types A and B are due to sphingomyelinase deficiency, but a third form, types C1 and C2, is caused by disrupted intracellular lipid trafficking due to alteration in proteins other than sphingomyelinase. Normal sphingomyelinase activity in a child with a Niemann-Pick phenotype therefore points to type C.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Hexosaminidase A deficiency causes Tay-Sachs disease, which has no hepatosplenomegaly.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Failure of peroxisome biogenesis causes Zellweger syndrome, a peroxisomal disorder with craniofacial anomalies and death before age 1, not a Niemann-Pick phenotype.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Galactocerebrosidase deficiency causes Krabbe disease, which spares the liver and spleen.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A defective ABC transporter for VLCFAs causes X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy, which presents with neurologic decline and adrenal issues rather than hepatosplenomegaly.

questions.topicName: Dyslipidemias, Lipid Storage Disorders, and other defects in Lipid Metabolism (2 of 2)

questions.stem: An epidemiologist is compiling the frequency of lysosomal storage diseases across a large population registry. Which of the following diseases is expected to be the most common lysosomal storage disease overall?

explanation.summary: Gaucher disease is collectively the most common lysosomal storage disease.
explanation.whyCorrect: Gaucher disease, caused by deficiency of glucocerebrosidase with accumulation of glucocerebroside, is collectively the most common lysosomal storage disease. Type 1 (non-neuronopathic) accounts for 99% of cases and affects the bone, spleen, and liver.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Tay-Sachs disease has a high prevalence in specific populations (Ashkenazi Jewish, Cajun, French Canadian) but is not the most common lysosomal storage disease overall.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Niemann-Pick disease is less common than Gaucher disease.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Fabry disease is an X-linked disorder that is less common than Gaucher disease.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Krabbe disease is less common than Gaucher disease.

questions.topicName: Dyslipidemias, Lipid Storage Disorders, and other defects in Lipid Metabolism (2 of 2)

questions.stem: A 19-year-old man with splenomegaly, thrombocytopenia, and chronic bone pain undergoes knee radiography, which shows loss of the normal curvature of the distal femur, described by the radiologist as an 'Erlenmeyer flask' deformity. Which of the following best explains this radiographic finding?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Lipid-laden macrophages filling the bone marrow

choices.label: B
choices.text: Sphingolipid deposition in the vascular endothelium

choices.label: C
choices.text: Excess osteoblast stimulation by circulating cytokines

choices.label: D
choices.text: Multinucleated globoid cells infiltrating the periosteum

explanation.summary: In Gaucher disease the Erlenmeyer flask deformity of the distal femur results from Gaucher cells filling the bone marrow.
explanation.whyCorrect: Splenomegaly, thrombocytopenia, and bone pain in a young adult indicate type 1 Gaucher disease. Lipid-laden macrophages called Gaucher cells infiltrate the bone marrow and joint space. On x-ray, an Erlenmeyer flask deformity of the distal femur appears because the normal curvature of the bone is lost as Gaucher cells fill up the bone marrow; bone destruction also manifests as osteopenia.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Sphingolipid accumulation in the vascular endothelial lining is the mechanism of early stroke in Fabry disease, not of femoral deformity.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The deformity reflects marrow expansion by storage cells, not osteoblast overstimulation; bone mass is actually reduced (osteopenia).
whyWrongByChoice.D: Globoid cells are pathognomonic of Krabbe disease and form in blood vessels and neuronal tissue, not bone.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Peroxisomal beta-oxidation defects cause Zellweger syndrome and adrenoleukodystrophy, which do not produce this bone deformity.

questions.topicName: Dyslipidemias, Lipid Storage Disorders, and other defects in Lipid Metabolism (2 of 2)

questions.stem: A 25-year-old woman with known type 1 Gaucher disease presents with sudden, excruciating pain in her left hip accompanied by warmth and swelling. Imaging demonstrates avascular necrosis of the femoral head with an early fracture. Which of the following is the most likely underlying mechanism of this bone crisis?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Pathologic fracture through a focus of osteoblastic metastasis

choices.label: C
choices.text: Vascular occlusion by abnormally large sphingolipid-engorged macrophages

choices.label: D
choices.text: Septic emboli originating from an infarcted spleen

choices.label: E
choices.text: Demyelination of the femoral nerve with neuropathic joint destruction

explanation.summary: Avascular necrosis of the femur in Gaucher disease results from vascular occlusion by abnormally large sphingolipid-engorged macrophages.
explanation.whyCorrect: Avascular necrosis of the femur is common in Gaucher disease and leads to femoral fractures because of vascular occlusion by the abnormally large sphingolipid-engorged macrophages. Acute infarctions produce bone crises, which present as sudden excruciating pain, sometimes with signs of inflammation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Although thrombocytopenia causes easy bruising in Gaucher disease, the bone crisis is an infarction from vascular occlusion, not bleeding into the joint.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Gaucher disease is a storage disorder, not a malignancy; the femoral lesion is necrosis from occlusion, not metastasis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The splenomegaly of Gaucher disease is due to Gaucher cell accumulation and is not a source of septic emboli.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Demyelination is the mechanism of Krabbe disease; Gaucher type 1 does not involve the nervous system.

questions.topicName: Dyslipidemias, Lipid Storage Disorders, and other defects in Lipid Metabolism (2 of 2)

questions.stem: A 31-year-old man with alpha-galactosidase A deficiency, angiokeratomas, and burning pain in his hands and feet is offered recombinant enzyme replacement therapy. He asks what benefit he should realistically expect. Which of the following is the most accurate counseling statement?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It reverses established renal failure and restores kidney function

choices.label: B
choices.text: It produces a normal life expectancy, as it does for patients with Gaucher disease

choices.label: C
choices.text: It clears the angiokeratomas and cures the underlying enzyme deficiency

choices.label: D
choices.text: It reliably prevents stroke by removing sphingolipid from the vascular endothelium

choices.label: E
choices.text: It alleviates some pain, but data are insufficient to show it extends life expectancy

explanation.summary: Recombinant enzyme replacement therapy for Fabry disease alleviates some pain, but there is insufficient data to demonstrate that it extends life expectancy.
explanation.whyCorrect: A recombinant enzyme replacement therapy is available for Fabry disease. This therapy alleviates some of the pain, but there is insufficient data to demonstrate that it extends life expectancy. This contrasts with Gaucher disease, where enzyme replacement allows relatively long, normal lives.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Enzyme replacement is not described as reversing established renal failure, one of the concerning complications of Fabry disease.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A relatively long, normal life with enzyme replacement is the expectation in Gaucher disease; the same benefit has not been demonstrated in Fabry disease.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Enzyme replacement supplies the missing enzyme but does not cure the underlying genetic deficiency or clear the rash.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Prevention of stroke has not been demonstrated; the documented benefit is partial pain relief.

questions.topicName: Dyslipidemias, Lipid Storage Disorders, and other defects in Lipid Metabolism (2 of 2)

questions.stem: A 29-year-old man reports decreased sweating, episodes of abdominal cramping with diarrhea, and tingling in his hands and feet. Examination shows clusters of raised, reddish-purple skin lesions on his trunk and thighs. Which substance is accumulating in his lysosomes?

explanation.summary: Fabry disease involves lysosomal accumulation of ceramide trihexoside due to alpha-galactosidase A deficiency.
explanation.whyCorrect: Hypohidrosis, gastrointestinal issues such as abdominal cramping and diarrhea, acroparesthesia, and angiokeratomas in an adult male are the distinctive features of Fabry disease. It is caused by deficiency of alpha-galactosidase A, leading to lysosomal accumulation of ceramide trihexoside.

whyWrongByChoice.A: GM2 ganglioside accumulates in Tay-Sachs disease, an infantile neurodegenerative disorder.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Sphingomyelin accumulates in Niemann-Pick disease, which features hepatosplenomegaly and a cherry red spot.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Glucocerebroside accumulates in Gaucher disease, which causes splenomegaly, cytopenias, and bone disease.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Galactocerebroside accumulates in Krabbe disease, an infantile demyelinating disorder.

questions.topicName: Dyslipidemias, Lipid Storage Disorders, and other defects in Lipid Metabolism (2 of 2)

questions.stem: A newborn boy has severe hypotonia, seizures, jaundice, and hepatomegaly. His face shows a high forehead, large fontanelles, widely spaced eyes, and a broad nasal bridge. Plasma very-long-chain fatty acids are markedly elevated, and fibroblast studies show that peroxisomes are essentially absent. The parents ask about his prognosis. Which of the following is the most accurate response?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Survival into adulthood is expected with enzyme replacement therapy

choices.label: B
choices.text: Lifespan is normal if adrenal insufficiency is treated with hormone replacement

choices.label: C
choices.text: Death typically occurs in adolescence from cirrhosis and pulmonary disease

choices.label: D
choices.text: Death usually occurs before the first year of age

choices.label: E
choices.text: Symptoms progress slowly, with neurologic decline beginning in later childhood

explanation.summary: Zellweger syndrome usually leads to death before the first year of age.
explanation.whyCorrect: Craniofacial abnormalities (high forehead, large fontanelles, widely spaced eyes, broad nasal bridge), hypotonia, seizures, jaundice, hepatomegaly, elevated VLCFAs, and absent peroxisomes define Zellweger syndrome, an autosomal recessive PEX gene disorder of peroxisomal biogenesis. VLCFAs accumulate in the liver and brain, and the defect usually leads to death before the first year of age.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Enzyme replacement therapy allowing long survival applies to Gaucher disease, a lysosomal disorder, not to the global peroxisomal biogenesis failure of Zellweger syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Adrenal issues characterize X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy rather than Zellweger syndrome, and no treatment is described that normalizes lifespan.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Death in adolescence or early adulthood from cirrhosis and pulmonary disease describes Niemann-Pick type B.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Later-childhood onset with neurological decline describes X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy, in which peroxisomes are present but VLCFA import is defective.

questions.topicName: Dyslipidemias, Lipid Storage Disorders, and other defects in Lipid Metabolism (2 of 2)

questions.stem: A 6-month-old infant with galactocerebrosidase deficiency has failure to thrive, irritability, and progressive vision loss, but a normal-sized liver and spleen. The parents ask why this storage disease affects the nervous system so severely while sparing the abdominal organs. Which of the following best explains this pattern?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The accumulating galactocerebroside is a major component of myelin

choices.label: B
choices.text: The deficient enzyme is normally expressed only in neurons

choices.label: C
choices.text: Macrophages of the liver and spleen contain few lysosomes

choices.label: D
choices.text: The stored lipid is rapidly excreted in bile before it can accumulate

choices.label: E
choices.text: Hepatocytes compensate by upregulating hexosaminidase A

explanation.summary: Galactocerebroside is a major component of myelin, so Krabbe disease manifests predominantly with neurological symptoms and progressive demyelination.
explanation.whyCorrect: Krabbe disease is caused by galactocerebrosidase deficiency with lysosomal accumulation of galactocerebrosides. Because galactocerebroside is a major component of myelin, this lysosomal storage disease predominantly manifests with neurological symptoms, and progressive demyelination leads to more severe neurological symptoms. There are no hepatic or spleen issues compared with other lysosomal storage diseases.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Lysosomal enzymes are present in all cells; the neurologic predominance reflects where the substrate is concentrated, not neuron-restricted enzyme expression.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Macrophages of the mononuclear phagocyte system contain many lysosomes, which is why other lysosomal storage diseases cause hepatosplenomegaly.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Biliary excretion of the substrate is not described; the sparing of liver and spleen reflects the myelin-centered distribution of galactocerebroside.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Hexosaminidase A degrades GM2 ganglioside and cannot compensate for galactocerebrosidase deficiency; each sphingolipid requires its own unique enzyme.

questions.topicName: Dyslipidemias, Lipid Storage Disorders, and other defects in Lipid Metabolism (2 of 2)

questions.stem: Brain tissue from an infant who died of a demyelinating lysosomal storage disease at 18 months of age shows multinucleated macrophages with abundant cytoplasm clustered around blood vessels. Biochemical analysis of the stored material identifies a specific galactocerebroside species. Which of the following is the accumulated compound?

explanation.summary: Krabbe disease features lysosomal accumulation of galactocerebrosides, specifically psychosine.
explanation.whyCorrect: Multinucleated macrophages with abundant cytoplasm in blood vessels and neuronal tissue are globoid cells, pathognomonic of Krabbe disease. Galactocerebrosidase deficiency leads to lysosomal accumulation of galactocerebrosides, specifically psychosine, with progressive demyelination and death by 1-3 years of age.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Sphingosine is the backbone from which all sphingolipids are built, not the specific substrate that accumulates in Krabbe disease.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Sphingomyelin accumulates in Niemann-Pick disease due to sphingomyelinase deficiency.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Ceramide trihexoside accumulates in Fabry disease due to alpha-galactosidase A deficiency.
whyWrongByChoice.E: GM2 ganglioside accumulates in Tay-Sachs disease due to hexosaminidase A deficiency.

questions.topicName: Dyslipidemias, Lipid Storage Disorders, and other defects in Lipid Metabolism (2 of 2)

questions.stem: A researcher incubates isolated peroxisomes with a 26-carbon fatty acid and monitors the initial enzymatic step of its degradation. Which enzyme catalyzes the first step of peroxisomal beta-oxidation?

explanation.summary: Acyl-CoA oxidase catalyzes the first step in peroxisomal beta-oxidation.
explanation.whyCorrect: Peroxisomal beta-oxidation involves peroxisome-specific enzymes. Acyl-CoA oxidase catalyzes the first step in peroxisomal beta-oxidation of very-long-chain fatty acids (larger than 22 carbons), which are too large for transport into mitochondria.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Catalase reduces the hydrogen peroxide generated by peroxisomal oxidation to water; it does not act on the fatty acid.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Carnitine acetyltransferase transports activated acyl groups out of the peroxisome to the mitochondria after chain shortening, not the first oxidative step.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Sphingomyelinase is a lysosomal enzyme deficient in Niemann-Pick disease, unrelated to peroxisomal beta-oxidation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Hexosaminidase A is a lysosomal enzyme deficient in Tay-Sachs disease, unrelated to peroxisomal beta-oxidation.

questions.topicName: Dyslipidemias, Lipid Storage Disorders, and other defects in Lipid Metabolism (2 of 2)

questions.stem: A cell biologist engineers a peroxisomal enzyme so that it is translated normally in the cytoplasm but lacks its peroxisome targeting signal (PTS). Peroxins in the peroxisomal membrane are intact. Which of the following outcomes is most likely?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The enzyme is redirected to the rough endoplasmic reticulum and secreted

choices.label: B
choices.text: The enzyme remains in the cytoplasm because peroxin receptors cannot recognize it

choices.label: C
choices.text: The enzyme is imported into mitochondria through the carnitine shuttle

choices.label: D
choices.text: The enzyme is delivered to lysosomes and degraded at pH 5

choices.label: E
choices.text: The enzyme is imported normally because peroxins bind any cytoplasmic protein

explanation.summary: Peroxisomal proteins carry a peroxisome targeting signal that PEX receptor proteins recognize to import them into the peroxisome.
explanation.whyCorrect: Peroxisomes form by budding off the endoplasmic reticulum, and translation of peroxisomal proteins occurs in the cytoplasm. Each peroxisomal protein contains a peroxisome targeting signal (PTS) that directs it to the peroxisome; peroxins (PEX) are receptor proteins in the peroxisomal membrane that recognize the PTS and import the protein. Without a PTS, the protein cannot be recognized and stays in the cytoplasm.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Peroxisomal proteins are translated in the cytoplasm, not on the rough ER, and loss of the PTS does not create a secretory signal.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Carnitine acetyltransferase moves activated acyl groups, not enzymes, between peroxisomes and mitochondria; a missing PTS does not target the protein to mitochondria.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Loss of the PTS leaves the protein cytoplasmic; it does not route the protein to lysosomes.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Peroxins specifically recognize the PTS; they do not import proteins that lack the signal.

questions.topicName: Dyslipidemias, Lipid Storage Disorders, and other defects in Lipid Metabolism (2 of 2)

questions.stem: A student compares the energetics of fatty acid oxidation in two organelles and notes that peroxisomal beta-oxidation, unlike mitochondrial beta-oxidation, does not drive ATP synthesis. Which of the following best explains this difference?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Peroxisomes lack acyl-CoA oxidase and cannot initiate oxidation

choices.label: B
choices.text: Medium-chain products are trapped inside the peroxisome

choices.label: C

explanation.summary: Peroxisomal beta-oxidation is not coupled to ATP synthesis because electrons are transferred to oxygen to form hydrogen peroxide rather than to reduced coenzymes.
explanation.whyCorrect: Peroxisomal beta-oxidation is not coupled to ATP synthesis via reduced coenzyme formation. Instead, electrons are transferred to oxygen, forming hydrogen peroxide as a byproduct, which is why the organelle contains catalase to reduce the toxic hydrogen peroxide to water.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Peroxisomes do contain acyl-CoA oxidase, which catalyzes the first step of peroxisomal beta-oxidation.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Medium-chain fatty acids produced by peroxisomal beta-oxidation are transported to mitochondria to complete the process; they are not trapped.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Catalase reduces hydrogen peroxide to water; it does not consume ATP.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Very-long-chain fatty acids are oxidized within the peroxisome; the lack of ATP reflects the electron acceptor, not a failure of activation.

questions.topicName: Dyslipidemias, Lipid Storage Disorders, and other defects in Lipid Metabolism (2 of 2)

questions.stem: After a very-long-chain fatty acid is shortened to a medium-chain fatty acid within a peroxisome, the activated acyl group must be delivered to the mitochondria for completion of beta-oxidation. Which peroxisome-specific enzyme is responsible for transporting the activated acyl group out of the peroxisome?

explanation.summary: Peroxisomes have their own carnitine acetyltransferase for transporting activated acyl groups out of the peroxisome and into the mitochondria.
explanation.whyCorrect: Peroxisomal beta-oxidation shortens very-long-chain fatty acids into medium-chain fatty acids, which are then transported to mitochondria to complete beta-oxidation. Peroxisomes have their own carnitine acetyltransferase for transporting activated acyl groups out of the peroxisome and into the mitochondria for further oxidation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Acyl-CoA oxidase catalyzes the first step of peroxisomal beta-oxidation, not export of the product.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Catalase reduces hydrogen peroxide to water and has no transport function.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Peroxins (PEX) recognize the peroxisome targeting signal to import peroxisomal proteins; they do not export acyl groups.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The ABC transporter imports VLCFA substrates into the peroxisome and is defective in X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy; it does not export shortened products.

questions.topicName: Dyslipidemias, Lipid Storage Disorders, and other defects in Lipid Metabolism (2 of 2)

questions.stem: A 7-year-old boy with progressive neurologic decline and adrenal insufficiency is found to have elevated very-long-chain fatty acids with structurally normal peroxisomes. His physician explains that the molecular defect belongs to the same class of transporter defect as two other disorders the student has studied. Which pair of disorders shares this class of defect?

explanation.summary: X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy is caused by a defective ABC transporter, the same class of transporter defect seen in Dubin-Johnson syndrome and Tangier disease.
explanation.whyCorrect: X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy occurs when transport of VLCFA substrates into the peroxisome is defective. Much like other transporter defects previously considered, namely Dubin-Johnson and Tangier, this occurs due to a defect in an ABC transporter that uses ATP hydrolysis to promote transport of materials. Peroxisomes still form, and the disease presents later in childhood with neurological decline and adrenal issues.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Zellweger syndrome is a PEX-related peroxisome biogenesis defect and Pompe disease is a lysosomal glycogen turnover defect; neither is an ABC transporter disorder.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hunter and Hurler syndromes are lysosomal disorders of glycosaminoglycan degradation, not transporter defects.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Tay-Sachs and Niemann-Pick are sphingolipidoses caused by deficient lysosomal hydrolases, not ABC transporters.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Gaucher and Fabry are sphingolipidoses caused by deficient lysosomal hydrolases, not ABC transporters.
